Exam Details

The Florida Building Contractor exam process includes Contract Administration and Project Management exam sections. These sections are part of the state contractor licensing examination pathway for Division I contractor categories, including Building Contractor candidates. The exams are designed to test whether candidates understand the administrative, contractual, technical, safety, code, estimating, and project management responsibilities connected to construction work.

The Contract Administration portion focuses on the business and documentation side of construction projects. Candidates should understand how contract documents are organized, how bidding instructions work, how contractor and subcontractor agreements assign responsibilities, how change orders are handled, how payment procedures are documented, and how claims, disputes, closeout, and project records are managed. Many questions require careful reading and the ability to identify the correct contract reference quickly.

The Project Management portion focuses on planning, coordinating, and managing building construction work. Candidates should be ready to study construction methods, safety standards, code requirements, estimating principles, cost awareness, project coordination, building systems, materials, concrete, reinforcing steel, trusses, gypsum panel products, accessibility requirements, energy conservation, residential construction, existing building work, and commercial construction procedures.

These exams require both reference knowledge and field understanding. Some questions can be answered by locating information directly in a book, while others require the candidate to apply construction experience and trade knowledge. A strong study plan should include reading, tabbing, highlighting when allowed, practice questions, timed drills, and repeated use of the indexes and tables of contents.

This complete book set gives students the references needed to support that preparation. The goal is not only to own the books, but to learn how to use them effectively. Candidates should work through the references consistently and build a system for finding information under exam conditions.

Open Book Test

The Florida Building Contractor Contract Administration and Project Management exams are open book tests. Candidates are allowed to use approved references during the exam, which makes book familiarity a major part of exam preparation. Open book testing rewards candidates who know how to navigate references quickly and accurately.

An open book exam is not the same as an easy exam. Students who bring the books but have not studied them often lose time searching through unfamiliar pages. The exam may require candidates to move between contract documents, code books, safety regulations, estimating resources, and technical construction references. Knowing which book to use is often the first challenge, and locating the exact section is the next.

Students should study this book set actively. That means learning the table of contents, index, chapter organization, article structure, definitions, tables, figures, and subject areas in each reference. Contract documents should be reviewed for responsibilities, procedures, deadlines, and relationships between parties. Code books should be reviewed for scope, chapter layout, tables, exceptions, and definitions. Technical books should be reviewed for construction methods, installation practices, safety considerations, and field procedures.

A practical study method is to work through practice questions with the books open. After reading a question, identify the subject, choose the most likely reference, locate the answer, and mark the area for later review. Over time, this builds speed and confidence. The better a candidate knows the books, the easier it becomes to manage time during the exam.

Licensing Steps

Florida Building Contractor candidates must complete the required examination process and meet the state’s licensing requirements before a license can be issued. The exam stage is a major part of the process, but candidates should also plan for the application and documentation requirements connected to licensure.

The typical path begins with selecting the correct license classification and reviewing the exam parts required for that classification. Building Contractor candidates prepare for the required exam sections, submit the appropriate exam application, schedule testing after approval, and complete the exams through the state’s testing process. Contract Administration and Project Management are major parts of the Building Contractor exam path.

After passing the required exams, candidates continue with the licensing application process. Candidates should keep records organized throughout the process so they are ready for the licensing stage after exam completion.

This complete book set supports the exam preparation stage by giving candidates access to the references used to study for Contract Administration and Project Management. Exam Details

The Florida Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is part of Florida's contractor certification process administered through the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Construction Industry Licensing Board (CILB).

The examination evaluates knowledge of underground construction activities, utility installations, excavation methods, safety, pipeline materials, construction plans, and trade procedures.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor
  • Trade Examination: Underground Utility General Trade Knowledge
  • Question Format: Multiple choice
  • Trade Examination Questions: 80
  • Exam Format: Open book
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing
  • Examination Provider: Pearson VUE
  • Examination Registration: Professional Testing, Inc.
  • Additional Examination: Business and Finance

The trade examination assesses knowledge of pre-installation requirements, underground excavation, soil conditions, utility location, pipeline installation, traffic control, construction safety, and system testing.

Candidates must be comfortable interpreting construction drawings, understanding technical specifications, and applying basic construction mathematics to underground utility situations.

The Business and Finance examination is a separate component involving the financial and administrative responsibilities of operating a contracting business.

Open Book Test

The Florida Underground Utility Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is an open-book test. Candidates may consult reference publications authorized by Florida's official examination reference list.

Open-book testing requires strong technical knowledge and efficient reference-navigation skills. Candidates must identify the subject of a question, choose the relevant reference, locate the appropriate information, and apply it to the construction situation.

For example, a question involving ductile iron pipe installation may require information from the DIPRA Installation Guide. Questions involving PVC pressure pipe may require consulting AWWA C900 or the Handbook of PVC Pipe Design and Construction.

Excavation safety questions may involve OSHA requirements, while underground utility damage prevention questions may require knowledge of Florida Statutes Chapter 556.

Students should become familiar with technical indexes, illustrations, pipe specifications, construction tables, installation procedures, and terminology used throughout the reference publications.

Florida's examination-room rules permit highlighting and underlining in approved references while restricting handwritten notes, unauthorized materials, and movable tabs. Publications must meet applicable binding and examination-room requirements.

The official reference list determines which publications and editions may be used during testing. This online course provides preparation associated with the listed references; it does not supply physical examination-room books.

Licensing Steps

Florida Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor certification requires professional qualifications, successful completion of applicable examinations, and submission of a licensing application.

  1. Understand the Contractor Classification: Review the scope of work authorized for Florida Underground Utility and Excavation Contractors.
  2. Evaluate Licensing Qualifications: Review the applicable construction experience, education, examination, and financial responsibility requirements.
  3. Organize Underground Utility Experience: Prepare information involving excavation, pipeline installation, utility construction, trenching, or project supervision.
  4. Prepare for the Trade Examination: Study utility materials, construction methods, underground safety, excavation, and installation requirements.
  5. Use the Online Exam Prep Course: Follow an organized review of the technical subjects associated with the examination.
  6. Study the Reference Publications: Become familiar with the technical books and standards related to the underground utility trade.
  7. Prepare for Business and Finance: Address the separate examination covering contractor business responsibilities.
  8. Register for Testing: Complete the construction examination registration process through Professional Testing, Inc.
  9. Complete Required Examinations: Take the applicable trade and Business and Finance examinations.
  10. Apply for Certification: Complete the required licensing application and remaining professional qualifications.

State Requirements

Florida regulates Underground Utility and Excavation Contractors under Chapter 489 of the Florida Statutes.

The classification addresses the construction, installation, maintenance, and repair of underground utility systems and related excavation activities within its authorized scope.

Underground utility work may involve water distribution lines, sewer systems, storm drainage, underground piping, excavation, backfilling, and related construction operations.

Florida Statutes Chapter 556 establishes requirements concerning underground facility damage prevention. The law addresses responsibilities associated with excavation and the protection of existing underground infrastructure.

Underground utility contractors must also understand applicable construction safety requirements, utility accommodation procedures, approved construction plans, and installation specifications.

Applicants must satisfy Florida's applicable examination, experience, financial responsibility, insurance, and administrative licensing requirements.

Reference Books

These study references cover the major technical areas involved in underground utility installation, from pipe materials and excavation planning to safety, directional boring, and regulatory responsibilities.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination covers several connected construction disciplines.

Pre-Installation Planning: Review plans, specifications, utility information, construction calculations, and project requirements.

Traffic Control: Study construction operations affecting roadways, access, and work-zone safety.

Excavation and Backfill: Review trench construction, excavation methods, soil conditions, bedding, compaction, and backfilling.

Pipe Installation and Repairs: Study pipeline handling, alignment, joining, repair, and installation procedures.

Piping, Valves, and Fittings: Review pipe materials, fittings, connections, valves, and underground distribution systems.

Testing and Closeout: Study pipeline testing, disinfection, inspection, and project completion procedures.

Drainage Systems: Review stormwater conveyance, concrete pipe, culverts, and drainage construction.

Equipment: Study excavation machinery, pipe installation equipment, boring systems, and construction safety.

Underground Water Distribution and Pipeline Installation

Underground utility contractors frequently work with water transmission and distribution systems that require proper pipe selection, installation, and protection.

Important subjects include trench dimensions, bedding, pipe handling, joint assembly, alignment, pressure systems, and backfilling.

The DIPRA Installation Guide and AWWA C900 provide complementary information involving ductile iron and PVC pressure pipe systems.

The Handbook of PVC Pipe Design and Construction adds technical background on PVC piping materials and installation considerations.

Studying these resources helps candidates understand how pipeline materials, soil conditions, and installation methods influence underground utility construction.

Excavation, Trenching, and Soil Compaction

Excavation is a central responsibility of underground utility construction. Proper trench preparation and soil management affect both project safety and pipeline performance.

Contractors must understand excavation dimensions, soil conditions, equipment selection, groundwater considerations, trench protection, bedding, and backfill.

Compaction is also important because properly prepared bedding and backfill help support underground piping systems.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 contains important excavation and trenching safety requirements, including protective systems and access considerations.

Reviewing excavation methods alongside safety regulations supports stronger preparation for underground construction questions.

Directional Boring and Jack-and-Bore Construction

Trenchless construction methods allow underground utilities to be installed beneath certain roads, structures, and other surface features while reducing the need for continuous open excavation.

Horizontal directional drilling involves creating a guided underground path for installing utility pipe or conduit.

Jack-and-bore construction involves advancing a casing or pipe through the ground using specialized boring and jacking equipment.

The listed 2026-2027 directional bore and jack-and-bore specifications support study of these construction methods.

Candidates should understand the general purpose of trenchless installation, equipment requirements, construction planning, alignment, and underground utility protection.

Concrete Pipe, Culverts, and Drainage Construction

Underground utility work also includes drainage systems designed to convey stormwater and other flows.

Concrete pipe and box culverts are used in drainage and infrastructure applications where installation procedures and support conditions are important.

The Concrete Pipe and Box Culvert Installation reference supports understanding of handling, bedding, placement, joining, and backfilling requirements.

Reviewing drainage construction helps candidates connect pipeline installation principles with broader underground utility and infrastructure work.

Florida Underground Utility Damage Prevention

Excavation near existing underground infrastructure requires careful planning and compliance with applicable damage prevention requirements.

Florida Statutes Chapter 556 addresses underground facility damage prevention and responsibilities associated with excavation activities.

The Damage Prevention Guide supports study of utility protection, existing underground facilities, and safe excavation practices.

Understanding damage prevention procedures is important for both examination preparation and the professional responsibilities of underground utility contractors.

Construction Estimating and Project Planning

Underground utility projects require planning for pipe quantities, excavation volumes, labor, equipment, materials, and construction sequencing.

Exam Details

The Florida Electrical Contractors Certification examination is administered in two parts: a Business examination and a Technical and Safety examination. Candidates seeking certification as Unlimited Electrical Contractors must satisfy both examination requirements and complete the applicable licensing process.

The Technical and Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows five hours for completion. The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows two and one-half hours.

Both examination parts are administered through computer-based testing. Candidates who have been approved to test schedule their examination appointments through the state’s designated examination vendor.

The Technical and Safety examination measures knowledge across a broad electrical-contracting scope. Candidates may encounter questions involving electrical theory, wiring methods, conductors, equipment, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, services, feeders, branch circuits, motors, transformers, generators, hazardous locations, emergency systems, fire alarms, life safety, lightning protection, telecommunications, electrical signs, and specialty systems.

National Electrical Code preparation should include efficient use of the index, article structure, definitions, tables, annexes, and cross-references. Candidates should be comfortable locating requirements related to conductor sizing, ampacity, wiring methods, raceways, boxes, equipment grounding, grounding-electrode systems, disconnecting means, overcurrent protection, voltage drop considerations, and special occupancies.

Fire-alarm preparation may include initiating devices, notification appliances, alarm signaling, supervisory signals, trouble signals, circuits, power supplies, inspection, testing, maintenance, system documentation, and installation requirements.

Life-safety preparation may involve occupancy classifications, means of egress, exit access, exits, exit discharge, emergency lighting, fire-protection features, occupant loads, travel distances, and requirements affecting electrical and alarm work.

Lightning-protection preparation may address air terminals, bonding, conductors, grounding, structural protection, surge protection, inspection, and installation considerations for different building types.

Candidates should also prepare for safety questions based on OSHA requirements. Topics may include electrical hazards, lockout and tagout, personal protective equipment, ladders, scaffolds, fall protection, tools, recordkeeping, hazard communication, and general workplace responsibilities.

Only one copy of each authorized reference may be brought into the testing room. Candidates should use the editions identified for their scheduled examination period because questions are based on the listed references.

Original-edition reference materials are generally required unless a reference is specifically authorized as a printable file. Any permitted printed material must be properly bound in accordance with the examination instructions.

References may contain underlining or highlighting. Handwritten and typewritten notes are not allowed. Existing notes must be completely removed, blackened out, or otherwise made unreadable before the book is taken into the examination room.

Moveable tabs, removable page flags, loose study sheets, formulas, sample questions, class notes, and unauthorized materials are not permitted. Candidates are also prohibited from making marks in their references during the examination.

An open-book format does not reduce the need for technical study. Five hours can pass quickly when a candidate is searching through a large library. Effective preparation includes learning which book applies to each subject and how that book is organized.

Practice should include timed lookups using the National Electrical Code, NFPA standards, OSHA regulations, the fire-alarm handbook, telecommunications material, sign references, and the contractor manual. Exam Details

The Florida Solar Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination evaluates technical knowledge associated with photovoltaic systems, solar domestic hot water, and solar swimming pool heating.

The examination is computer-based and consists of 80 equally weighted questions, with 5 hours allowed for completion.

Florida Solar Contractor Trade Exam Content Breakdown:

  • Photovoltaic Systems – 50%
    Photovoltaic principles, site evaluation, solar access, system sizing, modules, arrays, equipment selection, electrical components, conductors, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, disconnects, inverters, controls, installation, testing, troubleshooting, and maintenance.
  • Domestic Hot Water – 25%
    Solar water-heating collectors, system layouts, sizing, storage tanks, heat exchangers, pumps, piping, valves, controls, heat-transfer fluids, freeze protection, pressure protection, startup, testing, and maintenance.
  • Swimming Pools – 25%
    Solar pool-heating systems, collector orientation, hydraulic principles, flow requirements, piping arrangements, valves, controls, sizing, roof-mounted equipment, freeze protection, testing, troubleshooting, and safety.

Photovoltaic systems represent half of the examination. Candidates should devote substantial preparation time to electrical principles, photovoltaic equipment, system design, installation conditions, and code interpretation.

Domestic hot water and swimming pool heating each represent one-quarter of the examination. These subjects require familiarity with solar thermal systems, piping, circulation, controls, collector arrangements, and operating principles.

Candidates should also develop skills in interpreting plans, specifications, diagrams, tables, technical manuals, and equipment information.

Mathematical preparation may involve fractions, decimals, percentages, ratios, area, volume, unit conversions, square roots, powers, triangle calculations, and basic algebra.

Construction safety questions may require OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. Estimating questions may involve Walker's Building Estimator's Reference Book, while plumbing and residential construction questions may involve the appropriate Florida Building Code volume.

  1. Identify the Solar Subject: Determine whether the question involves photovoltaic systems, domestic hot water, pool heating, roofing, safety, or estimating.
  2. Select the Appropriate Reference: Choose the publication most closely associated with the subject.
  3. Locate Supporting Information: Use indexes, tables of contents, chapters, code articles, definitions, diagrams, and technical tables.
  4. Confirm Applicability: Review equipment conditions, exceptions, notes, calculations, and relevant technical provisions.
  5. Check Mathematical Work: Confirm units, formulas, quantities, and the type of result requested.

The Florida Residential Pool/Spa Contractor license is regulated through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Construction Industry Licensing Board. Applicants must complete the required examinations and satisfy the current licensing requirements associated with the certification.

The residential pool contractor classification covers residential swimming pool, spa, and hot tub construction, repair, and servicing work within the authorized scope. Applicants generally must document qualifying construction experience or an accepted combination of education and experience. Financial responsibility, fingerprints, insurance, identification, and business records may also be required depending on the application type. This coordinated library supports preparation for the technical, safety, installation, testing, and job-planning responsibilities associated with underground utility and excavation contracting.

Underground utility construction involves more than placing pipe in a trench. Candidates may need to understand pre-installation planning, site inspections, utility locating, excavation safety, traffic control, pipe bedding, dewatering, backfill, compaction, pressure piping, gravity sewer systems, drainage structures, valves, fittings, pump stations, directional boring, jack-and-bore installation, testing, disinfection, and project closeout.

They include manufacturer and industry guidance for ductile iron and PVC pipe, construction estimating information, OSHA safety regulations, concrete pipe installation procedures, excavation practices, Florida utility accommodation requirements, damage-prevention requirements, trenchless installation standards, and the Florida Plumbing Code.

Because the examination is open book, candidates should prepare with the actual references they plan to use. Effective study includes learning which book applies to each topic, locating important tables and procedures, practicing calculations, and completing timed reference-navigation exercises.

This listing is for the complete Trade Knowledge book set. Business and Finance books, online courses, highlighted and tabbed preparation, application services, and licensing services are not included unless specifically stated in another product package.

Exam Details

The Florida Underground Utility Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered through computer-based testing. The examination consists of 80 equally weighted questions and allows five hours for completion.

Questions are multiple choice and may require candidates to read and interpret plans, specifications, codes, technical standards, profiles, cross sections, equipment information, and construction calculations. Candidates should also prepare for basic mathematics involving fractions, decimals, percentages, area, volume, triangle calculations, square roots, powers, and simple algebra.

The published examination outline divides the trade examination into the following content areas:

  • Pre-Installation: 20%
  • Traffic Control: 5%
  • Excavating, Backfill and Compaction: 20%
  • Pipe Installation and Repairs: 15%
  • Piping, Valves and Fittings: 15%
  • Testing, Disinfecting and Job Closeout: 10%
  • Drainage Systems: 5%
  • Equipment: 10%

Pre-installation preparation may include site and equipment inspections, material quantities, plan review, shop drawings, applicable standards, federal and state requirements, excavation locations, soil and groundwater conditions, burial depth, pipe slope, utility locating, erosion control, material handling, pipe storage, plan scales, profiles, and geotechnical information.

Traffic-control topics may address compliance with traffic laws and contract requirements, placement of signs, cones, barricades, and detours, temporary pavement markings, flagger coordination, emergency access, and the location of stockpiled materials within or near rights-of-way.

Excavation, backfill, and compaction questions may involve trench construction, trench width, shoring, soil classification, OSHA requirements, dewatering, well points, sheet piling, trench boxes, tunneling, jack-and-bore work, non-cohesive soils, bedding, filter fabric, finish grades, invert elevations, surface replacement, compaction, and support of existing utilities.

Pipe installation and repair preparation may include pressure pipe, gravity sewer pipe, pipe slopes, bedding, deflection, fittings, valves, pump piping, manholes, lift stations, catch basins, grout, hydraulic cement, multiple pipes within one excavation, piers, slip lining, directional boring, testing, and trenchless installation procedures.

Piping, valves, and fittings topics may involve material selection, pump stations, fittings, meters, flow regulators, backflow prevention, pumps, motors, cathodic protection, hydrants, thrust restraint, taps, wall penetrations, underwater piping, pipe supports, coatings, mechanical connections, leak detection, and pressure testing.

Testing, disinfecting, and closeout preparation may include as-built drawings, infiltration and exfiltration testing, mandrel testing, low-pressure air testing, television inspection, hydrostatic testing, flushing, chlorination, bacteriological sampling, operating and maintenance manuals, signoffs, and final document submissions.

Drainage-system questions may address storm drainage installation, concrete pipe, box culverts, corrugated metal pipe, retention and detention systems, underdrains, perforated pipe, bedding, connections, cleaning procedures, and protection of installed systems.

Open Book Test

The Florida Underground Utility Contractor Trade Knowledge examination is open book. Candidates may bring only the references approved for the examination and must comply with the current testing-center rules.

The official reference list allows one copy of each authorized reference. Original editions are required except for specific documents identified as available in printable PDF form. Printed PDF references must be properly bound and remain bound during the examination.

References containing underlining or highlighting may be used. Handwritten and typewritten notes are not permitted. Moveable tabs, removable page flags, writing tablets, and electronic tablets are not allowed. Permanently attached tabs containing ordinary chapter or page headings may be accepted under the general construction-examination rules.

Open-book testing still requires extensive preparation. Candidates should know whether a question is most likely answered by the ductile iron guide, AWWA C900 standard, PVC handbook, excavation reference, concrete pipe manual, FDOT utility documents, OSHA regulations, damage-prevention guide, estimating book, or Florida Plumbing Code.

Practice should include timed searches for pipe dimensions, bedding procedures, joint assembly, allowable deflection, trench safety, utility-location requirements, bore procedures, testing methods, backfill calculations, and code provisions. The goal is to locate and apply information efficiently rather than reading entire chapters during the exam.

Licensing Steps

  1. Review the license classification. Confirm that the Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor classification matches the work you intend to perform.
  2. Review the qualification requirements. Evaluate the applicable experience, education, financial, insurance, background-screening, and business requirements.
  3. Apply for the required examinations. Complete the examination application process for General Trade Knowledge and Business and Finance.
  4. Prepare with the approved references. Study the official content areas and practice locating information within the listed books.
  5. Schedule the examinations. After receiving authorization, schedule the computer-based testing appointments through the designated examination provider.
  6. Pass the required examination parts. Complete both examination areas required for the Division II contractor classification unless an applicable exemption applies.
  7. Submit the licensing application. File the appropriate Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor application.
  8. Provide supporting documentation. Submit required experience records, education information, fingerprints, credit information, insurance documentation, and business qualification materials.
  9. Complete final licensing requirements. Address workers’ compensation coverage or exemption and any additional items requested during application review.

State Requirements

Individuals seeking licensure as Florida Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractors must generally take and pass the state certification examinations before obtaining an active license.

Applicants are required to document four years of qualifying experience or an acceptable combination of college education and experience. Complete experience and education requirements are provided in the applicable licensing application.

A fingerprint-based background check is required as part of the licensing process. Applicants must submit fingerprints through a registered Livescan provider after submitting the license application.

Applicants must demonstrate financial stability and responsibility by providing a personal credit report containing a FICO-derived credit score and the required local, state, and federal public-record searches.

Applicants must attest that they have obtained public-liability and property-damage insurance in the amounts required by board rule. Workers’ compensation insurance or an applicable exemption must also be obtained within the period established for the license.

The required application depends on whether the applicant seeks an individual license, intends to qualify a business, plans to qualify an additional business, or is using another authorized licensing pathway.

Begin preparation with pre-installation and excavation because each represents 20% of the published examination outline. The Florida Service Pool Contractor trade examination focuses on the knowledge involved in servicing, maintaining, repairing, and operating swimming pools and spas within the authorized scope of the license category. Candidates should understand practical service procedures as well as the written standards and regulations that apply to different installations.

Trade subjects may include circulation systems, filtration equipment, pumps, piping, valves, drains, inlets, heaters, sanitation systems, chemical feeders, controls, water testing, water balance, electrical components, safety equipment, and troubleshooting.

The ANSI/APSP standards separate pool and spa requirements by installation type. ANSI/APSP-3 addresses permanently installed residential spas. ANSI/APSP-2 covers public spas. ANSI/APSP-1 addresses public swimming pools, while ANSI/APSP/ICC-5 applies to residential inground swimming pools.

Chapter 64E-9 supports preparation involving Florida public swimming pools and bathing places. It addresses subjects connected with operation, sanitation, water quality, safety, equipment, and facility requirements.

The 2026 Pool and Spa Operator Handbook supports practical preparation involving circulation, filtration, disinfectants, pH, alkalinity, water testing, equipment operation, maintenance, and troubleshooting.

NFPA 70, the 2023 National Electrical Code, includes Article 680 for swimming pools, fountains, spas, hot tubs, and similar installations. Candidates should become familiar with the electrical provisions involving bonding, grounding, wiring, equipment, and safety protection.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports workplace-safety preparation. The Florida Building Code - Building supports study of building requirements that may affect barriers, accessibility, equipment areas, structures, and other regulated pool-related conditions.

Open Book Test

The professionally highlighted and tabbed books help create a more organized navigation system. Tabs provide visible access points for pool categories, spa standards, electrical provisions, water-quality topics, contract documents, accounting subjects, regulations, and safety requirements.

A question involving a permanently installed residential spa may require ANSI/APSP-3. A public-spa question may require ANSI/APSP-2. Public swimming pool questions may require ANSI/APSP-1 or Chapter 64E-9, while residential inground pool questions may require ANSI/APSP/ICC-5.

Pool-operation questions may require the Pool and Spa Operator Handbook. Electrical questions may require NFPA 70 Article 680. Safety questions may require OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, and building-related questions may require the Florida Building Code - Building.

Business contract questions may require A201, A401, or A701. Accounting questions may require Builder’s Guide to Accounting or the Contractors Manual. Professional-regulation questions may require Florida Statutes Chapter 455.

The online courses include book overviews and reference-navigation practice to help students understand which publication applies to each subject. Simulated practice exams allow candidates to practice selecting books, locating information, and managing time.

Highlighting and tabs are navigation aids rather than answer keys. Candidates should read surrounding definitions, exceptions, tables, notes, and related provisions before selecting an answer.

Complete the required examination registration process and review the current candidate information for the trade and Business and Finance examinations. Confirm that the books and editions used during preparation match the references identified for the scheduled testing period.

Create separate study plans for the trade and business portions. Divide trade preparation into residential pools, public pools, residential spas, public spas, water quality, circulation, filtration, electrical requirements, workplace safety, public-pool regulations, and building requirements.

Divide Business and Finance preparation into contracts, bidding, accounting, financial management, insurance, taxes, employment responsibilities, contractor administration, and professional regulation.

Use the self-study courses together with the physical books. Review the course lesson, locate the related section in the reference, and complete practice questions that require active book use.

Complete simulated practice exams under timed conditions. Track missed questions and identify whether the difficulty involved trade knowledge, selecting the wrong book, interpreting the text, calculation errors, or time management.

After passing the required examinations, submit the appropriate Florida licensing application and supporting documentation. Passing the examinations does not automatically issue a license. Applicants must meet all applicable qualifications and receive approval before performing regulated work.

State Requirements

Florida Service Pool Contractor applicants must satisfy the requirements established for the license category. These requirements may include passing the applicable examinations, documenting qualifying experience, demonstrating financial responsibility, completing background requirements, maintaining insurance, and submitting the required application materials.

The Service Pool Contractor credential has a defined scope of work. Candidates should understand which pool and spa service activities are authorized and should not assume that passing the examinations permits work assigned to another contractor classification or separately regulated trade.

Applicants should maintain accurate records of employment, pool and spa service experience, equipment work, supervisory responsibilities, education, and training. Organized documentation can support a more efficient application process.

Prepare for the Florida Specialty Structure Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination with an online exam prep course built around the trade subjects and reference books connected to the state exam. The course helps candidates organize their study of foundations, wall systems, roof systems, windows, insulation, post-and-beam structures, roofovers, siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, downspouts, estimating, construction safety, and Florida building-code requirements.

Specialty structure construction requires knowledge of several materials and installation methods. Candidates may encounter questions involving aluminum components, wood framing, concrete masonry, concrete finishing, vinyl siding, high-wind construction, structural connections, weather protection, fasteners, anchors, flashing, sealants, and exterior building systems. This online course provides a trade-focused structure for reviewing those connected subjects.

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractor examination is open book, making reference navigation an important part of preparation. Candidates must be able to identify the subject of a question, choose the correct reference, locate the applicable chapter or table, and interpret the information within the available testing time. The course supports this process by connecting exam topics with the books used to study them.

Online preparation gives working contractors and license applicants the flexibility to study around jobsite, business, and personal responsibilities. Candidates can build a consistent study routine, review difficult subjects, practice calculations, and spend additional time becoming familiar with the references.

This product is an online preparation course for the Florida Specialty Structure Contractor Trade Knowledge examination. The listed books are the references used for preparation and are not included with the online course unless a separate product option or package specifically states that books are included.

What You Get

  • Online Trade Exam Preparation: Organized review focused on the Florida Specialty Structure Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination.
  • Trade-Focused Study Guidance: Preparation covering foundations, walls, roofs, insulation, windows, post-and-beam structures, roofovers, siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, and downspouts.
  • Reference Navigation Support: Guidance for connecting examination subjects with the appropriate estimating, safety, masonry, concrete, aluminum, siding, wood-construction, and Florida code references.
  • Practice-Oriented Preparation: A study approach that reinforces trade knowledge, construction calculations, code research, and open-book lookup skills.
  • Flexible Online Study: Course preparation that can be incorporated into a schedule built around work and personal responsibilities.

The course is intended to help candidates study more efficiently, but it does not replace the official reference books. Candidates should obtain the required editions, become familiar with every reference, and use the books throughout their preparation.

Exam Details

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based testing format. The trade exam contains 80 equally weighted questions.

The official content outline identifies the following examination areas:

  • Foundations: 7.5%
  • Wall Sections: 15%
  • Roof Sections: 15%
  • Insulation: 7.5%
  • Windows: 15%
  • Post and Beam Structures: 15%
  • Roofovers: 15%
  • Siding, Soffits, Fascias, Gutters and Downspouts: 10%

Candidates should be prepared to read and interpret plans, specifications, technical illustrations, construction tables, installation instructions, and building-code provisions. Questions may also require the application of basic construction mathematics.

Foundation topics may involve excavation, layout, forms, pier-type post footings, reinforcing materials, vapor barriers, grading, compaction, concrete placement, finishing, masonry kneewalls, mortar, concrete masonry units, reinforcement, and joint construction.

Wall-section topics may include screen walls, framed solid walls, composite metal-panel walls, storm doors, screen doors, anchoring, bracing, fasteners, sealants, flashing, span information, wind resistance, and compatibility between materials.

Roof-section preparation may include standing-seam roofs, pan roofs, screen roofs, support spacing, structural connections, fastening, sealing, flashing, wind loads, roof attachments, panel sizing, gussets, and common roof configurations.

Insulation questions may address rigid insulation, batt insulation, thermal resistance, protective coverings, moisture considerations, and compatible caulking or sealing materials.

Window preparation may involve installation in wood, masonry, or metal walls. Candidates should review measurement, rough openings, anchoring, fastening, flashing, sealing, weather protection, reinforcement, and high-wind requirements.

Post-and-beam topics may include wood and metal structures, carports, patios, roof framing, bracing, anchors, fasteners, structural connections, and safe construction practices. Roofover questions may address raised and flat-down systems, laminated systems, vinyl blanket systems, ventilation, insulation, sealing, spacing, drainage, and weather resistance.

Siding and exterior-component questions may involve aluminum siding, vinyl siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, downspouts, vents, starter strips, furring strips, expansion and contraction, fastening, weather barriers, drainage, and replacement of damaged sheathing.

Open Book Test

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractor Trade Knowledge examination is open book and consists of multiple-choice questions. Candidates may use the references authorized for the examination, provided the books comply with the current examination-room rules.

An open-book exam still requires detailed preparation. Candidates cannot rely on searching every reference from the beginning for each question. They must recognize the subject, select the most likely book, find the applicable section, and determine how the information applies.

Reference navigation should be practiced throughout the course. Candidates should become comfortable using tables of contents, indexes, chapter headings, illustrations, span tables, definitions, appendices, and code sections.

Practice exercises should include topics such as concrete finishing, masonry reinforcement, aluminum connections, vinyl siding expansion, wood durability, OSHA fall protection, construction quantities, window installation, roof attachments, and Florida code requirements.

The state reference rules permit authorized books that meet the applicable preparation and binding requirements. Candidates should review the current testing instructions before exam day and bring only permitted references and materials.

Licensing Steps

  1. Review the license classification. Confirm that the Certified Specialty Structure Contractor classification corresponds with the construction work you plan to perform.
  2. Review the qualification requirements. Examine the applicable experience, education, financial, insurance, background-screening, and business requirements.
  3. Apply for the required examinations. Complete the examination registration process for the applicable Florida contractor examination parts.
  4. Prepare for Trade Knowledge. Study the official content areas and use the required references while completing the online course.
  5. Prepare for Business and Finance. The Business and Finance examination is separate and requires its own references and preparation.
  6. Schedule the examinations. After receiving authorization, schedule the applicable computer-based examination appointments through the designated testing provider.
  7. Pass the required examination parts. Complete the examination requirements associated with the Certified Specialty Structure Contractor license.
  8. Submit the licensing application. File the appropriate initial licensure application and supporting documentation.
  9. Complete the remaining requirements. Address the applicable experience verification, financial documentation, fingerprints, insurance, workers’ compensation, and business qualification requirements.

State Requirements

Florida applicants seeking licensure as certified specialty contractors must generally pass the required state certification examinations before completing initial licensure. Passing the examinations does not automatically issue a contractor license.

Applicants must submit the proper application and satisfy the qualifications that apply to their circumstances. Florida generally requires four years of qualifying experience or an accepted combination of college education and experience. Applicants should review the complete application instructions to determine how their education and work history may be credited.

The licensing process also includes financial responsibility requirements. Applicants may need to provide credit reports containing the information required by the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

Fingerprint-based background screening is part of the application process. Insurance requirements may include public-liability and property-damage coverage, along with workers’ compensation coverage or an applicable exemption.

Applicants seeking to qualify a company must provide the required business information. The appropriate application depends on whether the applicant is seeking individual licensure, qualifying a business, qualifying an additional business, or using another available licensing pathway.

Florida requires applicants to obtain their license within the applicable period after receiving their examination score. Candidates should plan their examination preparation and licensing documentation as connected parts of the overall process.

Reference Books

  • Walker's Building Estimator’s Reference Book, Walker’s, 33rd Edition
    A construction-estimating reference covering labor, materials, equipment, measurements, quantities, unit costs, and calculations used in construction planning and estimating.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926
    The federal construction-safety regulations covering fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, electrical hazards, personal protective equipment, tools, material handling, excavation, and jobsite practices.
  • Concrete Masonry Handbook for Architects, Engineers, Builders, 6th Edition, 2008
    A technical reference covering concrete masonry materials, mortar, reinforcement, structural concepts, installation practices, details, and construction applications. This book is out of print and may be supplied used in like-new condition when purchased through an applicable book package.
  • Design of Wood Frame Structures for Permanence, Wood Construction Data No. 6, 2006
    A wood-construction reference addressing moisture control, decay prevention, termite protection, material selection, ventilation, durability, and detailing for long-term structural performance.
  • Vinyl Siding Installation Manual, 2020
    An installation reference covering surface preparation, fastening, panel installation, accessories, expansion and contraction, flashing, weather resistance, soffits, fascia, and common siding details.
  • Guide to Aluminum Construction in High Wind Areas, Student Edition, 2010
    A specialty construction guide addressing aluminum members, connections, spans, anchoring, fastening, bracing, screen enclosures, roof systems, and construction in high-wind conditions.
  • Concrete Finishers Guide, 2017
    A practical reference covering concrete placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, joints, tools, surface preparation, defects, and commonly used finishing procedures.
  • Florida Building Code – Building, 2026
    The building volume of the 8th Edition Florida Building Code, containing provisions related to structural systems, exterior walls, roofs, weather protection, materials, accessibility, and commercial construction.
  • Florida Building Code – Residential, 2026
    The residential code covering applicable one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, including foundations, walls, roofs, windows, insulation, exterior coverings, structural connections, and weather-resistant construction.

The listed books serve as references for course study and exam preparation. They are not included with this online course unless the selected product package specifically states that books are included.

Test Information and Study Materials

Begin preparation by dividing the official content outline into manageable study blocks. Wall sections, roof sections, windows, post-and-beam structures, and roofovers each account for substantial portions of the examination and should receive consistent review.

Foundation study should combine the concrete, masonry, estimating, and Florida code references. Review footing layout, excavation, concrete quantities, reinforcement, forms, placement, finishing, masonry units, mortar, and kneewall construction.

Wall and roof preparation should emphasize spans, support spacing, anchors, fasteners, bracing, flashing, sealing, panel systems, screen systems, roof forms, structural connections, and high-wind considerations.

For window questions, study rough openings, measurements, fastening, anchoring, flashing, sealants, weather protection, wall materials, and wind-resistant installation. Compare the requirements and installation methods used in wood, masonry, and metal walls.

For siding and exterior components, review panel installation, starter strips, trim, expansion allowances, fastening placement, soffit ventilation, fascia, gutters, downspouts, drainage, weather barriers, and substrate preparation.

OSHA preparation should include fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, electrical safety, cutting tools, personal protective equipment, material handling, and general workplace responsibilities. Learn how the OSHA book is arranged so individual standards can be found efficiently.

Construction mathematics should be included in every stage of preparation. Practice area, volume, material quantities, percentages, spacing, unit conversions, concrete calculations, and simple algebra. Pay close attention to units and rounding instructions.

Timed reference drills help turn technical knowledge into practical exam skills. Select a topic, choose the appropriate book, locate the information, and confirm the answer. Review slow or incorrect searches to identify books and subjects that require additional practice.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps candidates organize the broad Florida Specialty Structure Contractor trade outline into focused study areas. Rather than approaching every reference without direction, candidates can connect each subject with the books most likely to contain the required information.

Trade-focused review brings together foundations, masonry, concrete, aluminum systems, wood-frame durability, vinyl siding, windows, roofs, estimating, OSHA safety, and Florida building codes. This coordinated approach reflects the way specialty structure work combines multiple materials and construction systems.

Practice-oriented preparation encourages candidates to apply what they study through calculations, technical questions, code research, and reference lookups. Reviewing missed questions and locating the supporting information can reinforce both trade knowledge and open-book navigation skills.

Reference-navigation guidance helps candidates become familiar with indexes, chapter structures, tables, illustrations, definitions, and code organization. Repeated practice can make it easier to identify the appropriate reference and locate relevant material during the examination.

An organized online study routine can help candidates track progress, revisit weak subjects, and approach the Florida Specialty Structure Contractor Trade Knowledge examination with greater familiarity and confidence. Examination results still depend on the candidate’s preparation, construction knowledge, reference skills, time management, and performance on test day.

Prepare for the Florida Residential Pool Contractor Trade Knowledge examination with a complete set of the technical references used for the exam. This Florida Residential Pool Contractor exam book set brings together the pool and spa standards, estimating reference, OSHA construction regulations, concrete and masonry resources, shotcrete guidance, electrical code provisions, reinforcing steel reference, pool operations handbook, and Florida Building Code material needed for organized trade exam preparation.

Residential pool contracting requires knowledge across several construction disciplines. Candidates must understand site preparation, excavation, plumbing, electrical work, steel reinforcement, concrete and shotcrete placement, pool finishes, equipment installation, water circulation, safety requirements, and building-code compliance. The examination also requires candidates to read plans, interpret technical standards, navigate codes, and complete basic construction calculations.

This 10-book collection is assembled for candidates who want the primary Florida Residential Pool Contractor trade references in one package. It includes the editions identified for the applicable reference cycle, including ANSI/APSP residential pool and spa standards, Walker’s Building Estimator’s Reference Book, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, the Concrete Masonry Handbook, the ACI Guide to Shotcrete, the 2020 National Electrical Code, Placing Reinforcing Bars, the 2026 Pool & Spa Operator Handbook, and the 2026 Florida Building Code - Building.

Owning the correct references is an important part of open-book exam preparation, but effective study also requires familiarity with each book. Candidates should know which publication addresses a particular subject, how each index is organized, where important definitions appear, and how to locate tables, formulas, illustrations, installation requirements, and safety provisions under timed testing conditions.

The books support preparation for residential swimming pool and spa work from initial planning through startup. Topics include site dimensions, excavation, soil conditions, dewatering, backfilling, piping, pumps, filters, electrical bonding, grounding, reinforcing steel, shotcrete, masonry, interior finishes, pool equipment, residential spa requirements, code compliance, and safe construction practices.

Exam Details

The Florida Residential Pool Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based testing format. The exam contains 80 equally weighted questions, and candidates are allowed five hours to complete the examination.

The examination uses multiple-choice questions and may test a candidate’s ability to apply information from technical references to practical construction situations. Questions may involve plans, specifications, codes, standards, calculations, materials, equipment, installation methods, field conditions, or accepted trade practices.

Candidates should be prepared to read and interpret plans and specifications, read and apply code provisions, and complete basic mathematics. Mathematical work may include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, decimals, percentages, areas, volumes, triangle calculations, square roots, powers, and simple algebraic equations.

Major examination subjects may include:

  • Pre-installation planning and site preparation
  • Residential pool and spa design criteria
  • Permitting, inspections, and building-department requirements
  • Site dimensions, elevations, setbacks, and soil conditions
  • Excavation, grading, dewatering, de-mucking, and well-pointing
  • Backfilling, compaction, drainage, and debris removal
  • Pool plumbing, recirculation lines, fittings, and valves
  • Pumps, filters, skimmers, heaters, and chemical feeders
  • Hydraulics, flow rates, pipe sizing, and pressure testing
  • Electrical wiring, grounding, bonding, and pool equipment
  • Concrete, masonry, shotcrete, and structural installation
  • Reinforcing steel placement and support
  • Decks, coping, tile, interior surfaces, and finishes
  • Residential spa construction and installation requirements
  • Pool startup, water treatment, operation, and safety
  • OSHA construction safety and jobsite hazard control

The exam may also include questions based on field experience and knowledge of trade practices. Candidates should combine book study with practical understanding of residential pool construction methods, materials, equipment, sequencing, and safety.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Pool Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates may bring the approved references into the testing room, provided the books comply with the current examination rules.

Only one copy of each approved reference may be brought into the examination site. Original-edition materials are required unless a reference is specifically identified as available in an approved PDF format. Printed PDF references must be properly bound and remain bound throughout the examination.

References containing underlining made with a pen or highlighter may be used. Handwritten and typewritten notes are not permitted. Existing notes must be removed or completely blacked out so they cannot be read. Candidates are not allowed to add marks to their books during the examination.

Permanently attached tabs containing normal chapter or page headings may be permitted. Removable tabs, pull-off labels, page flags, and similar materials are not accepted. Candidates should review the current testing rules before preparing or modifying any examination reference.

An open-book format does not remove the need for structured study. Searching unfamiliar books during a timed examination can use valuable minutes. Candidates should practice identifying the topic of a question, selecting the correct reference, using the index or table of contents, and confirming the applicable section efficiently.

Licensing Steps

  1. Review the license scope. Confirm that the Florida Certified Residential Pool/Spa Contractor classification matches the work you plan to perform.
  2. Review the examination requirements. Residential Pool/Spa Contractor applicants generally complete the Business and Finance examination and the Residential Pool Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination.
  3. Apply for examination eligibility. Complete the required examination registration process through the designated Florida construction examination administrator.
  4. Schedule the examinations. After receiving approval, arrange the applicable computer-based testing appointments through the designated testing provider.
  5. Prepare with the approved trade books. Study the tested subjects and practice locating information throughout the reference set.
  6. Complete the required examinations. Take the Business and Finance and Trade Knowledge portions required for the certification.
  7. Submit the correct license application. Select the application that matches whether you are applying as an individual, qualifying a business, or using another available licensing path.
  8. Document experience and education. Provide the records required to establish the qualifying experience or accepted combination of education and experience.
  9. Submit supporting information. Complete the applicable financial, identity, fingerprint, insurance, and business-document requirements.
  10. Receive the license before contracting. Passing the examinations does not independently authorize regulated contracting work. The required Florida contractor license must be issued before operating under the classification.

State Requirements

The Florida Residential Pool/Spa Contractor license is regulated through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Construction Industry Licensing Board. A certified residential pool contractor may perform residential swimming pool, hot tub, and spa work within the scope established for the license.

The residential pool contractor scope includes construction, repair, and servicing work associated with residential pools and spas. The work may involve layout, excavation, dewatering, steel reinforcement, light niches, pool floors, shotcrete or gunite, tile, coping, perimeter piping, filtration equipment, chemical feeders, interior finishes, decks, equipment housing, and package pool heaters when performed within the authorized scope.

Applicants seeking certified-contractor licensure generally must pass the required state examinations and satisfy current experience or education requirements. Florida licensing information identifies four years of qualifying experience or an accepted combination of college education and experience as the general standard, subject to the detailed application instructions.

Applicants should maintain clear records of employers, project dates, job responsibilities, supervisory duties, and the types of residential pool or spa work completed. Financial responsibility, credit information, fingerprints, insurance, and business records may also be required depending on the application type.

Candidates who intend to qualify a business must complete the requirements associated with the business entity and qualifying-agent relationship. Forming a company or passing an examination does not replace the need for formal license approval.

    A residential spa standard covering design, construction, installation, equipment, circulation, safety, and performance requirements for permanently installed spas.
  • ANSI/APSP/ICC-5 American National Standard for Residential Inground Swimming Pools, 2025
    A core residential pool standard addressing design criteria, dimensions, construction requirements, materials, circulation systems, safety considerations, and other requirements for inground swimming pools.
  • Walker’s Building Estimator’s Reference Book, 33rd Edition
    A construction estimating reference used for material quantities, labor considerations, measurements, calculations, and practical estimating information relevant to pool construction projects.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926
    Federal construction safety regulations covering excavation, trenching, personal protective equipment, electrical hazards, tools, equipment, material handling, fall protection, and jobsite safety responsibilities.
  • Concrete Masonry Handbook for Architects, Engineers, Builders, 6th Edition, 2008
    A technical resource covering concrete masonry materials, construction methods, structural considerations, reinforcement, mortar, detailing, and practical masonry applications. This out-of-print reference is supplied in used, like-new condition.

    The electrical code reference used for swimming pool and spa wiring, grounding, bonding, underwater lighting, equipment connections, receptacles, disconnecting means, and related electrical safety requirements.
  • Placing Reinforcing Bars, 10th Edition
    A reinforcing steel reference covering bar placement, supports, splices, bends, detailing, tolerances, handling, and installation practices used in reinforced concrete construction.
  • Pool & Spa Operator Handbook, 2026
    A pool and spa operations reference covering circulation, filtration, water chemistry, disinfection, equipment, maintenance, troubleshooting, safety, and operating practices.
  • Florida Building Code - Building, 2026
    The Florida construction code reference addressing building requirements, materials, structural provisions, accessibility, safety, inspections, and code requirements applicable to residential pool construction.

Study construction sequencing as well as individual requirements. A residential pool project may move from site layout and excavation to steel placement, plumbing, electrical work, shotcrete, tile, coping, decking, equipment installation, finishing, filling, and startup. Understanding that sequence helps connect information from several books.

  • Domestic Hot Water: 25% of the trade examination.
  • Swimming Pools: 25% of the trade examination.

Applicants should use the application that matches their intended license status. Florida provides separate application paths for individuals, contractors qualifying a business, contractors qualifying an additional business, and applicants pursuing an available endorsement path.

Exam Details

Florida Residential Contractor candidates fall within the Division I contractor examination category. Division I candidates must pass three required examination parts: Business and Finance, Contract Administration, and Project Management.

Business and Finance focuses on the responsibilities involved in operating and financially managing a contracting business. Study areas may involve accounting, estimating, job costing, business organization, contracts, payroll, taxes, insurance, financial management, and contractor obligations.

Contract Administration addresses bidding procedures, agreements, project documentation, contractual relationships, payment responsibilities, changes, claims, and the duties of owners, contractors, subcontractors, architects, and other project participants.

Project Management emphasizes the practical administration and execution of construction work. Preparation may involve Florida building codes, safety regulations, construction methods, materials, energy requirements, concrete, reinforcement, gypsum products, wood trusses, estimating, scheduling, and project coordination.

Florida construction examinations in this category are administered in a computer-based testing format. Candidates apply for the applicable examination parts through Professional Testing, Inc. After receiving approval, candidates schedule their examination appointments through the state’s designated computer-based testing provider.

Passing all required examination parts is one stage of the licensing process. A passing score does not automatically issue a contractor license. Applicants must also complete the appropriate initial licensure application and satisfy the requirements established by the Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Contractor examination is open book. Candidates may use permitted references during the applicable examination sessions, subject to the current testing rules and official reference instructions.

An open-book format requires strong navigation skills. Candidates need to determine which publication contains the answer, locate the correct chapter or section, read the applicable language, and use the information to solve the question. A large collection of books can become difficult to manage without regular practice, which is why organized highlighting and tabs can be valuable preparation tools.

The highlighted sections help direct attention to frequently studied concepts and important provisions. The tabs help divide books by subject, chapter, code section, or major topic. Together, these features can support quicker movement through the references while candidates practice answering timed questions.

Tabs and highlighting should be treated as navigation aids rather than answer keys. Examination questions may require information from surrounding paragraphs, definitions, exceptions, charts, tables, footnotes, or related code sections. Candidates should read beyond a highlighted sentence whenever necessary and understand how the provision applies to the question.

Testing rules can govern book condition, binding, notes, attachments, tabs, and other materials. Candidates should review the current candidate information before their scheduled appointment and bring only the references permitted for the examination session being taken.

Licensing Steps

The process begins by reviewing the qualifications for Florida certified residential contractor licensure. Prospective candidates should understand the examination, experience, education, financial, and application requirements before registering to test.

Candidates then register for the required examination parts. Division I Residential Contractor candidates generally complete Business and Finance, Contract Administration, and Project Management. Approved candidates schedule the computer-based examinations through the designated testing provider.

After passing the required examinations, an individual seeking certification submits the appropriate initial licensure application. Florida provides different application paths depending on whether the applicant will be licensed as an individual, qualify a business entity, qualify an additional business, or pursue another authorized licensing route.

The application process may require documentation addressing experience or education, financial responsibility, background information, examination results, insurance, and other items included in the applicable application instructions. Applicants should complete the form that matches their intended licensing and business status.

Passing the examination alone does not authorize a person to perform contracting work that requires licensure. The applicant must receive the appropriate Florida license before offering or performing regulated contracting services.

State Requirements

Florida certified construction contractors are regulated by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Construction Industry Licensing Board. A certified contractor holds a state-issued certificate of competency and may work within the authorized license scope throughout Florida, subject to applicable permitting, code, and local administrative requirements.

Florida defines a residential contractor as a contractor whose services are limited to the construction, remodeling, repair, or improvement of one-family, two-family, or three-family residences that are not more than two stories, together with associated accessory-use structures.

Applicants for certified residential contractor licensure are generally required to document four years of qualifying experience or an accepted combination of college education and construction experience. The experience must meet the standards established for the license category and must be documented according to the current application instructions.

Applicants must also satisfy additional licensing requirements, which may include demonstrating financial responsibility, meeting background and character requirements, paying applicable fees, and obtaining required insurance or workers’ compensation coverage. The exact documentation depends on the applicant’s circumstances and selected application type.

Applicants should confirm that they qualify for the residential contractor category before paying examination and application expenses. Passing an examination does not override unmet licensing qualifications or expand the legal scope of the residential contractor license.

Test Information and Study Materials

Candidates should review rebar placement, reinforcement support, cover, bends, splices, shotcrete placement, concrete masonry concepts, and construction sequencing.

Pool and spa operation topics should also be included in the study routine. Candidates should study personal protective equipment, excavation safety, fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, tools, materials, hazard communication, signs, signals, barricades, and general jobsite safety responsibilities.

Exam Details

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered through computer-based testing. The examination consists of 80 equally weighted questions.

Candidates should be prepared to read and interpret plans, specifications, and construction codes. The published examination content also requires basic mathematics, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, decimals, percentages, area and volume calculations, triangle calculations, square roots, powers, and simple algebraic equations.

The official trade examination outline divides the content into the following areas:

  • Foundations: 7.5%
  • Wall Sections: 15%
  • Roof Sections: 15%
  • Insulation: 7.5%
  • Windows: 15%
  • Post and Beam Structures: 15%
  • Roofovers: 15%
  • Siding, Soffit, Fascias, Gutters and Downspouts: 10%

The foundations category includes knowledge associated with excavating, laying out, forming, and placing pier-type post footings. Candidates may need to review measuring, grading, reinforcing materials, concrete mixtures, vapor barriers, compaction, and cement-finishing methods. This category also includes concrete masonry kneewalls, mortar mixtures, block placement, reinforcement, and joint thickness.

The wall-sections category includes screen walls that support screen or metal roofs, framed solid walls, composite metal-panel walls, storm and screen doors, bracing, fastening, anchoring, caulking, flashing, material compatibility, span tables, wind-load considerations, and safe use of tools and access equipment.

The roof-sections category addresses standing-seam and pan roofs, screen roofs, support spacing, span tables, fastening, sealing, flashing, wind loads, roof attachment, screen-panel sizing, gusseting, and common roof forms such as dome, hip, flat, and gable configurations.

Insulation questions may involve rigid and batt insulation, insulation types, thermal resistance, protective coverings, and caulking compatibility. Window questions may involve vinyl and glass windows installed in wood, masonry, or metal walls, including measurement, fastening, sealing, wall reinforcement, and wind-load requirements.

Post-and-beam preparation includes wood-roof and metal-roof applications, anchoring, fastening, carport construction, patio construction, and jobsite safety. Roofovers may include raised or flat-down metal systems, laminated systems, vinyl blanket systems, ventilation, insulation, structural spacing, sealing, and safe tool use.

The siding and exterior-components category includes aluminum and vinyl siding, gutters, downspouts, soffits, fascia, water diverters, expansion joints, vents, starter strips, furring strips, weatherproofing, vapor barriers, sheathing replacement, drainage, spacing for expansion and contraction, and fastening requirements.

The approved reference list permits one copy of each authorized reference. Original editions are required except where an approved reference is specifically identified as available in printable PDF form. Approved PDF materials must be properly bound and remain bound during the examination.

      Isometrics Portion – 5 drawings at 10 points each

      Each of the isometric drawings is worth up to a maximum of 10 points. Based on the criteria listed below, each drawing will be independently evaluated by three graders. At least two of the graders must agree that a criterion is correct in order for that criterion to be graded as correct and points to be awarded. If one or more criterion is determined to be incorrect by at least two of the graders, points will not be awarded for that criterion. The awarded points for all criteria will be summed and converted to a 10 point scale to determine the score for each drawing.

      The following are the criteria and points used by the graders to evaluate each of the five isometric drawings.

      a. Legibility. Drawing is clear and readable. Drawing is sufficient in size. Lines and labels are distinguishable. (8 points)

      b. Orientation. All fixtures are shown in the correct location relative to each other. (20 points)

      c. Flow. Direction of flow is shown when going from vertical to horizontal. The direction of flow must be indicated even if the direction is implied for all waste lines and all fixture connections. Direction of flow is not required for vent lines. (12 points)

      d. Angles. Isometric drawing uses 30-60-90 degree angles. All angles used on the drawing are displayed at the appropriate orientation. (8 points)

      e. Piping. All pipes, fittings, traps, clean-outs, and similar portions of the piping structure are included on the drawing. All piping is shown exactly as on the drawing (regardless of specific code requirements). The piping must display the correct elevation in reference to the floor plan. (20 points)

      f. Labeling. All fixtures are labeled according to the legend provided in the examination instructions. (4 points)

      g. Vents. All vents are properly indicated. (16 points)

      h. Fixtures. All fixtures shown on the floor plan are appropriately indicated on the isometric drawing. (12 points)
