Exam Details

The Florida Residential Pool Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based format. The trade examination contains 80 equally weighted questions, and candidates are allowed five hours to complete it.

The examination evaluates a candidate’s knowledge of residential pool and spa construction, trade practices, code requirements, jobsite safety, structural work, electrical systems, plumbing, equipment, estimating, and related technical subjects. Questions may require candidates to interpret standards, plans, specifications, tables, diagrams, calculations, or practical construction situations.

Mathematical preparation may include whole numbers, fractions, decimals, percentages, area, volume, ratios, square roots, powers, triangle calculations, and basic algebra. Candidates should be comfortable applying calculations to estimating, dimensions, material quantities, pool volume, flow, pressure, structural work, and jobsite conditions.

Major examination areas may include:

  • Pre-installation planning and jobsite preparation
  • Residential swimming pool and spa design requirements
  • Plans, specifications, dimensions, elevations, and construction details
  • Estimating, material quantities, and basic construction mathematics
  • Excavation, grading, trenching, dewatering, and soil conditions
  • Backfill, compaction, drainage, and site restoration
  • Concrete, masonry, shotcrete, and structural pool-shell construction
  • Reinforcing steel placement, supports, bends, laps, and tolerances
  • Pool plumbing, piping, valves, fittings, drains, and circulation systems
  • Pumps, filters, skimmers, heaters, chemical feeders, and related equipment

  • Electrical wiring, grounding, bonding, receptacles, lighting, and equipment

The examination may also draw on practical trade knowledge. Candidates should understand how residential pool projects progress from layout and excavation through structural installation, plumbing, electrical work, finishing, equipment startup, and final inspection.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Pool Contractor trade examination is an open-book test. Candidates may bring approved reference books into the testing room when those materials comply with the current examination rules.

Open-book testing requires efficient navigation. Candidates may not have enough time to read an entire chapter each time a question appears. They should know which book applies to the subject, how the publication is organized, and where to find the relevant definition, table, formula, standard, code provision, or construction requirement.

The highlighted and tabbed books in this package are prepared to support that process. Permanent tabs identify major sections and common subject areas. Highlighting draws attention to important provisions, definitions, tables, and technical content. Applicants must complete the required examinations and satisfy the current application requirements associated with the certification.

A Florida Residential Pool/Spa Contractor classification covers residential swimming pool, spa, and hot tub construction, repair, and servicing work within the authorized scope. Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Exam - Online Exam Prep Course

Prepare for the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Exam with structured online exam preparation from 1 Exam Prep. Designed for residential electricians, electrical supervisors, electrical contractors, and professionals pursuing Florida residential electrical contractor certification, this course focuses on electrical theory, residential wiring, National Electrical Code requirements, electrical safety, fire alarm systems, lightning protection, and contractor business knowledge.

Becoming a residential electrical contractor requires more than practical installation experience. Candidates must understand electrical calculations, wiring methods, services, grounding, bonding, circuit protection, construction safety, and the technical requirements that apply to residential electrical work.

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Online Exam Prep Course helps candidates organize these subjects into a focused preparation plan. Study guidance emphasizes technical knowledge, reference navigation, and practical strategies for approaching examination questions.

Residential electrical professionals regularly encounter electrical panels, service equipment, branch circuits, feeders, switches, receptacles, lighting fixtures, motors, and appliances. Understanding how these installations relate to electrical codes is essential for examination preparation and professional development.

This course supports candidates preparing for Florida's Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination while also providing study structure around the contractor and safety references associated with the certification process.

Whether you are an experienced electrician preparing to pursue contractor certification or a residential electrical professional strengthening your technical knowledge, organized preparation can help you approach the examination with greater confidence.

PACKAGE INCLUSION: This product includes ONLINE EXAM PREPARATION ONLY, with organized study guidance focused on residential electrical systems, code interpretation, calculations, construction safety, reference navigation, and examination preparation strategies.

IMPORTANT NOTE: THIS PACKAGE DOES NOT INCLUDE ANY PHYSICAL BOOKS. The six reference publications listed below are separate study materials and can be purchased separately.

Exam Details

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification examination includes two examination components: Technical/Safety and Business.

The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows 5 hours for testing. The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows 2½ hours.

Technical preparation covers electrical theory, residential wiring, electrical services, calculations, grounding, protection, safety, and related electrical installation requirements.

Important examination preparation areas include:

  • Electrical Theory: Voltage, current, resistance, power, circuit relationships, and electrical principles.
  • Plans and Specifications: Reading electrical drawings, interpreting symbols, and understanding installation information.
  • Wiring and Protection: Conductors, wiring methods, overcurrent protection, and electrical installation requirements.
  • Electrical Services: Service conductors, service equipment, disconnecting means, and related requirements.
  • Branch Circuits and Feeders: Circuit ratings, conductor sizing, residential distribution, and protection.
  • Grounding and Bonding: Grounding electrode systems, equipment grounding, and electrical bonding requirements.
  • Load Calculations: Demand loads, neutral loads, appliance loads, and residential electrical calculations.
  • Box and Conduit Fill: Electrical box calculations, raceway fill, and conductor installation conditions.
  • Motors: Motor-related electrical principles, equipment requirements, and protection concepts.
  • Voltage Drop: Electrical calculations and conductor relationships affecting voltage drop.
  • OSHA Safety: Construction hazards, electrical safety, tools, equipment, and workplace requirements.
  • Fire Alarm Systems: Fire alarm equipment, signaling concepts, and related requirements.
  • Lightning Protection: Lightning protection components, installation concepts, and grounding considerations.
  • Life Safety: Requirements associated with fire protection, building safety, and life safety systems.

The examination requires candidates to connect electrical knowledge with technical reference material. A question involving service calculations may require electrical theory, load calculation methods, conductor sizing, and National Electrical Code interpretation.

Candidates should become familiar with the purpose and organization of the references used during preparation rather than attempting to memorize isolated answers.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Both the Technical/Safety and Business examination components allow authorized reference materials under the applicable examination rules.

Open-book testing requires effective study and strong reference-navigation habits. Candidates must recognize the topic, identify the appropriate publication, locate the controlling requirement, and apply it accurately.

The 2023 National Electrical Code is a central reference for residential electrical preparation. Candidates should practice using its index, articles, definitions, technical tables, exceptions, and related provisions.

Electrical questions may involve branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, equipment, or calculations. Safety and specialized system questions may involve OSHA, NFPA 72, NFPA 780, or NFPA 101.

Recommended open-book preparation strategies include:

  1. Identify the Subject: Determine whether the question involves theory, wiring, calculations, safety, fire alarms, lightning protection, or life safety.
  2. Select the Appropriate Reference: Begin with the publication most closely related to the question.
  3. Locate the Requirement: Use indexes, chapter headings, code articles, definitions, and tables.
  4. Review Technical Conditions: Read exceptions, notes, qualifying language, and applicable installation details.
  5. Complete the Calculation: When necessary, identify the formula and apply the correct values.
  6. Maintain Examination Pace: Confirm the relevant information and proceed without unnecessary searching.

Repeated navigation practice can help candidates become more comfortable moving between technical subjects and understanding how the references are organized.

Candidates must follow current examination instructions concerning approved publications, permitted editions, tabs, highlighting, annotations, and materials allowed inside the testing room.

Licensing Steps

Florida Residential Electrical Contractor candidates must complete the applicable examination, qualification, and certification procedures established for the license classification.

General licensing steps include:

  1. Confirm the License Classification: Identify the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification and its authorized scope of work.
  2. Review Eligibility Requirements: Understand the professional experience, education, training, and character requirements associated with certification.
  3. Prepare Professional Documentation: Organize records supporting your qualifying electrical experience and other application information.
  4. Apply for the Examination: Complete the applicable Florida examination application process.
  5. Obtain Study References: Purchase the relevant electrical, safety, contractor, and technical publications separately.
  6. Begin Online Exam Preparation: Study electrical theory, National Electrical Code requirements, calculations, safety, and related subjects.
  7. Practice Reference Navigation: Develop familiarity with locating provisions across the reference publications.
  8. Prepare for the Required Examination Components: Review Technical/Safety subjects and the separate Business examination requirements.
  9. Schedule and Take the Examinations: Follow the applicable examination registration, identification, and testing procedures.
  10. Complete the Certification Application: Submit the required information and supporting documentation.
  11. Satisfy Remaining Licensing Requirements: Complete the applicable financial, insurance, background, business, and administrative requirements.

Passing the examination is an important step toward certification, but it does not automatically issue a Florida contractor license.

State Requirements

Florida residential electrical contractor certification is regulated by the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board within the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

The Residential Electrical Contractor classification is a specialty electrical contractor certification associated with residential electrical installations.

The specialty scope includes qualifying electrical wiring and related work in one-, two-, three-, and four-family residences not exceeding two stories in height, together with associated accessory-use structures.

Electrical service within this specialty scope is limited to a single-phase, 400-ampere single service.

Applicants must satisfy the qualifications established for Florida electrical contractor certification, including applicable experience or approved education and training pathways.

Florida also requires applicants to meet the applicable professional character and licensing requirements.

Important areas of professional preparation include:

  • Residential electrical installation requirements
  • Electrical services and distribution systems
  • Branch circuits and feeders
  • Conductor sizing and load calculations
  • Grounding and bonding
  • Electrical equipment and protective devices
  • National Electrical Code compliance
  • OSHA construction safety
  • Fire alarm and life safety concepts
  • Contractor business responsibilities
  • Technical reference interpretation

Electrical contractors must understand the limitations of their authorized work and comply with applicable licensing and electrical installation requirements.

The online course supports examination preparation while candidates pursue the required Florida certification process.

Reference Books

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Online Exam Prep Course is aligned with six technical references covering contractor procedures, construction safety, electrical code requirements, fire alarms, lightning protection, and life safety.

IMPORTANT: These physical reference books are not included with the online course and can be purchased separately.

  • Contractors Manual, 2025
    A contractor reference supporting study of business procedures, project coordination, administrative responsibilities, construction practices, safety organization, and contractor-related knowledge.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction safety reference addressing workplace hazards, fall protection, tools, equipment, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, and construction safety requirements.
  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023
    The primary electrical code reference covering services, feeders, branch circuits, wiring methods, conductors, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, equipment, and residential electrical installation requirements.
  • NFPA 72 – National Fire Alarm Code, 2019
    A fire alarm and signaling reference addressing detection, initiating devices, notification appliances, system functions, and related installation requirements.
  • NFPA 780 – Installation of Lightning Protection Systems, 2017
    A lightning protection reference covering protection system components, air terminals, conductors, bonding, grounding, and installation principles.
  • NFPA 101 – Life Safety Code, 2018 Edition
    A life safety reference addressing fire protection, means of egress, occupancy-related safety requirements, and provisions intended to protect building occupants.

These references support several aspects of residential electrical examination preparation. The National Electrical Code addresses electrical installations, OSHA covers construction safety, and the NFPA publications support specialized fire alarm, lightning protection, and life safety subjects.

The Contractors Manual supports the contractor-related knowledge associated with professional business responsibilities.

Test Information and Study Materials

Effective preparation for the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor examination combines electrical theory, code knowledge, calculations, safety review, and consistent reference-navigation practice.

1. Electrical Theory

Review voltage, current, resistance, power, circuit relationships, and basic electrical principles. Understanding electrical theory provides a foundation for load calculations and technical questions.

2. National Electrical Code Review

Study the organization of the 2023 National Electrical Code. Become familiar with chapters, articles, definitions, tables, exceptions, and installation requirements associated with residential electrical work.

3. Electrical Services

Review service conductors, service equipment, disconnecting means, grounding, bonding, and related installation conditions.

4. Branch Circuits and Feeders

Study dwelling-unit branch circuits, feeder requirements, conductor selection, circuit ratings, and overcurrent protection.

5. Load Calculations

Practice electrical demand calculations, appliance loads, neutral loads, service calculations, and related mathematical concepts.

6. Wiring Methods

Review cables, raceways, electrical boxes, conductors, connections, and applicable installation requirements.

7. Grounding and Bonding

Study grounding electrode systems, equipment grounding, bonding methods, and electrical safety requirements.

8. Motors and Equipment

Review electrical equipment requirements, motor-related concepts, protective devices, and technical installation considerations.

9. Box and Conduit Fill

Practice calculations involving conductor quantities, electrical boxes, conduit fill, and related NEC tables.

10. OSHA Safety

Review construction safety requirements involving electrical hazards, tools, personal protective equipment, elevated work, and workplace conditions.

11. Fire Alarm Systems

Use NFPA 72 to review fire alarm components, detection, initiating devices, signaling functions, and notification concepts.

12. Lightning Protection

Use NFPA 780 to study lightning protection components, conductors, bonding, grounding, and installation concepts.

13. Life Safety Requirements

Review NFPA 101 concepts involving building safety, means of egress, fire protection, and occupant protection.

14. Contractor Procedures

Study contractor business responsibilities, project coordination, administrative concepts, and related subjects using the Contractors Manual.

15. Open-Book Practice

Read technical questions carefully, identify the relevant subject, select the appropriate reference, and locate the supporting provision before determining the answer.

16. Study Review and Improvement

After practice sessions, revisit difficult calculations and unfamiliar code subjects. Review incorrect answers and practice locating the supporting material again.

A consistent study schedule helps candidates divide preparation into manageable subjects rather than attempting to review every reference at once.

Combining technical study with repeated code navigation helps strengthen understanding and supports a more organized approach to examination questions.

Florida Solar Contractor Exam Complete Book Set - Trade Books

Prepare for the Florida Solar Contractor Trade Knowledge examination with a comprehensive collection of technical references covering solar thermal systems, photovoltaic systems, electrical requirements, plumbing provisions, roofing practices, workplace safety, construction estimating, and residential building requirements.

The Florida Solar Contractor Exam Complete Book Set brings together the trade books listed for this product in one convenient package. Rather than locating each technical reference separately, candidates can build a coordinated study library designed around the major knowledge areas associated with solar contracting in Florida.

Solar contractor work can involve several interconnected construction disciplines. A contractor may need to evaluate a site, interpret plans, calculate system requirements, install collectors or photovoltaic components, coordinate electrical and plumbing connections, protect roof assemblies, follow safety standards, and verify that the completed system operates correctly. The books in this set support preparation across those overlapping responsibilities.

This collection includes references devoted to photovoltaic system design, solar water and pool heating, electrical installations, OSHA construction safety, roofing systems, estimating, plumbing, and residential construction. Together, they provide candidates with material for studying both solar-specific concepts and the building systems that support a complete installation.

The book set is intended for candidates preparing for the Florida Solar Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination. It is a trade-reference package and does not replace the separate study materials that may be needed for the Business and Finance examination.

Because Florida construction examinations use approved references, effective preparation involves more than reading technical material from beginning to end. Candidates should become comfortable locating definitions, tables, diagrams, formulas, installation provisions, safety rules, and system requirements under time pressure. A well-organized reference library can make that process more efficient.

Exam Details

The Florida Solar Contractor classification is a Division 2 contractor category. The state examination requirement for this category includes the Business and Finance examination and the Solar Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination.

The Solar Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based testing format. The trade examination consists of 80 equally weighted questions and allows five hours for completion. Construction examination questions are multiple choice, with four possible answers for each question.

The official examination content outline identifies three principal content areas:

  • Swimming Pools: 25% of the trade examination.
  • Domestic Hot Water: 25% of the trade examination.
  • Photovoltaic Systems: 50% of the trade examination.

Candidates should also be prepared to read and interpret plans, specifications, and codes. Basic mathematics may include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, percentages, fractions, decimals, area and volume calculations, square roots, powers, triangle calculations, and simple algebraic equations.

The swimming-pool portion may address site surveys, collector orientation, system sizing, pool and spa heating design, hydraulics, piping, controls, collector installation, freeze protection, troubleshooting, safety, permitting, and code compliance.

The domestic-hot-water portion may include collector orientation, solar water-heating design, direct and indirect systems, piping materials, pumps, heat exchangers, pressure-relief provisions, storage, controls, heat-transfer fluids, system testing, commissioning, and owner instruction.

The photovoltaic portion may cover site analysis, array orientation, system sizing, structural attachment, electrical theory, conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, inverters, batteries when applicable, equipment installation, controls, monitoring, troubleshooting, commissioning, electrical testing, documentation, tools, safety, and applicable codes.

A passing score of 70% is required on Florida construction examinations. Scores are not rounded to the nearest percentage.

Open Book Test

The Florida construction examinations are open book. Candidates may bring only the books and materials included on the approved reference list for their examination. Bringing a large library is helpful only when the candidate knows where information is located, so reference navigation should be treated as an essential part of exam preparation.

Approved books must remain in an acceptable published format. Original-edition references are generally required unless an official reference is specifically provided as a printable file. Approved printed files must be properly bound according to testing rules.

Underlining and highlighting are permitted in approved references. Permanently attached tabs may also be used when they contain ordinary chapter names or page headings. Removable notes, loose labels, detachable tabs, handwritten study sheets, and unauthorized reference materials are not permitted.

Before exam day, candidates should organize each book consistently. Useful tab categories may include major chapters, code articles, system types, design tables, formulas, safety standards, roof assemblies, electrical calculations, plumbing provisions, and troubleshooting topics. Tabs should identify locations without becoming detailed notes.

Practice should include locating information directly from the books. A candidate who understands a subject but cannot find the supporting table or provision quickly may lose valuable examination time. Regular timed lookup drills help develop familiarity with indexes, tables of contents, chapter structures, definitions, illustrations, and cross-references.

Licensing Steps

  1. Review the Florida licensing classification. Confirm that the Certified Solar Contractor license matches the scope of work you plan to perform.
  2. Review the qualification requirements. Florida applicants must satisfy the applicable age, experience, education, financial, insurance, background-screening, and application requirements.
  3. Register for the required examinations. Solar contractor candidates generally complete the Business and Finance examination and the Solar Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination.
  4. Prepare with the approved references. Study the official content areas and develop an efficient system for navigating the trade books.
  5. Schedule the computer-based examinations. After examination registration and approval, candidates schedule their testing appointments through the state’s examination vendor.
  6. Pass the required examination parts. Candidates must receive passing results on every examination part required for the license.
  7. Submit the contractor license application. After meeting the examination requirements, complete the appropriate Certified Solar Contractor application and submit all required documentation.
  8. Complete supporting requirements. This may include fingerprints, a credit report, proof of insurance, workers’ compensation coverage or an applicable exemption, experience documentation, and other materials required by the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

State Requirements

An individual applying for Florida contractor certification must be at least 18 years old. Certified Solar Contractor applicants are generally required to document four years of qualifying experience or an approved combination of college education and experience. The application instructions determine how education and different types of experience may be credited.

Applicants must complete the state certification examination requirements unless a specific exemption or endorsement provision applies. Passing an examination does not by itself create a contractor license. The applicant must also satisfy the Construction Industry Licensing Board’s licensing qualifications and complete the appropriate application.

A background check is part of the licensing process. Applicants are instructed to submit fingerprints through a registered Livescan service provider after submitting the license application.

Financial responsibility is also reviewed. Applicants must provide an acceptable personal credit report containing a FICO-derived credit score and the required records search information.

Applicants must attest that they have obtained public-liability and property-damage insurance in the amounts required by board rule. Workers’ compensation insurance or a valid exemption must also be obtained within the period established for the license.

Florida requires candidates to pass all required examination parts within the applicable four-year examination period. Candidates should review the current application and examination instructions before registering because forms, procedures, and administrative requirements may change.

Reference Books

  • Walker's Building Estimator’s Reference Book, Walker’s, 33rd Edition
    A construction-estimating reference containing labor, material, equipment, measurement, and cost-related information useful for interpreting estimating questions and construction calculations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926
    The federal construction-safety regulations addressing topics such as fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, material handling, excavation, tools, and workplace hazards.
  • National Electrical Code Handbook, 2023
    An illustrated electrical reference that combines the 2023 National Electrical Code with explanatory commentary and supporting examples for electrical installations, photovoltaic systems, grounding, wiring, protection, and equipment.
  • Photovoltaic System Design, Course Manual
    A solar-focused manual supporting the study of photovoltaic site evaluation, system layout, component selection, array design, electrical characteristics, installation planning, and system performance.
  • Solar Water & Pool Heating Manual, 2006
    A technical reference covering solar thermal applications for domestic water and swimming pools, including collectors, piping, pumps, controls, sizing, installation, operation, and troubleshooting.
  • Photovoltaic Systems, 2012, 3rd Edition
    A detailed photovoltaic reference addressing system principles, electrical fundamentals, array configurations, equipment, batteries, inverters, wiring, commissioning, maintenance, safety, and code-related installation practices.
  • The N.R.C.A. Roofing Manual: Membrane Roof Systems, 2023
    A roofing-industry reference covering membrane roof assemblies, materials, design considerations, installation methods, roof details, drainage, flashing, and practices relevant to rooftop solar work.
  • The N.R.C.A. Roofing Manual: Metal Panel and SPF Roof Systems, 2024
    A technical manual addressing metal-panel roofing and spray polyurethane foam roof systems, including materials, construction details, attachment considerations, maintenance, and rooftop coordination.
  • The N.R.C.A. Roofing Manual: Steep-Slope Roof Systems, 2025
    A reference for steep-slope roof coverings and assemblies, including underlayments, flashing, drainage, attachment methods, penetrations, and installation practices that affect solar collector and photovoltaic mounting.
  • Florida Building Code – Plumbing, 2026
    The plumbing volume of the 8th Edition Florida Building Code, providing requirements for plumbing systems, water distribution, piping, fixtures, valves, drainage, materials, and related installations.
  • Florida Building Code – Residential, 2026
    The residential code for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses within its scope, including structural, roofing, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, and building-planning requirements relevant to residential solar projects.

Test Information and Study Materials

Begin by dividing the books into the three major trade-exam categories: swimming-pool heating, domestic-hot-water systems, and photovoltaic systems. Because photovoltaic systems represent half of the published content allocation, they deserve a substantial portion of the study schedule. The remaining time should include balanced review of pool heating and domestic water heating.

Create a separate study block for electrical work. Practice locating photovoltaic articles, conductor requirements, disconnecting means, grounding and bonding provisions, overcurrent protection rules, equipment requirements, and relevant definitions in the National Electrical Code Handbook.

Roofing preparation should focus on identifying roof-system types, understanding acceptable attachment principles, recognizing flashing and waterproofing concerns, and protecting the integrity of membrane, metal, spray-foam, and steep-slope assemblies. Rooftop solar installations require candidates to connect solar knowledge with practical roof-system knowledge.

For solar thermal preparation, review collector selection, orientation, array sizing, piping arrangements, valves, pumps, controls, pressure conditions, freeze protection, heat exchangers, storage, system activation, owner instruction, and troubleshooting. Pay particular attention to the differences between pool-heating, direct domestic-water, and indirect closed-loop systems.

Safety preparation should include fall hazards, ladder use, scaffolding, electrical hazards, tools, personal protective equipment, material handling, and general construction-site responsibilities. Use the OSHA index frequently so that common standards can be located quickly.

Complete timed practice sessions with the actual books. When reviewing a question, identify the likely reference, select the probable chapter or article, locate the supporting information, and confirm the answer. This method develops technical understanding and exam-day reference skills at the same time.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps contractor candidates turn a demanding collection of codes, manuals, and technical references into a more organized preparation plan. Instead of studying unrelated books without direction, candidates can focus on the trade topics connected to the official Florida Solar Contractor examination outline.

Trade-focused review helps connect photovoltaic design, solar thermal systems, electrical work, plumbing, roofing, estimating, safety, and residential construction. This coordinated approach is especially valuable for solar candidates because examination questions may require knowledge from more than one construction discipline.

Reference-navigation practice helps candidates learn where information is located and how to retrieve it efficiently. Familiarity with indexes, code articles, tables, diagrams, and chapter structures can reduce unnecessary searching during an open-book examination.

Practice-oriented preparation also helps identify weak areas before test day. Candidates can review missed questions, return to the supporting reference, and strengthen both subject knowledge and book-navigation skills.

With an organized study structure, realistic practice, and repeated use of the trade references, candidates can approach the Florida Solar Contractor examination with greater familiarity, stronger preparation habits, and more confidence in their ability to work through technical questions.

Exam Details

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based testing format. It consists of 80 equally weighted questions.

The examination measures knowledge of construction practices associated with specialty structures. Candidates should be prepared to read and interpret plans, specifications, technical manuals, tables, illustrations, and applicable building-code provisions.

The published examination content areas include:

  • Foundations: 7.5%
  • Wall Sections: 15%
  • Roof Sections: 15%
  • Insulation: 7.5%
  • Windows: 15%
  • Post and Beam Structures: 15%
  • Roofovers: 15%
  • Siding, Soffits, Fascias, Gutters and Downspouts: 10%

Foundation preparation may include pier-type post footings, excavation, layout, forming, concrete placement, reinforcing materials, vapor barriers, grading, compaction, and finishing. Candidates may also encounter concrete masonry kneewalls, mortar, block installation, reinforcement, and masonry construction practices.

Wall-section preparation may include screen walls, framed solid walls, composite metal panels, wall bracing, storm and screen doors, anchoring, fastening, flashing, caulking, and wind-resistant construction. Candidates should understand how wall components connect to foundations, roof systems, doors, windows, and adjacent materials.

Roof-section topics may include standing-seam roofs, pan roofs, screen roofs, span information, structural supports, fastening, flashing, sealing, roof attachments, wind loads, gussets, and common roof configurations. Candidates should be able to locate installation and structural information in the aluminum guide and Florida code references.

Window questions may address measurements, rough openings, installation in wood, metal, or masonry walls, anchoring, fastening, flashing, sealing, weather resistance, reinforcement, and high-wind requirements.

Post-and-beam construction may include wood and metal structural components, anchoring methods, connections, bracing, carports, patios, roof framing, and safe use of construction tools and access equipment.

Roofovers may involve raised systems, flat-down systems, laminated materials, vinyl blanket systems, ventilation, insulation, fasteners, sealing, structural spacing, drainage, and weather protection.

Siding and exterior-component preparation may include vinyl and aluminum siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, downspouts, vents, starter strips, furring strips, expansion and contraction, drainage, vapor barriers, weatherproofing, and replacement of damaged sheathing.

Candidates should also prepare for basic construction mathematics, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, decimals, percentages, areas, volumes, square roots, powers, triangle calculations, unit conversions, and simple algebra.

The Florida Specialty Structure Contractor Trade Knowledge examination is open book and consists of multiple-choice questions. Candidates may bring authorized references that comply with the applicable examination-room requirements.

Open-book testing does not mean every answer can be found quickly without preparation. Candidates must recognize the subject of a question, identify the most likely reference, locate the applicable chapter or table, and evaluate the information before selecting an answer.

  8. Submit the initial licensing application. File the appropriate application with the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  9. Provide supporting documentation. Submit the applicable experience records, financial information, fingerprints, insurance documents, workers’ compensation information, and business qualification materials.

State Requirements

Individuals seeking Florida licensure as certified specialty contractors must generally pass the state certification examination before applying for initial licensure. Passing the examination does not automatically issue a contractor license.

Applicants must complete the appropriate licensing application and satisfy the qualification requirements that apply to their circumstances. These requirements may include documentation of construction experience or an accepted combination of education and experience.

The application process may also include financial responsibility requirements, personal and business credit information, fingerprint-based background screening, public-liability insurance, property-damage insurance, and workers’ compensation coverage or an applicable exemption.

Applicants intending to qualify a business must provide information about the business entity and their relationship to that company. Different application forms may apply to individuals, applicants qualifying a business, contractors qualifying an additional business, or applicants using an available endorsement pathway.

Florida licensing information states that applicants must obtain the license within four years of receiving the examination score. Candidates should plan the examination and application process carefully so required documents can be completed within the applicable period.

The Florida Electrical Contractors Certification examination is offered in two parts: a Business section and a Technical/Safety section. The Technical/Safety section for Alarm Systems Contractor I includes 100 scored questions. The exam content outline lists the following question ranges: General Theory and Electrical Principles, 14 to 16 questions; Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation, 18 to 20 questions; Wiring and Protection, 2 to 4 questions; Wiring Methods and Materials, 2 to 4 questions; Special Occupancies and Situations, 2 to 4 questions; OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing and Use of Tools and Equipment, 8 to 10 questions; Life Safety and Americans with Disabilities Act, 4 to 6 questions; Limited Energy/Low Voltage, 6 to 8 questions; Central Station Facilities and Signaling, 6 to 8 questions; Premises Protective Signaling Systems, 7 to 9 questions; Initiating Devices, 7 to 9 questions; and Burglar Alarms, 12 to 14 questions.

Exam Details

Florida Roofing Contractor candidates prepare for roofing trade examinations and the Business and Finance examination. This Ultimate package provides books, courses, flash cards, and application support for both areas.

The roofing trade examinations address technical knowledge associated with roofing construction, repair, maintenance, reroofing, waterproofing, estimating, jobsite safety, and Florida building-code compliance. Candidates should be prepared to work with several types of roof systems and supporting construction disciplines.

Membrane roof preparation may include built-up roofing, modified bitumen, thermoset membranes, thermoplastic membranes, roof decks, vapor retarders, insulation, cover boards, attachment methods, surfacing, flashing, drainage, penetrations, and perimeter conditions.

Metal panel and spray polyurethane foam preparation may include panel configurations, fasteners, clips, substrates, sealants, thermal movement, flashing, spray foam application, protective coatings, repairs, and installation details.

Steep-slope preparation may include asphalt shingles, tile, slate, wood roofing products, underlayments, ventilation, valleys, ridges, hips, eaves, rakes, fastening, flashing, and penetrations.

Architectural metal subjects may involve copings, gutters, downspouts, roof edges, joints, transitions, counterflashing, drainage, expansion, and metal movement. Condensation and air-leakage topics address moisture and uncontrolled airflow through roofing and building-envelope assemblies.

Waterproofing preparation may cover below-grade and above-grade systems, substrates, drainage, transitions, joints, protection, penetrations, and installation methods. Estimating preparation may include roof dimensions, slopes, areas, waste factors, material quantities, labor, productivity, unit conversions, and project costs.

The Business and Finance examination focuses on operating and managing a contracting business. Subjects may include accounting, contracts, bidding, financial statements, job costing, taxes, insurance, business organization, employment responsibilities, licensing requirements, and contractor administration.

The live, recorded, and self-study course formats allow candidates to approach these subjects in different ways. Live instruction provides guided review, recorded classes support repeated study, and self-study resources help candidates maintain progress between lessons.

Open Book Test

The Florida Roofing Contractor trade and Business and Finance examinations are open book. Candidates may use approved references during the applicable examination session when those books comply with current testing requirements.

Open-book testing still requires strong preparation. Candidates must identify the subject of a question, select the correct publication, locate the applicable information, interpret the material, and apply it within the available testing time.

The highlighted and tabbed books help candidates build a more organized lookup method. A membrane roofing question may require the NRCA manual covering membrane roof systems. A metal panel or spray polyurethane foam question may require the corresponding NRCA roofing manual. A steep-slope question may require the NRCA steep-slope volume.

Architectural sheet-metal, flashing, condensation, and air-leakage questions may require the applicable NRCA reference or the SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual. Waterproofing questions may require the NRCA Waterproofing Manual. Estimating questions may require Walker’s Building Estimator’s Reference Book or Roofing Construction and Estimating.

Safety questions may require OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. Florida code and high-wind questions may require the Florida Building Code - Building or the Florida Building Code - Test Protocols for High-Velocity Hurricane Zones.

Business questions may require the Contractors Manual, Builder’s Guide to Accounting, A201, A401, A701, or Florida Statutes Chapter 455. Candidates should learn which reference applies to accounting, contracts, bidding, contractor responsibilities, and professional regulation.

Tabs and highlighting provide useful starting points, but candidates should read surrounding definitions, exceptions, tables, notes, and related provisions before choosing an answer. The correct response may depend on information beyond a single highlighted sentence.

Books brought into the testing center must comply with current rules for permitted editions, binding, tabs, highlighting, notes, loose materials, and book condition. Candidates should review the current examination instructions before every scheduled appointment.

Exam Details

The Florida electrical contractor certification examination is divided into a Business section and a Technical/Safety section. Residential Electrical Contractor candidates are required to complete the Business component as well as the Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination.

The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows 2 1/2 hours. The business content covers subjects associated with operating and managing a contracting business, including maintaining cash flow, estimating and bidding, contracts and agreements, purchasing control, scheduling, insurance and bonding, contracting laws and rules, personnel management, payroll and sales tax laws, financial statements, and management accounting.

The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows 5 hours. The examination measures knowledge of residential electrical work as well as the ability to locate, interpret, calculate, and apply information from applicable references.

Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety subject areas include:

  • General Theory and Electrical Principles
  • Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation
  • Wiring and Protection
  • OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing, and Use of Tools and Equipment
  • Residential Life Safety and ADA
  • Motors
  • Box Fill
  • Demand Loads
  • Conduit Fill
  • Grounding Conductors
  • Neutral Loads
  • Appliance Loads
  • Service
  • Voltage Drop

Because these areas combine code knowledge, electrical theory, calculations, safety requirements, and reference lookup, study time should include both content review and repeated practice locating information in the books.

Open Book Test

Both the Florida Electrical Contractors Business examination and the Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination are open-book exams. Candidates may bring authorized references that comply with the testing program’s reference-material rules.

Open-book does not mean that every study aid can be taken into the testing room. Florida’s examination rules restrict candidates to approved reference materials. Class notes, sample questions, formulas, loose study materials, and similar preparation materials are not permitted as substitutes for approved references. Permanently attached tabs may be used in reference books, while removable tabs such as pull-off labels and Post-it-style flags are not permitted.

This makes reference navigation an important part of Florida Residential Electrical Contractor exam preparation. During your study period, practice identifying the correct book first, then locating the relevant chapter, article, table, section, or index entry. The objective is to become comfortable enough with the references that you can move through them efficiently under exam conditions.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the appropriate Florida license category. The Residential Electrical Contractor examination is one of the specialty electrical contractor categories administered through the Florida Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.
  2. Apply for authorization to take the examination. Candidates use the Florida DBPR electrical contractor examination application and select Residential Electrical Contractor as the examination category.
  3. Receive examination approval. After DBPR processes and approves the examination application, the candidate becomes eligible to schedule the required computer-based examination components.
  4. Schedule the examinations. Florida DBPR electrical contractor computer-based examinations are delivered through Pearson Professional Assessments, formerly Pearson VUE.
  5. Prepare for both Business and Technical/Safety. Residential Electrical Contractor candidates must prepare for the required Business component as well as the residential trade examination.
  6. Pass the required examination portions. Passing the examination is one part of the Florida licensing process and does not replace the other licensing qualifications.
  7. Submit the initial certification application. After passing the required examination components, applicants pursuing certification submit the appropriate initial certification application to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  8. Complete the remaining licensing requirements. The application requires documentation relating to qualifications such as experience, financial responsibility, insurance, and other applicable licensing information.

State Requirements

Florida’s initial certification application requires electrical, alarm, and electrical specialty contractor applicants to be at least 18 years of age, satisfy the applicable character and qualification requirements, meet education or experience requirements, and complete the required licensing process.

The application provides several experience pathways. These include three years of management experience in the applicable trade within the preceding six years; four years of experience as a foreman, supervisor, or contractor within the preceding eight years; or qualifying combinations of training, technical education, supervisory experience, governmental or military technical experience, and other recognized experience within the specified periods established by Florida. A qualifying electrical professional engineer pathway is also included in the state application requirements.

For an electrical specialty category such as Residential Electrical Contractor, applicants must document experience applicable to the specialty for which they are seeking certification. Florida’s application includes Residential Electrical as a specific work-experience category in the employment verification section.

Applicants should also be prepared to provide the employment and experience documentation required by the state application. Depending on how the experience was obtained, documentation may include employer verification, employment records, and project history. Additional licensing documentation relating to financial responsibility, business qualification, insurance, and background information may also apply based on the applicant’s circumstances and the type of license status requested.

Exam Details

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification examination is administered in two parts: a Business examination and a Technical/Safety examination. Both sections are computer-based examinations administered through Pearson VUE after the candidate receives authorization from the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and provides 2½ hours of testing time. The Business component is required for the electrical certification categories covered by the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.

The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and provides 5 hours of testing time. Additional unscored pilot questions may also appear on the examination.

The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination covers a broad range of subjects. The current examination outline includes:

  • General Theory and Electrical Principles: 13–15 questions
  • Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation: 12–14 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 6–8 questions
  • OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing and Use of Tools and Equipment: 8–10 questions
  • Residential Life Safety and ADA: 4–6 questions
  • Motors: 4–6 questions
  • Box Fill: 4–6 questions
  • Demand Loads: 5–7 questions
  • Conduit Fill: 2–4 questions
  • Grounding Conductors: 7–9 questions
  • Neutral Loads: 3–5 questions
  • Appliance Loads: 6–8 questions
  • Service: 8–10 questions
  • Voltage Drop: 4–6 questions

Every examination question is multiple choice. Candidates should be prepared to apply electrical principles, interpret plans and specifications, perform calculations, and locate applicable requirements in the NEC and other applicable references.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Business and Technical/Safety examinations are open book. Candidates may use authorized reference materials in accordance with the examination administrator’s rules.

An open-book electrical exam still requires significant preparation. With 100 scored Technical/Safety questions and a five-hour testing period, there is not enough time to search every book from beginning to end. Candidates should know which reference is most likely to contain the information needed for a particular question and should become comfortable navigating indexes, articles, chapters, tables, definitions, and calculations.

Florida examination rules permit permanently attached tabs in reference books. Removable tabs, Post-it notes, pull-off labels, handwritten notes, class notes, formulas, sample questions, and other unauthorized study materials are not allowed in the examination room. Reference materials are subject to examination-center rules and inspection.

A practical preparation strategy is to organize major sections before exam day. Become familiar with frequently used NEC articles, electrical calculation tables, OSHA safety topics, life safety provisions, and the organization of the other technical references. The faster you can identify the right book and section, the more time you can devote to solving the question itself.

Licensing Steps

  1. Apply for examination approval. Candidates pursuing Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification begin by submitting the applicable examination application to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  2. Receive authorization to test. After the examination application is approved, candidates become eligible to schedule the required examinations.
  3. Schedule the examinations. Florida electrical contractor examinations are delivered through Pearson VUE in a computer-based testing format.
  4. Prepare for the Business and Technical/Safety sections. Study contractor-related material for the Business examination and electrical, safety, calculations, code, and residential subjects for the Technical/Safety examination.
  5. Pass both required examination portions. Initial certification by examination requires successful completion of both portions of the Florida Electrical Contractors examination.
  6. Submit the initial certification application. After completing the examination requirements, candidates must apply for initial certification in the appropriate specialty category.
  7. Provide required supporting documentation. The application process includes documentation related to experience, financial responsibility, and other requirements established for Certified Specialty Electrical Contractors.
  8. Complete the DBPR licensing process. Applicants must satisfy the requirements of the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board before the license can be issued.

State Requirements

Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification is regulated through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board under Florida’s electrical contractor licensing framework.

Applicants seeking initial Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor licensure by examination must demonstrate that they meet the applicable education or experience requirements identified in the state application. Candidates must also have passed both portions of the State of Florida Electrical Contractors examination. Examination scores used for initial certification may not be more than three years old at the time of application.

The initial certification process also requires financial documentation. Current state requirements for Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor applicants include a personal credit report, as well as a business credit report and business financial statement. The business financial statement must demonstrate the net-worth requirement established for specialty electrical contractor certification.

Passing the examination is therefore an important step, but it does not by itself issue the contractor license. Candidates must complete the appropriate certification application and meet the licensing requirements established by the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong preparation plan for the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor exam should begin with the National Electrical Code. Many examination subjects involve calculations or requirements that require candidates to move between NEC articles and tables. Instead of attempting to memorize every code provision, concentrate on understanding the NEC structure and learning how to quickly locate the information you need.

Electrical theory should also receive dedicated study time. Candidates should be comfortable working with voltage, current, resistance, power, electrical formulas, conductor characteristics, and other principles that support practical electrical calculations. Theory questions may require direct calculations or may provide the foundation needed to solve more detailed residential electrical problems.

Plan and specification reading represents another significant part of the Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Practice interpreting electrical drawings, symbols, circuit information, schedules, dimensions, and written specifications. The ability to connect a plan detail with an applicable NEC requirement is particularly useful during technical testing.

Load calculations deserve focused preparation because several examination categories involve demand loads, neutral loads, appliance loads, and service calculations. Practice identifying the correct calculation method before entering numbers into a formula. Learn which NEC article or table applies and become comfortable checking your work.

Grounding and bonding are also important study areas. Review grounding electrode systems, grounding electrode conductors, equipment grounding conductors, bonding requirements, conductor sizing, and the distinctions between different grounding and bonding functions. These concepts are easier to apply when candidates understand the purpose behind the requirement instead of relying solely on memorized table values.

Other targeted study areas should include box fill and conduit fill. These subjects often combine code navigation with calculation skills. Candidates should practice determining conductor allowances, equipment allowances, raceway fill, and applicable table values using the NEC.

Life safety preparation can include review of NFPA 101, NFPA 72, and related concepts associated with fire protection, alarms, emergency conditions, and occupant safety. What books are included in the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Exam Complete Book Set?

Is the Florida Residential Electrical Contractor exam open book?

How many questions are on the Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety exam?

What subjects should I study for the Residential Electrical Contractor exam?

Exam Details

Candidates should understand the technical principles involved in sheet metal construction and become familiar with the publications used to support applicable installation requirements.

Important examination preparation areas include:

Open Book Test

Architectural flashing, gutters, copings, and roof-edge details may involve the SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual. Questions concerning industrial exhaust or commercial kitchen ventilation may require the relevant NFPA standard.

  1. Identify the Technical Subject: Determine whether the question concerns duct construction, sheet metal, ventilation, exhaust, calculations, safety, or mechanical codes.
  2. Select the Appropriate Reference: Choose the SMACNA, NFPA, OSHA, contractor, or Florida code publication associated with the topic.
  3. Locate Supporting Information: Use indexes, chapter headings, technical tables, diagrams, definitions, and standard-numbering systems.
  4. Confirm Applicability: Review pressure classifications, installation conditions, exceptions, notes, and related provisions.
  5. Check Calculations: Confirm airflow values, dimensions, velocity, friction loss, and units when solving numerical questions.
  6. Maintain Examination Pace: Avoid spending excessive time searching after locating the controlling information.

Florida State Business and Finance Flash Cards

Prepare for the Florida State Business and Finance examination with a focused set of 250 flash cards designed to reinforce important concepts, terminology, and reference-book knowledge connected to the Business and Finance portion of Florida construction contractor testing.

The Florida State Business and Finance exam requires more than memorizing isolated facts. Candidates need to understand business practices, accounting concepts, contracts, bidding documents, regulatory information, and other subjects that can appear throughout the approved reference materials. Because the examination is open book, preparation also involves becoming familiar with where information is located and how key topics are organized inside the books and documents used for the test.

These Florida State Business and Finance Flash Cards give candidates a practical way to review important information in short, repeatable study sessions. Instead of relying only on long reading assignments, you can work through individual questions and answers, identify areas that need more attention, and return to difficult concepts as often as needed.

The set contains 250 flash cards. The test questions in this study product focus on material associated with the principal Business and Finance references, including AIA contract documents, accounting material, the Contractors Manual, and Florida regulatory statutes.

Flash cards can be especially useful when preparing for an open-book contractor examination because they encourage active recall. Rather than simply reading a chapter and moving on, you are prompted to retrieve an answer, recognize terminology, distinguish between similar concepts, and connect a question with the reference material where the subject is discussed.

Use the cards independently, combine them with your reference-book study, or work through them alongside a broader Florida contractor exam preparation program. A consistent review schedule can help you become more comfortable with the language used throughout construction business, contracting, and financial-management references.

What You Get

  • 250 Florida State Business and Finance flash cards for focused exam-preparation review.
  • Questions built around important concepts associated with the Business and Finance reference materials.
  • Practice that supports active recall rather than passive reading alone.
  • A convenient format for reviewing terminology, business concepts, contract documents, accounting material, and regulatory subjects.
  • A study tool that can be used repeatedly as you become more familiar with the Florida Business and Finance examination references.

Exam Details

The Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board Business and Finance examination is part of the state examination process for Florida construction contractor licensing. The Business and Finance examination is administered as a computer-based test.

The examination contains 120 scored questions and provides 6.5 hours of examination time. Florida identifies the Business and Finance examination as a daily computer-based testing examination.

Florida construction examinations use multiple-choice questions. Business and Finance candidates should be prepared to work with information drawn from approved references as well as applicable business and trade knowledge. The exam is designed to evaluate familiarity with the business and financial responsibilities associated with professional construction contracting.

For many candidates, the challenge is not simply knowing a definition. The examination may require you to recognize the correct business concept, understand a contractual relationship, interpret information from a reference, or identify where an answer can be found within the approved materials. That makes reference familiarity an important part of preparation.

The 250 flash cards are intended to complement that preparation by giving you repeated exposure to concepts connected with the books and documents used for Business and Finance study.

Open Book Test

The Florida construction Business and Finance examination is an open-book examination. Candidates may bring approved reference materials into the testing room when those materials comply with Florida's examination rules.

An open-book test still requires substantial preparation. With 120 scored questions and a limited testing period, searching unfamiliar books from beginning to end for every answer can consume valuable time. Candidates benefit from knowing the structure of their references, recognizing important sections, and becoming comfortable with the terminology used throughout the material.

Flash-card practice can support this process. When you repeatedly encounter a subject during study, you begin to associate the concept with the source material in which it appears. That familiarity can make it easier to decide which reference is most likely to contain the information you need during the examination.

Florida's current Business and Finance reference rules require examination materials to meet specific conditions before they may be used in the testing room. Approved references must remain properly bound. Underlining and highlighting are permitted, while handwritten and typewritten notes are not allowed. Moveable tabs such as removable flags are not permitted, and candidates may not make marks in their references during the examination.

Because examination-reference rules can affect how you prepare your books, candidates should organize permitted materials well before the test date rather than waiting until the day of the examination.

Licensing Steps

The Business and Finance examination is one component of Florida's construction contractor examination and licensing process. The exact examinations and licensing requirements that apply depend on the contractor classification being pursued.

Florida directs candidates who need to take construction examinations to apply for examination eligibility through Professional Testing, Inc. Once approved, candidates taking computer-based construction examinations may schedule their examination through Florida's examination vendor, Pearson VUE.

A typical candidate preparing for the Business and Finance portion should plan to:

  1. Determine the Florida contractor classification or specialty being pursued.
  2. Review the examinations required for that classification.
  3. Apply for the required construction examination or examinations through the state's designated examination-registration process.
  4. Prepare using the current examination content information and approved reference list.
  5. Schedule the computer-based examination after receiving examination approval.
  6. Take and pass the examinations required for the applicable contractor classification.
  7. Complete the applicable contractor-license application requirements for the license being sought.

Different Florida contractor classifications have different licensing requirements, so candidates should use the application that corresponds to their specific classification and status.

State Requirements

The Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board is responsible for licensing and regulating the state's construction industry. Applicants pursuing certified contractor licensure generally must satisfy the examination and application requirements associated with the specific contractor category they are seeking.

The Business and Finance examination does not by itself constitute a Florida contractor license. It is an examination component used within the broader licensing process. Depending on the contractor category, additional examinations and application requirements may apply.

For example, Florida identifies different examination combinations for different construction classifications. Division I contractor categories such as General, Building, and Residential require Business and Finance along with additional required examination parts. Other contractor specialties may use a different examination structure.

Because this product is specifically focused on Florida State Business and Finance, the 250 flash cards concentrate on preparation for that examination area rather than attempting to replace trade-specific preparation for another contractor examination.

Reference Books

The Florida Business and Finance examination relies on designated reference materials. The following titles are central to the flash-card study focus and correspond to the major Business and Finance references:

  • AIA A201 – General Conditions of the Contract for Construction, 2017
    This AIA document addresses the general conditions governing construction contracts and establishes important contractual relationships, responsibilities, procedures, and administrative concepts used in construction projects.
  • AIA A401 – Standard Form of Agreement Between Contractor-Subcontractor, 2017
    This contract document addresses the agreement between a contractor and subcontractor and is useful for studying responsibilities, contractual relationships, payment concepts, and obligations between the parties.
  • AIA A701 – Instructions to Bidders, 2018
    This document covers instructions and procedures associated with the construction bidding process and helps candidates become familiar with terminology and responsibilities related to bidding.
  • Builder's Guide to Accounting, 2001
    This construction-oriented accounting reference supports preparation for financial and accounting concepts relevant to operating and managing a contracting business.
  • Contractors Manual, 2025 Edition
    The Contractors Manual is a major Florida Business and Finance examination reference and covers business, financial, administrative, and contractor-related material used in examination preparation.
  • Florida Statutes Chapter 455
    Chapter 455 contains Florida statutory provisions relating to business and professional regulation and is among the regulatory references associated with the Business and Finance examination.

Becoming familiar with these materials is an important part of preparing for the open-book examination. The goal is not necessarily to memorize every page. Instead, candidates should learn what each reference is designed to cover and develop the ability to recognize which book or document is most relevant to a particular subject.

Exam Room Approved Books

Florida's Business and Finance reference list identifies the materials candidates may bring into the testing room. The approved Business and Finance references include:

  • AIA A201 – General Conditions of the Contract for Construction, 2017
    Approved AIA contract reference for the Business and Finance examination.
  • AIA A401 – Standard Form of Agreement Between Contractor-Subcontractor, 2017
    Approved contractor-subcontractor agreement reference.
  • AIA A701 – Instructions to Bidders, 2018
    Approved bidding-document reference for the examination.
  • Builder's Guide to Accounting, 2001
    Approved accounting reference for Business and Finance testing.
  • Contractors Manual, 2025 Edition
    The 2025 edition is used for the examination beginning February 1, 2026.
  • Florida Statutes Chapter 455, 2025
    The current 2026 Business and Finance reference list identifies the 2025 edition of Chapter 455. A properly bound PDF version is permitted under the examination reference rules.

Candidates should prepare the approved books in accordance with Florida's testing-room requirements. Knowing that the exam is open book does not eliminate the need to study. Successful preparation includes developing familiarity with the books, learning their organization, and practicing how to identify the correct reference quickly when faced with a question.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida State Business and Finance Flash Cards are designed as a supplementary study tool for candidates who want additional repetition while preparing with the official reference materials.

A productive study method is to combine several types of preparation. Begin by reviewing the reference books and learning their general structure. Next, use flash cards to test recall and identify topics that are not yet comfortable. When a flash-card question exposes a weak area, return to the appropriate reference and review the surrounding material. This creates a stronger connection between the question, the concept, and the location of the information.

You can also separate the 250 flash cards into smaller study groups. Working with 25 to 50 cards at a time can make review easier to manage. After completing a group, set aside the cards you answer confidently and spend more time on those that require additional review.

Another useful strategy is to practice reference selection. When reading a flash-card question, ask yourself which source you would consult during the actual exam. A bidding question may direct your attention toward AIA A701, while a contractor-subcontractor relationship may make AIA A401 the more logical starting point. Accounting questions may require a different reference entirely.

This type of repetition helps develop the reference-navigation habits that matter in an open-book examination. The objective is to move beyond recognizing words and toward understanding how the books fit together within the Business and Finance subject area.

The goal is to build a structured study routine that combines reading, active recall, repeated review, and reference navigation. Candidates can use the flash cards at home, during short study periods, or as a review tool after working through larger sections of the Business and Finance materials.

By breaking preparation into manageable pieces, 1 Exam Prep helps students approach the Florida Business and Finance examination with a clearer study structure and greater familiarity with the material they will encounter.

Exam Details

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification examination includes a Business examination and a Technical/Safety examination. The examinations are computer based and are scheduled after candidates receive authorization through the Florida licensing and examination process.

The Business examination contains 50 scored questions with 2½ hours of testing time. The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions with 5 hours of testing time. Additional pilot questions may appear and are not counted toward the candidate's examination score.

The Residential Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination covers multiple areas of electrical knowledge and application. Candidates should prepare for subjects involving general electrical theory and principles, plan and specification interpretation, wiring and protection, OSHA and jobsite safety, residential life safety, motors, box fill, demand loads, conduit fill, grounding conductors, neutral loads, appliance loads, services, and voltage drop.

These subjects require more than memorization. Candidates may need to perform calculations, interpret technical information, identify applicable code requirements, and locate details within reference books. Familiarity with the structure of the NEC and supporting references is therefore an important part of effective preparation.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor Business and Technical/Safety examinations are open book. Candidates may use authorized reference materials according to the examination administrator's rules.

Open-book testing makes reference navigation a critical skill. Even with several hours available, searching through six large technical books without a clear system can consume valuable testing time. Highlighting and tabs help candidates identify important sections and move through their references more efficiently while studying and practicing.

The National Electrical Code alone contains a large number of articles, tables, definitions, exceptions, and calculation requirements. Permanent organization can help candidates move more quickly between commonly studied areas such as branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, raceways, boxes, conductor sizing, appliances, and motors.

The same principle applies to OSHA and NFPA references. A candidate who already understands where major safety, fire alarm, life safety, or lightning protection topics are located can devote more attention to interpreting the question and applying the correct requirement.

Florida examination reference rules permit highlighting and permanently attached tabs within authorized reference materials. Candidates should become familiar with their books before exam day so the highlighting and tabs serve as navigation tools rather than substitutes for studying.
