  7. Submit the applicable certification application. After satisfying examination requirements, complete the licensing application for the appropriate electrical contractor category.
  8. Meet the remaining state licensing requirements. Provide the required documentation and complete the licensing process established by the Florida Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

State Requirements

Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification falls under the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board. Candidates pursuing certification must complete the required examination process and satisfy the applicable licensing qualifications.

Florida's certification process includes requirements beyond passing an exam. Applicants pursuing initial Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor licensure by examination must meet the applicable experience or education requirements and complete the required application process.

Applicants also need to satisfy applicable financial responsibility requirements and provide required supporting documentation during the certification process. Examination results form one part of the overall licensing process and do not by themselves issue a Florida contractor license.

Important subjects include employee protection, electrical safety, tools and equipment, ladders, scaffolding, fall protection, excavation hazards, personal protective equipment, and other jobsite safety topics.
  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023
    The 2023 National Electrical Code is a major technical reference for residential electrical preparation. Candidates use the NEC to study branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, raceways, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, boxes, motors, appliances, calculations, and other electrical installation requirements.

The highlighted and tabbed references can help candidates create a more structured approach to large code books and standards, but candidates should still work through the material regularly before testing.

NFPA 72, NFPA 780, and NFPA 101 should each be treated as separate references. Learn the type of information contained in each publication so you know which book to reach for when a question involves fire alarms, lightning protection, or life safety.

  2. Apply for Examination Approval: Submit the appropriate examination application through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  3. Prepare for Both Examinations: Study the Technical/Safety and Business subjects using relevant references and structured examination preparation.

  5. Pass Both Examination Components: Earn the required passing score on each component.
  6. Apply for Initial Certification: Complete the applicable initial licensure application and provide the required supporting documentation.
  7. Obtain Licensing Approval: The Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board reviews initial certified licensure applications and determines whether the applicant satisfies licensing requirements.

Passing the examinations is an essential part of the certification process, but it does not independently authorize a candidate to perform work requiring a contractor license. Applicants must also satisfy the applicable requirements for initial licensure.

State Requirements

Florida regulates certified alarm system contractors under Chapter 489, Part II, Florida Statutes, and applicable administrative rules.

Applicants seeking Certified Alarm System Contractor I licensure must meet requirements involving examination performance, qualifying experience, financial documentation, and licensing approval.

  • Minimum Age: Examination applicants must be at least 18 years old.
  • Examination: Candidates must pass the required Technical/Safety and Business components.
  • Experience: Applicants must demonstrate qualifying professional experience under an applicable statutory pathway.
  • Fire Alarm Experience: At least 40% of the qualifying experience must involve the types of fire alarm systems typically used in commercial settings.
  • Financial Documentation: Initial certification requires applicable personal and business credit documentation and business financial information.
  • Business Net Worth: Florida's initial certification checklist requires a business financial statement demonstrating a net worth of at least $10,000.
  • Board Approval: Initial certified licensure applications are subject to review and approval by the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

Florida distinguishes between certified contractors and registered contractors. Certified licensure generally provides statewide contracting authority within the license classification, while registration is associated with specified local jurisdictions.

In Florida, “master-level” electrician testing is closely tied to state electrical contractor certification. That means the exam isn’t just about knowing the code—it’s about proving you can think like the person responsible for electrical contracting work: applying the National Electrical Code (NEC) accurately, understanding safety and compliance expectations, and handling business responsibilities that come with certification.

This Florida 2026 Master Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide is built for the way Florida’s electrical certification exams are structured: two parts—a Business section and a Technical/Safety section—administered through Pearson VUE for DBPR’s Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board. You’ll get 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams to help you build exam-ready performance: faster lookups, better pacing, cleaner decision-making, and fewer avoidable mistakes.

Practice exams are the difference between “I know electrical work” and “I can score it under pressure.” With repeated exam-style practice, you build a steady method you can trust on test day:

  • Read carefully (so you don’t miss one word that changes the answer)
  • Find what you need fast (open-book doesn’t help if you search too long)
  • Apply the rule correctly (not “close enough” guessing)
  • Protect your time across two exam parts and a long testing day

Who this is for:

  • Candidates preparing for Florida’s Electrical Contractors Certification exams (Business + Technical/Safety)
  • Electricians aiming for the Unlimited Electrical Contractor (or other Florida electrical certification areas listed by DBPR)
  • Test-takers who want a structured plan built around practice and realistic review
  • Working electricians who want to strengthen NEC navigation, safety knowledge, and exam pacing

Exam Details

Florida’s Electrical Contractors Certification examinations are administered on behalf of the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board and are given in two parts: technical/safety and business. They are offered in a computer-based testing format through Pearson VUE. Candidates can schedule after the department approves their exam application, and DBPR notes candidates are eligible to schedule within 72 hours after the examination application is approved.

DBPR’s Electrical Contractors Candidate Information Booklet explains the exam structure clearly:

  • Business section: 50 scored questions, 2.5 hours
  • Technical/Safety section: 100 scored questions, 5 hours
  • Format: Computer-based, multiple choice
  • Open-book: Both parts are open book (with strict reference rules)
  • Passing score: 75% minimum on the Business section and 75% minimum on the Technical/Safety section

For Florida’s Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety exam, the Candidate Information Booklet lists major topic areas and typical question ranges, including:

  • General Theory and Electrical Principles
  • Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation
  • Wiring and Protection
  • Wiring Methods and Materials
  • Special Occupancies and Situations
  • OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing, and Use of Tools and Equipment
  • Life Safety and Americans with Disabilities Act
  • Electrical Signs, Outline Lighting, and Structural Considerations
  • Alarms / Limited Energy

That outline tells you how broad Florida’s electrical contractor testing is: code application, safety and OSHA knowledge, specialty systems, and plan reading—not just one narrow slice of the trade. That’s why a practice-heavy approach works so well. When you practice across the blueprint repeatedly, your study becomes more efficient and your test-day confidence rises.

Open Book Test

Florida’s electrical certification examinations are open book for both the Business section and the Technical/Safety section. Candidates are strongly encouraged to bring approved reference materials to the exam site and use only the references allowed for their specific certification area.

What open-book really means in Florida: it’s not “anything goes.” Florida’s reference list and exam rules are strict. Your advantage comes from being prepared with compliant books and a trained lookup strategy.

High-impact reference rules you should train for:

  • No handwritten or typewritten notes are allowed in references; any existing handwritten notes must be completely blackened out or whited out so they are not legible.
  • Moveable tabs (such as Post-it flags) are not allowed.
  • You cannot make marks in your references during the examination.
  • No scratch paper, class notes, formulas, sample questions, or bound/loose-leaf study materials are allowed in the examination room.
  • Only the references listed for the exam are allowed at the exam site (and typically only one copy of each reference is allowed).

Open-book strategy that actually works:

  • Don’t look up everything. Use references to confirm uncertain details, table values, and tricky exceptions—then move on.
  • Use keywords and structure. The fastest lookups come from recognizing what the question is testing and going directly to the likely chapter/article/table.
  • Protect momentum. If a question becomes a time sink, make the best code-supported choice you can and keep moving. Consistent points beat perfect certainty with poor pacing.

Licensing Steps

Florida’s state electrical certification exams support contractor certification through DBPR’s Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board. While application documentation requirements depend on the certification area, DBPR’s exam guidance and the Candidate Information Booklet outline the exam-centered flow:

  1. Apply for approval to sit for the examination. DBPR requires exam candidates to be approved before scheduling.
  2. Schedule through Pearson VUE. DBPR states approved candidates schedule using the department’s examination vendor, Pearson VUE, and candidates are eligible to schedule within 72 hours after the exam application is approved.
  3. Take the Business exam. The Business section is 50 scored questions with a 2.5-hour time limit and requires a 75% minimum passing score.
  4. Take the Technical/Safety exam for your electrical certification area. For Unlimited Electrical Contractor, the Technical/Safety exam is 100 scored questions with a 5-hour time limit and requires a 75% minimum passing score.
  5. Follow DBPR/ECLB instructions after passing. Use the official DBPR licensing process for final certification steps, including any remaining application items required for issuance.

This product is designed to support the exam portion of that pathway with practice-driven preparation that matches Florida’s two-part format.

State Requirements

Florida’s statewide electrical credentialing is structured around electrical contractor certification and specialty certification areas rather than a single statewide “master electrician” license title. DBPR’s electrical exam program includes multiple certification areas, such as Unlimited Electrical Contractor and Residential Electrical Contractor, with each area having its own Technical/Safety outline and approved references.

Because eligibility requirements can vary by certification area and applicant pathway, the most reliable way to stay on track is to align your preparation to the exact exam(s) you are taking:

  • Business exam readiness: contracts, estimating, scheduling, insurance/bonding, personnel management, payroll/sales tax, and financial reports
  • Technical/Safety readiness: NEC-based code application, wiring methods, protection, special occupancies, OSHA and safety, plan reading, and the specialty topics included in Florida’s outline

If your goal is Florida’s Unlimited Electrical Contractor certification area, this guide is designed to help you prepare in the proportions the state outlines—so your study time produces measurable improvement.

Reference Books

Florida publishes an official Electrical Contractors’ Reference List with titles and editions allowed for each certification area. Below are references shown as applicable to the Unlimited Electrical Contractor (UE) category on the official list.

  • Florida Contractors Manual, 2021
    Core business and regulatory reference for Florida contractor exams. The official reference list notes that a bound PDF version of the index to this book may be brought into test centers for use on the exam.
  • MANCOMM Code of Federal Regulation, Title 29 (OSHA) Parts 1926, 1910, 1904 – July 2020 edition
    OSHA safety reference listed for Florida electrical contractor examinations.
  • NFPA 70 – National Electrical Code, 2023 edition
    The NEC reference listed for Florida electrical contractor technical/safety testing. Effective-date notes for future code updates are listed on Florida’s reference list.
  • NFPA 72 – National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 edition
    Fire alarm and signaling reference listed for Florida electrical contractor certification areas.
  • NFPA 780 – Lightning Protection Code, 2017 edition
    Lightning protection reference listed on Florida’s approved reference list for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • NFPA 101 – Life Safety Code, 2018 edition
    Life safety reference listed on Florida’s approved reference list for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • Fire Alarm Signaling Systems Handbook, Bukowski & Moore (3rd Ed., 2003 or 4th Ed., 2010)
    Supplemental fire alarm signaling handbook listed as an approved reference.
  • UL 681 – Installation and Classification of Burglar and Holdup Alarm Systems
    Approved alarm-system reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor (with edition notes shown on Florida’s reference list).
  • UL 365 – Police Station Connected Burglar Alarm Units and Systems
    Approved alarm-system reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • Engineering Sign Structures: An Introduction to Analysis and Design (1998)
    Approved sign-structure reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • NEON, Techniques and Handling (1997, 4th edition)
    Approved neon/sign reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (16th or 17th edition)
    Approved reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor, tied to structural considerations in specialty work and exam topics.
  • Telecommunication Wiring (2001, 3rd edition)
    Approved telecommunications wiring reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor.
  • NTC Blue Book Low Voltage Systems, 2020 edition
    Approved low-voltage systems reference listed for Unlimited Electrical Contractor (with effective-date notes for later editions shown on Florida’s reference list).

Test Information and Study Materials

Florida’s electrical contractor testing is long and broad—two parts, open book, and timed. The challenge isn’t only knowing the material. It’s managing time, staying accurate, and using references efficiently.

Use your practice exams to train like the real test:

  • Business exam mindset: These questions reward careful reading and familiarity with how Florida contractor requirements are framed. Practice helps you avoid second-guessing.
  • Technical/Safety mindset: These questions reward NEC navigation and correct application. Practice helps you reduce search time and answer with confidence.
  • Two-part endurance: Florida’s exam day can be long. Training with full-length practice sessions helps you build stamina so performance doesn’t drop late.

How to study with the 12 practice exams:

  • Start with a baseline exam. Take a timed practice test early. Use the results to identify where you lose points (and where you lose time).
  • Create a “miss list.” Track missed questions by topic area: wiring methods, protection, special occupancies, alarms/low voltage, OSHA/safety, plan reading, and general theory.
  • Fix the cause, not just the answer. Most misses come from misreading, slow lookup, or weak understanding. When you address the cause, your score improves quickly.
  • Practice lookups on purpose. For NEC-based questions, redo the lookup until you can find the right place quickly and consistently.
  • Rotate heavy-weight areas. Don’t study only your comfort zones. Cycle wiring/protection, wiring methods/materials, special occupancies, OSHA/safety, and alarms/limited energy so your prep stays balanced.

How to use the 2 full final exams:

  • Save them for late-stage prep. Finals are most valuable after you’ve improved through multiple practice rounds and targeted review.
  • Simulate test rules. Use only compliant references and follow the open-book restrictions: no scratch paper, no extra materials, no moveable tabs.
  • Review with intention. Your final exams should show you what to tighten: a weak category, a slow question type, or a lookup habit that wastes time.

Quick open-book habits that pay off in Florida:

  • Use the index and structure. The NEC is built for navigation—practice using it like a tool, not a textbook.
  • Know your tables. Many time-consuming questions are table-driven. Practice locating and reading them efficiently.
  • Watch for “allowed vs. required” wording. These are common traps. Practice trains you to slow down just enough to catch the qualifier.
  • Keep momentum. If a question becomes a search spiral, make the best supported choice you can and move forward.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep supports Florida electrical contractor candidates by focusing on what these exams really are: performance tests. You don’t just need knowledge—you need a method that works under time pressure, in an open-book environment, across a wide range of topics.

  • Organized study guidance: Practice exams give you a clear routine, so you always know what to do next.
  • Practice-oriented preparation: Repetition builds faster lookups, stronger pacing, and better accuracy.
  • Trade-focused review: You train applied understanding—how to interpret requirements and choose the best answer under exam conditions.
  • Reference navigation support: Open book becomes an advantage when you practice using your books efficiently and compliantly.
  • Confidence-building structure: Familiarity reduces stress. When you’ve practiced the format repeatedly, test day feels manageable.

This guide is built for working electricians: practice, review, correct, repeat—then rehearse with full finals so you walk into Florida’s exams ready to perform.

FAQ Section

Is the Florida electrical contractor certification exam open book?

Yes. DBPR’s Candidate Information Booklet states the Electrical Contractors Certification exam is offered in two parts (Business and Technical/Safety) and that both parts are open-book exams.

How is the Florida electrical exam structured?

The Candidate Information Booklet states the exam has two parts: a Business section with 50 scored questions (2.5 hours) and a Technical/Safety section with 100 scored questions (5 hours).

What score do I need to pass?

The Candidate Information Booklet states the minimum percentage score needed to pass both the Business section and the Technical/Safety section is 75 percent.

Who administers the Florida electrical exams?

DBPR states the electrical examinations are offered in a computer-based testing format through the department’s examination vendor, Pearson VUE.

Can I bring any book I want since it’s open book?

No. DBPR states candidates are encouraged to bring approved reference materials and that no other references are allowed at the examination site. Florida’s reference list also prohibits handwritten notes and moveable tabs.

What is the Technical/Safety exam time limit for Unlimited Electrical Contractor?

The Candidate Information Booklet lists the Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination as open book with a five-hour time limit and 100 scored questions.

What topics show up on the Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety exam?

The Candidate Information Booklet lists major areas such as general theory, plan reading, wiring/protection, wiring methods/materials, special occupancies, OSHA/safety, life safety/ADA, electrical signs, and alarms/limited energy.

How should I use the two full final exams?

Use them late in your study plan as full dress rehearsals. Take each final timed and uninterrupted, then review your results to target the last weak areas before your scheduled exam date.

Exam Details

The Florida Electrical Contractors Certification examination is administered in two parts: a Business examination and a Technical and Safety examination. Candidates seeking the Unlimited Electrical Contractor certification must satisfy both examination requirements before completing the applicable licensing process.

The Technical and Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows five hours for completion. The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows two and one-half hours.

The Technical and Safety examination measures knowledge across a broad electrical-contracting scope. Candidates should be prepared to interpret electrical codes, fire-alarm standards, life-safety requirements, lightning-protection provisions, OSHA regulations, technical diagrams, tables, formulas, equipment information, and practical installation scenarios.

National Electrical Code preparation may include conductor sizing, ampacity, wiring methods, services, feeders, branch circuits, raceway fill, box fill, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, motors, transformers, generators, emergency systems, standby systems, special occupancies, special equipment, communications systems, and electrical signs.

Fire-alarm preparation may address initiating devices, notification appliances, alarm signals, supervisory signals, trouble signals, circuits, pathways, power supplies, emergency communications, system documentation, inspection, testing, and maintenance.

Life-safety preparation may involve occupancy classifications, occupant loads, exit access, exits, exit discharge, means of egress, emergency lighting, travel distances, fire-protection features, and electrical systems that support occupant protection.

Lightning-protection topics may include air terminals, conductors, bonding, grounding, surge protection, structural protection, installation practices, and inspection requirements.

OSHA preparation may include construction safety, general-industry safety, electrical hazards, personal protective equipment, fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, lockout and tagout, tools, hazard communication, workplace records, and employer responsibilities.

Specialty-system preparation may include telecommunications wiring, structured cabling, electrical advertising signs, sign supports, foundations, neon tubing, electrodes, transformers, concrete mixtures, and field-oriented electrical calculations.

The Business examination focuses on contractor responsibilities and business operations. Preparation may include project administration, contracts, financial management, employment matters, regulatory responsibilities, recordkeeping, business organization, and requirements affecting licensed electrical contractors.

Open Book Test

The Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical and Safety examination is open book. Candidates may use authorized references that comply with the testing-room rules for the applicable examination period.

Open-book testing still requires extensive preparation. Five hours can pass quickly when a candidate is searching through a large technical library. Successful preparation depends on knowing which reference applies to each subject and how that reference is organized.

The professionally highlighted and tabbed books in this package support that process. Tabs provide visible access points to major chapters and code articles, while highlighting helps selected information stand out during study and review.

Candidates should practice using indexes, definitions, tables, chapter headings, diagrams, annexes, exceptions, and cross-references. Important answers may depend on a related definition, table note, exception, or secondary code section, so candidates should read the complete applicable provision.

Useful timed lookup subjects include conductor ampacity, service calculations, feeder calculations, grounding-electrode systems, raceway fill, box fill, motors, transformers, fire-alarm circuits, notification appliances, emergency lighting, means of egress, lightning-protection components, OSHA electrical safety, telecommunications pathways, neon installations, and sign-support requirements.

Authorized references may contain approved highlighting and underlining. Handwritten notes, typewritten notes, loose study sheets, removable page flags, moveable tabs, unauthorized formulas, sample questions, and class notes are not permitted in the examination room.

Candidates should review every tab before test day and practice moving between references without relying entirely on the table of contents. Repeated use of the books can improve familiarity and reduce unnecessary search time.

Prepare for the Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Trade Exam with an online exam preparation course from 1 Exam Prep. Designed for window installers, door installation professionals, remodeling contractors, construction supervisors, and experienced tradespeople, this course provides organized preparation for the technical knowledge required for Florida specialty contractor certification.

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Online Exam Prep Course focuses on the installation, repair, and servicing of residential and commercial windows, exterior doors, and hurricane protection systems. Study topics include Florida building codes, construction estimating, installation techniques, manufacturer specifications, window performance, safety, and construction plan reading.

Florida's construction environment creates unique challenges for window and door contractors. Proper installation requires understanding wind resistance, water intrusion prevention, structural openings, product approvals, flashing, fastening systems, and the performance requirements of building components.

This online course helps students organize their preparation around the examination's major trade knowledge areas and the six technical publications associated with the course.

Whether you have years of field experience or are preparing to pursue Florida specialty contractor certification, structured review can help you strengthen technical knowledge and develop better habits for answering reference-based examination questions.

Product Format: Online Trade Knowledge Exam Prep Course. The six publications listed below are study references and are not included as physical books, rentals, or downloadable copies. This product focuses on trade examination preparation rather than the separate Business and Finance examination.

Exam Details

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is part of the statewide construction contractor certification program administered through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR).

The examination evaluates a candidate's knowledge of window and door installation practices, materials, construction requirements, and professional trade responsibilities.

  • License Classification: Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor
  • Trade Examination: Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Trade Knowledge
  • Number of Questions: 55
  • Question Format: Multiple choice
  • Examination Format: Open book
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Construction Industry Licensing Board
  • Additional Examination: Business and Finance

The official trade examination content outline identifies eight major subjects: introduction to window and door installation; tools, equipment, and materials; construction plans and manufacturer specifications; installation techniques; hurricane protection devices and shutters; repair and service; customer service and communication; and health and safety.

Installation techniques and the interpretation of construction plans and specifications are especially important areas of preparation. Candidates should also understand product performance, hurricane protection, proper equipment selection, and repair practices.

The course helps organize these topics into a practical study approach centered on professional window and door installation knowledge.

Open Book Test

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is an open-book test. Candidates may consult authorized reference publications during the examination, subject to Florida's examination-room rules.

Open-book testing rewards familiarity with technical information. Candidates need to recognize the subject of a question, identify the appropriate reference, locate the relevant section, and apply the information correctly.

For example, a question concerning window energy performance may involve concepts covered in Residential Windows: A Guide to New Technologies and Energy Performance. Questions about construction estimating may require familiarity with Walker's Building Estimator's Reference Book.

Installation questions may involve Florida Building Code provisions related to exterior openings, safety glazing, structural requirements, weather protection, or residential construction.

Florida permits underlining and highlighting in authorized reference books. Handwritten and typewritten notes, movable tabs, and unauthorized materials are prohibited. Examination references must also meet applicable binding requirements.

Building Code Edition Information: The course's supplied study reference list includes the 2026 editions of the Florida Building Code - Building and Residential. Florida's examination reference list effective January through December 2026 identifies the 2023 editions as the editions used to develop examination answers. The state allows earlier or later editions of authorized titles at the candidate's risk.

Developing familiarity with authorized references and the organization of technical requirements is an important part of preparing for this examination.

Licensing Steps

Pursuing Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor certification involves meeting professional qualifications, completing required examinations, and submitting the appropriate licensing application.

  1. Understand the License Classification: Review the scope of work associated with window and door installation specialty contracting in Florida.
  2. Review Professional Qualifications: Become familiar with applicable construction experience, financial responsibility, and licensing requirements.
  3. Organize Relevant Experience: Review work involving window installation, door replacement, exterior openings, hurricane protection, repairs, and related construction activities.
  4. Prepare for Trade Knowledge: Study installation techniques, tools, materials, construction specifications, building codes, and safety.
  5. Use the Online Exam Prep Course: Follow a structured approach to reviewing examination subjects.
  6. Review Technical References: Become familiar with the six listed publications and their relevant subject areas.
  7. Prepare for Business and Finance: Address the separate examination covering contractor business and financial responsibilities.
  8. Register for Required Testing: Follow the applicable Florida contractor examination procedures.
  9. Complete the Examinations: Satisfy the examination requirements associated with certification.
  10. Complete the Licensing Application: Submit the required information and meet Florida's remaining certification requirements.

State Requirements

Florida construction contractor licensing is regulated under Chapter 489 of the Florida Statutes and the rules of the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

The Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor classification involves specialized construction work related to installing, replacing, and servicing qualifying window and door systems within the authorized scope of the license.

Contractors working in Florida must understand requirements involving exterior openings, weather protection, wind resistance, safety glazing, installation specifications, and applicable product approvals.

Florida's hurricane exposure makes proper installation especially important. Windows and doors form part of a building's exterior envelope, and their performance depends on appropriate products, fastening methods, flashing, sealing, and installation practices.

Contractors must follow applicable building codes, manufacturer instructions, approved construction documents, and safety regulations.

Applicants must also meet the experience, examination, financial responsibility, and administrative requirements associated with Florida specialty contractor certification.

Reference Books

The online exam preparation course is organized around the following six technical study references. Physical books are not included with this online-only course.

  • Walker's Building Estimator's Reference Book, 33rd Edition, 2024
    A construction estimating publication addressing material quantities, labor, equipment, measurements, construction costs, and project planning. Useful for understanding estimating methods applicable to window and door installation work.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    Contains federal construction safety regulations covering personal protective equipment, ladders, scaffolding, fall protection, power tools, material handling, and jobsite hazards relevant to window and door installers.
  • Contractors Manual, 2025
    Addresses contractor responsibilities, construction business practices, project administration, and professional construction operations. The 2025 edition became the designated examination edition on July 1, 2026.
  • Residential Windows: A Guide to New Technologies and Energy Performance, 2007 (3rd ed.)
    Explores residential window systems, glazing technologies, energy performance, thermal efficiency, materials, design considerations, and factors affecting window selection and performance.
  • Florida Building Code - Building, 2026
    Covers building construction requirements involving exterior openings, structural design, wind resistance, weather protection, safety glazing, and other provisions affecting window and door installation.
  • Florida Building Code - Residential, 2026
    Addresses residential building requirements involving windows, doors, exterior openings, emergency escape and rescue openings, flashing, safety glazing, and weather-resistant construction.

These references support preparation across estimating, safety, window technology, contractor administration, and Florida building requirements.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor examination covers several areas of technical knowledge. Understanding how the subjects connect helps candidates build a more complete preparation strategy.

Introduction to Window and Door Installation: Review professional terminology, industry standards, certification concepts, and code requirements related to hurricane protection.

Tools, Equipment, and Materials: Study common installation tools, fasteners, sealants, flashing materials, window components, door systems, and construction equipment.

Construction Plans and Specifications: Review drawings, dimensions, schedules, manufacturer instructions, installation details, and product requirements.

Installation Techniques: Study opening preparation, fastening, alignment, flashing, sealing, glazing, and proper installation practices.

Hurricane Protection: Review wind-resistant products, hurricane shutters, protection devices, and relevant construction requirements.

Repair and Service: Study common window and door problems, maintenance practices, replacement work, and repair methods.

Customer Communication: Understand project coordination, communicating requirements, and managing installation expectations.

Health and Safety: Review OSHA requirements, safe equipment use, material handling, elevated work, and workplace hazards.

Window and Door Installation Fundamentals

Window and door installation requires careful preparation of structural openings and correct positioning of the selected products.

Installers must understand how windows and doors interact with walls, framing, exterior finishes, and weather-resistant assemblies.

Proper measurements, alignment, fastening, flashing, and sealing contribute to the performance and durability of installed products.

The examination also addresses the relationship between field installation practices and manufacturer's written specifications.

The online course supports review of these fundamentals, helping candidates connect practical construction experience with the technical concepts assessed during testing.

Florida Building Codes and Exterior Openings

Florida's building codes establish important requirements affecting window and door construction.

Depending on the building and installation, relevant subjects include structural openings, safety glazing, emergency escape and rescue openings, accessibility, weather protection, and wind resistance.

Exterior openings must be considered as part of the building envelope, particularly where wind-driven rain and severe weather can affect performance.

Understanding how to locate requirements within the Building and Residential code publications is an important part of open-book examination preparation.

Students should also study the relationship between applicable code provisions, manufacturer instructions, and approved installation details.

Hurricane Protection and Wind-Resistant Installation

Florida's exposure to hurricanes creates demanding performance requirements for exterior windows, doors, and protective devices.

Window and door contractors must understand wind resistance, impact protection concepts, proper fastening, product selection, and installation requirements.

Hurricane shutters and other protection devices form a separate examination subject involving their applications, installation considerations, and relevant construction standards.

Preparation should address how products are secured to a building and how installation details affect their performance under demanding environmental conditions.

Studying these topics supports trade knowledge relevant to both the examination and professional installation work.

Construction Plans and Manufacturer Specifications

Construction drawings and manufacturer specifications provide essential information for window and door installations.

Plans may identify opening dimensions, product types, locations, installation details, and related construction requirements.

Manufacturer specifications address product handling, placement, fasteners, installation procedures, and other details relevant to the selected system.

Installers need to understand how to interpret these documents and apply the appropriate instructions to the work being performed.

The examination emphasizes the ability to understand construction plans, specifications, and installation requirements rather than relying exclusively on memorized procedures.

Window Energy Performance and Residential Technology

Modern windows incorporate glazing technologies, frame materials, and design features that affect energy performance and occupant comfort.

The reference Residential Windows: A Guide to New Technologies and Energy Performance supports study of window efficiency, thermal performance, glazing characteristics, and product selection.

Important concepts include heat transfer, insulation, solar performance, and the relationship between window construction and building energy use.

Understanding these topics can help candidates interpret technical product information and recognize the performance characteristics of residential window systems.

Estimating Window and Door Installation Projects

Estimating is an important part of construction planning and professional project management.

Window and door installation estimates may involve measurements, material quantities, labor, equipment, disposal, and related construction activities.

Walker's Building Estimator's Reference Book provides background for understanding construction quantities, cost calculations, and estimating terminology.

Candidates should be familiar with reading dimensions, identifying project components, and applying construction calculations appropriately.

Developing these skills helps prepare students for estimating-related examination questions and supports broader construction trade knowledge.

OSHA Safety for Window and Door Installers

Window and door installation can involve elevated work, glass handling, ladders, scaffolding, power tools, and construction debris.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 addresses workplace safety requirements relevant to these activities.

Important areas include fall protection, personal protective equipment, safe tool operation, material handling, and hazard recognition.

Safety preparation also includes understanding responsibilities associated with maintaining appropriate working conditions during installation, replacement, and repair projects.

Repair, Replacement, and Service Knowledge

The examination includes knowledge of diagnosing and addressing problems involving windows, doors, and hurricane protection devices.

Common considerations include damaged components, operational difficulties, weather-related deterioration, sealing problems, and installation defects.

Replacement work may require assessing existing openings, removing old products, preparing surfaces, and installing new components according to applicable requirements.

Understanding maintenance and service principles helps candidates recognize how installation quality affects long-term product performance.

It is also relevant for professionals who already own the examination references and want organized trade-focused preparation without purchasing an additional physical book package.

Exam Details

The Florida Gas Line Specialty Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination assesses knowledge associated with natural gas transmission and distribution systems, pipeline installation, joining methods, testing, maintenance, excavation, and safety.

The examination is part of Florida's contractor certification program overseen by the Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

  • Licensing Board: Construction Industry Licensing Board

Candidates should become familiar with pipeline terminology, applicable material standards, underground installation techniques, and requirements associated with safe gas system operation.

Welding, fusion, excavation, and construction safety are especially important areas for structured review because they connect installation quality with pipeline integrity and workplace protection.

Open Book Test

The Florida Gas Line Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is an open-book test. Candidates may consult reference materials authorized for their examination category and scheduled testing period.

Open-book examinations require the ability to identify the technical subject, select the relevant publication, locate the appropriate information, and apply it accurately.

For example, questions about steel line pipe may involve API specifications, while questions about polyethylene gas piping may involve ASTM material standards. Pipeline construction and safety questions may require familiarity with federal regulations or construction safety requirements.

Highlighted and tabbed references help candidates develop familiarity with publication organization and practice finding information efficiently.

Regular practice using indexes, diagrams, technical tables, safety provisions, and specifications supports more efficient reference navigation during examination preparation.

State Requirements

Florida regulates Gas Line Specialty Contractors through the state's construction licensing framework.

Florida Administrative Code Rule 61G4-15.100 defines the Gas Line Specialty Contractor classification.

The scope includes installing, modifying, altering, testing, repairing, and maintaining natural gas transmission and distribution systems and their appurtenances within rights-of-way or easements, or terminating at the meter.

Contractors must understand the limitations of their specialty classification and comply with applicable gas transportation safety, construction, and utility requirements.

Technical responsibilities include appropriate pipeline materials, construction methods, testing, excavation practices, and underground facility damage prevention.

Federal pipeline safety regulations and Florida Public Service Commission rules provide regulatory information relevant to natural gas transportation systems.

Prepare for the Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor License Exam with a complete 12-reference trade book set covering underground and aboveground storage tanks, petroleum storage systems, tank installation, vapor recovery, leak detection, tank closure, excavation safety, and environmental protection.

The Florida Pollutant Storage Contractor Exam Complete Book Set - Trade Books brings together industry standards, federal regulations, Florida environmental rules, construction references, and professional technical guides to support preparation for the Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination.

Pollutant storage contracting requires specialized knowledge of tank systems used to store petroleum products and other regulated substances. Contractors must understand site preparation, storage tank components, piping connections, excavation, backfill, anchorage, testing, corrosion protection, and safe construction practices.

This collection includes technical resources from the Petroleum Equipment Institute (PEI), the American Petroleum Institute (API), the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), and federal and Florida regulatory authorities.

Designed for experienced petroleum equipment installers, underground storage tank professionals, environmental contractors, construction supervisors, and individuals pursuing Florida contractor certification, this package provides an organized foundation for studying pollutant storage systems.

The references address the different stages of a storage tank project's lifecycle, from planning and installation to inspection, maintenance, closure, and removal.

Product Type: Complete physical trade-reference book set containing 12 listed reference items. This package does not include an online exam preparation course, highlighted-and-tabbed preparation, or licensing application services.

Exam Details

The Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination evaluates technical knowledge associated with pollutant storage tank construction, equipment installation, system maintenance, safety, and environmental requirements.

The examination is part of Florida's construction contractor certification program, overseen by the Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

  • Examination: Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor Trade Knowledge
  • Licensing Authority: Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation
  • Licensing Board: Construction Industry Licensing Board
  • Examination Format: Open book
  • Question Format: Multiple choice
  • Examination Delivery: Computer-based testing
  • Examination Registration: Professional Testing, Inc.
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE
  • Additional Certification Examination: Business and Finance

The trade examination covers practical knowledge of tank installations, underground construction, material handling, piping systems, safety devices, leak detection, corrosion protection, and tank removal.

Florida's examination content outline includes the following areas:

  • Pre-installation and site preparation
  • Material handling
  • Excavating
  • Supports and anchorage
  • Backfill
  • Tank installation
  • Piping, valves, and fittings
  • Above-tank covering
  • Leak detection
  • Cathodic protection systems
  • Tank removal and abandonment
  • Equipment

These subjects require an understanding of construction procedures, technical standards, system components, and the environmental responsibilities associated with storage tank work.

Open Book Test

The Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor Trade Knowledge Examination is an open-book test. Candidates may use reference publications authorized for the examination category and their scheduled testing period.

Open-book testing requires more than possessing technical manuals. Candidates must understand the question, identify the appropriate reference, locate relevant information, and apply the correct standard or installation principle.

Questions involving underground tank installation may require familiarity with PEI/RP100. Aboveground storage system questions may involve PEI/RP200, while vapor recovery topics may involve PEI/RP300.

Questions about flammable liquids and motor fuel dispensing facilities may require knowledge of NFPA 30 and NFPA 30A.

Florida publishes official examination reference lists identifying which publications are authorized for each testing period. Candidates must use the approved list applicable to their scheduled examination when selecting books for examination-room use.

Practicing with indexes, illustrations, installation details, technical definitions, and regulatory provisions helps candidates develop stronger reference-navigation habits.

A coordinated book set makes it easier to study related storage tank subjects together and recognize the publications that address different technical responsibilities.

Licensing Steps

Florida Certified Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor licensing involves technical examination requirements and professional qualifications established through the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

  1. Understand the Contractor Classification: Review the authorized work associated with Florida Pollutant Storage Systems Contractor certification.
  2. Evaluate Licensing Qualifications: Review applicable experience, education, and professional requirements.
  3. Organize Trade Experience: Document relevant tank installation, maintenance, excavation, environmental construction, or supervisory experience.
  4. Prepare for Trade Knowledge: Study storage tank systems, site preparation, installation methods, piping, leak detection, and safety.
  5. Review Technical References: Become familiar with the 12 listed publications and their principal subjects.
  6. Practice Reference Navigation: Locate installation procedures, safety provisions, technical diagrams, and regulatory requirements.
  7. Prepare for Business and Finance: Study the separate examination addressing contractor business responsibilities.
  8. Register for Testing: Complete the applicable Florida construction examination registration process.
  9. Complete Required Examinations: Satisfy the examination requirements associated with certification.
  10. Apply for Certification: Submit the appropriate licensing application and meet remaining qualifications.

Structured trade examination preparation helps candidates connect field experience with the published standards and construction requirements associated with pollutant storage systems.

State Requirements

Florida regulates Pollutant Storage Systems Contractors under Chapter 489 of the Florida Statutes.

The classification covers installing, maintaining, repairing, altering, extending, and performing legally authorized design work involving pollutant storage tanks and related materials and components.

Florida law requires pollutant storage tank installations to comply with the applicable standards adopted under the state's environmental regulations.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection regulates petroleum storage systems through rules that address underground and aboveground storage facilities.

Chapter 62-761 of the Florida Administrative Code addresses underground storage tank systems, while Chapter 62-762 addresses aboveground storage tank systems.

Contractors must understand applicable installation standards, inspection requirements, environmental protection procedures, and safety practices associated with regulated storage systems.

Certification also involves meeting the applicable examination, experience, financial responsibility, insurance, and administrative requirements.

State Requirements

Florida

To become a licensed contractor in Florida, you are required to:

  • Pass a state certification examination (Florida Business & Finance and Trade Knowledge exams).
  • Be at least 18 years old.
  • Prove that you are financially stable. (credit score of 660 or higher; otherwise, you must obtain a licensing bond).
  • Present evidence of liability and workers' compensation insurance.
  • Demonstrate good moral character.
  • NOT have any outstanding debts owed to the state (related to construction).
  • Comply with IRS rules by providing your federal employer identification number or social security number (if you are an individual).
  • Fulfill the experience/education requirements (as applicable).
  • Submit an electronic fingerprint.
Click Here to Get Insured. Talk to a Licensing Expert Application Assistance Package
Scope of Work

Residential Contractor means a contractor whose services are limited to construction, remodeling, repair, or improvement of one-family, two-family, or three-family residences not exceeding two habitable stories above no more than one uninhabitable story and accessory use structures in connection therewith.


Applications

Applications for the Florida Residential Contractor License must be submitted to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation. For application instructions and assistance, call 850-487-1395. The application process includes proof of financial stability, insurance coverage details, and electronic fingerprinting among other requirements.


Reciprocity

Florida has a limited form of reciprocity with other states. If you have passed the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors, you may be exempt from the Florida Trade Knowledge exam. You are still required to pass the Florida Business and Finance exam and fulfill other specific state requirements.


Continuing Education

Florida requires all licensed contractors to complete 14 hours of continuing education during each biennial renewal period. This education must include 1 hour on workplace safety, 1 hour on workers' compensation, 1 hour on business practices, 1 hour on laws and rules, 1 hour on wind mitigation, and the remaining hours on general subjects.


Exam

To obtain a Florida Residential Contractor license, you must pass two exams: the Florida Business and Finance exam and the Trade Knowledge exam. These exams cover topics such as financial management, contract administration, project management, safety, building codes, and specialty contracting practices. The exams are administered by Professional Testing, Inc. (PTI).


Training

Training for the Florida Residential Contractor exam is available through various providers, offering courses that include both Business and Finance and Trade Knowledge preparation. These courses are designed to help applicants pass their exams on the first attempt by providing them with the necessary knowledge and test-taking strategies.

Exam Details

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor Trade Knowledge examination is composed of 50 questions. It is administered in one computer-based testing session.

Questions are multiple choice and may be based on the approved references, field experience, basic mathematics, and knowledge of accepted trade practices. The official examination content outline identifies eight major subject areas.

Introduction to Window and Door Installation accounts for approximately 7% of the examination. This area includes certification, standards, licensure, contractor responsibilities, legal considerations, and the scope of work associated with the specialty classification.

Tools, Equipment, and Materials account for approximately 14.5%. Candidates should understand commonly used hand tools, power tools, measuring devices, access equipment, fasteners, sealants, flashing materials, shims, anchors, glazing-related materials, and other products used during installation and service work.

Construction Plans, Specifications, and Manufacturers’ Specifications account for approximately 18%. Candidates should be prepared to read construction documents, identify relevant details, interpret installation requirements, and adjust installation practices to match product specifications and approved construction plans.

Installation Techniques account for approximately 22%. This is the largest content area. It includes pre-installation procedures, exterior window and door installation, retrofit work, replacement of window bucks, flashing, sealing, finishing, alignment, adjustment, and methods used to achieve proper operation.

Hurricane Protection Devices and Shutters account for approximately 14.5%. Candidates should understand different types of hurricane-protection systems, applicable installation methods, anchoring considerations, code requirements, and standards affecting protective products.

Repair and Service account for approximately 11%. This area includes diagnosing problems, repairing windows and doors, servicing hurricane-protection devices, maintaining operating components, and correcting installation-related issues.

Customer Service and Communication account for approximately 4%. Candidates may be tested on communicating with customers, understanding project expectations, managing timelines, explaining work, and maintaining professional jobsite relationships.

Health and Safety account for approximately 9%. Topics may include personal protective equipment, ladders, scaffolds, fall hazards, tools, material handling, emergency procedures, jobsite housekeeping, and disposal of construction debris.

The percentages shown in the official examination outline may vary slightly. Candidates should prepare for questions from every content area rather than concentrating only on the largest categories.

Open Book Test

Only one copy of each approved reference may be brought into the testing room. The examination questions are based on the editions listed for the applicable testing period, although some questions may also rely on practical experience and accepted trade knowledge.

Original-edition books are required unless a particular reference is officially identified as an authorized printable document. All printed references must remain securely bound during the examination.

References containing underlining or highlighting may be used. Handwritten notes and typewritten notes are not permitted. Existing notes must be removed or completely blacked out so they cannot be read.

Moveable tabs, removable page flags, loose study pages, unbound materials, writing tablets, and electronic tablets are not allowed. Candidates may not make marks in the references during the examination.

Exam Details

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor examination is associated with the statewide certification administered by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

The examination pathway evaluates both trade knowledge and the business and financial management responsibilities of a contracting firm.

  • License Classification: Certified Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor.
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.
  • Trade Examination: Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractors Trade Knowledge.
  • Trade Examination Questions: 55 multiple-choice questions.
  • Trade Examination Time Limit: 2 hours and 30 minutes.
  • Additional Examination: Business and Finance.
  • Passing Standard: 70% on each required examination.
  • Examination Format: Open book.
  • Trade Examination Delivery: Computer-based testing.

The trade examination emphasizes installation methods, manufacturer instructions, hurricane protection devices, materials, tools, repair procedures, and workplace safety.

Technical questions also evaluate candidates' ability to interpret construction plans, identify installation conditions, and apply sound trade practices.

Open Book Test

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor examination is an open book test. Florida permits candidates to use reference publications authorized for the examination.

Open book does not mean that every answer can be found quickly. Candidates need to understand terminology, recognize the construction issue involved, and know where to look for related information.

A question involving impact-resistant window installation may require a different reference section from one addressing general material estimating, workplace safety, or residential construction requirements.

Authorized books must comply with Florida's examination-room policies. Reference materials must remain properly bound. Underlining and highlighting are permitted, but handwritten and typewritten notes are not allowed.

Moveable tabs are prohibited, and candidates cannot add markings to references during the examination. Only one copy of each authorized reference is permitted.

Practice using chapter headings, indexes, illustrations, tables, and product installation terminology. Learn how to distinguish a manufacturer's installation requirement from a general construction code provision.

ACE encourages candidates to strengthen reference-navigation skills through targeted review, explanation-based practice, and better organization of technical subjects.

Licensing Steps

Becoming a Florida Certified Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor involves completing the examinations and satisfying the state's professional certification requirements.

  1. Understand the certification: Review the authorized specialty scope involving exterior windows, exterior doors, hurricane protection devices, shutters, and related hardware.
  2. Evaluate your qualifications: Review qualifying construction experience, foreman responsibilities, college education, or applicable military experience.
  3. Gather supporting documents: Organize records of installation experience, employment, and construction responsibilities.
  4. Prepare for Trade Knowledge: Study installation procedures, materials, specifications, hurricane shutters, repair work, and safety.
  5. Prepare for Business and Finance: Review contractor accounting, contracts, estimating, and financial management.
  6. Review authorized books: Become familiar with the designated building codes, estimating publication, safety standards, and window reference.
  7. Complete examination requirements: Follow the state's applicable registration, authorization, scheduling, and testing procedures.
  8. Apply for certification: Submit the appropriate application through Florida DBPR.
  9. Complete remaining qualifications: Provide required documentation and satisfy the applicable financial responsibility, background screening, and insurance conditions.

Florida identifies application CILB 5-AP for individuals seeking this specialty certification and CILB 6-AP for contractors qualifying a business.

The ACE free demo provides examination preparation support rather than contractor application processing or professional licensing services.

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractors under Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, and Florida Administrative Code Rule 61G4-15.100.

A Certified Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractor is authorized to install, replace, adjust, repair, and service exterior windows and doors, hurricane protection devices, shutters, and associated hardware.

Work must follow accepted engineering information and applicable manufacturer specifications. The specialty does not authorize structural alterations, except for replacement of window bucks during retrofit work as permitted by its defined scope.

The classification differs from the broader Building Contractor and General Contractor classifications. Its purpose is to provide specialized contracting authority for the defined window, door, and hurricane protection work.

Florida provides multiple qualification pathways involving construction experience and education. One pathway recognizes four years as a worker or foreman, including at least one year as a foreman. Other pathways recognize approved combinations of college education, work experience, and qualifying military service.

Applicants must satisfy the applicable examination, professional qualification, character, and financial responsibility requirements.

Understanding the limits of the specialty license is important for professionals working on projects that also involve structural framing, electrical equipment, masonry, or other separately regulated construction activities.

Florida's building environment makes wind resistance, appropriate product selection, approved installation details, and weather protection especially important subjects for this trade.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida Window and Door Installation Specialty Contractors Trade Knowledge examination covers eight major content areas.

Introduction to Window and Door Installation – 7%: Review certification responsibilities, licensing requirements, professional scope, standards, and regulatory considerations.

Tools, Equipment, and Materials – 14.5%: Study equipment selection, measuring tools, fastening products, sealants, glazing components, and common installation materials.

Construction Plans, Specifications, and Manufacturer Instructions – 18%: Practice interpreting drawings and manufacturer details, recognizing installation conditions, and applying product specifications.

Installation Techniques – 22%: Review pre-installation preparation, exterior window and door installation, replacement of window bucks, finishing, flashing, sealing, adjustment, and alignment.

Hurricane Protection Devices and Shutters – 14.5%: Study hurricane protection products, fastening methods, installation requirements, and applicable construction standards.

Repair and Service – 11%: Review diagnosing performance problems, adjusting components, repairing hardware, and maintaining windows and doors.

Customer Service and Communication – 4%: Study customer expectations, project communication, scheduling, and service responsibilities.

Health and Safety – 9%: Review safe tool operation, personal protection, handling construction materials, disposal procedures, and emergency practices.

Installation Techniques is the largest category, accounting for 22% of the trade examination. Construction Plans and Specifications represents another 18%, making installation knowledge and document interpretation particularly valuable study priorities.

Window Installation and Retrofit Techniques

Exterior window installation requires attention to openings, dimensions, alignment, fastening, and weather protection.

Study the steps involved in preparing an opening and evaluating existing construction conditions.

Review window frames, shims, anchors, sealants, flashing, and related installation materials.

Become familiar with the differences between installing windows in new construction and replacing windows in existing buildings.

Retrofit projects may involve removing existing products and replacing window bucks within the specialty's authorized scope.

Practice interpreting installation diagrams that identify anchor spacing, edge distances, fastener types, and permitted substrate conditions.

Understanding these concepts helps connect hands-on installation experience with questions involving manufacturer requirements and Florida construction practices.

Exterior Door Installation and Adjustment

Exterior doors must fit their openings, operate correctly, and provide appropriate protection against weather exposure.

Study door frames, jambs, thresholds, hardware, hinges, fastening systems, and weatherstripping.

Review the importance of level, plumb, square, and appropriate alignment during installation.

Become familiar with adjustment procedures involving hinges, locks, latches, and door operation.

Practice recognizing how improper flashing, fastening, or sealing can contribute to performance problems.

Door installation questions often involve multiple components, making careful interpretation of specifications and product details an important preparation skill.

Hurricane Protection and Shutter Systems

Florida's wind exposure makes hurricane protection a significant part of window and door installation work.

Study hurricane shutters, impact-resistant products, opening protection concepts, and attachment methods.

Review how installation requirements depend on the product, supporting substrate, fastener selection, and approved construction details.

Become familiar with the differences between various shutter systems and their installation considerations.

Practice reading product approval information and identifying the construction conditions associated with a permitted installation.

Hurricane Protection Devices and Shutters represents 14.5% of the examination outline, so this subject deserves consistent attention during study.

Construction Plans and Manufacturer Specifications

Effective window and door installation depends on correctly interpreting the technical information associated with each product.

Study plans, elevations, schedules, opening dimensions, and product installation diagrams.

Reference books cannot contain additional loose or attached papers. Candidates must bring their own authorized reference materials.

PSI permits a silent, battery-operated, nonprinting, nonprogrammable calculator without an alphabetic keyboard.

Florida's licensing framework distinguishes between Certified Electrical Contractors, who hold broader electrical contracting authority, and specialty electrical contractors whose authorized work is limited to their classification.

Applicants pursuing initial Florida electrical contractor licensure without a qualifying license from another jurisdiction must follow Florida's applicable examination and licensing process.

Florida also requires applicants to satisfy the applicable endorsement qualifications and provide the documentation required by the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

Exam Details

The Florida Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Principle and Practice Licensure Examination contains 50 scored questions. The examination is computer based and is administered through Pearson VUE for the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

The official examination content outline is divided as follows:

  • Building Construction Standards: 13 questions, 26%
  • Contracting: 5 questions, 10%
  • Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board: 22 questions, 44%

This category includes Chapter 468, Part XII, Florida Statutes; Rule 61G19, Florida Administrative Code; Chapter 455, Florida Statutes; and Chapter 112, Part III, Florida Statutes.

Building Construction Standards account for 13 questions. This section includes Chapter 553, Florida Statutes; Rule 61-41, Florida Administrative Code; Chapter 760, Part II, Florida Statutes; the 2023 Florida Building Code - Accessibility; and the 2023 Florida Building Code - Energy Conservation.

Open Book Test

The Florida Principle and Practice examination is an open-book test based on the approved reference materials identified for the examination.

Open-book testing makes organization and reference navigation extremely important. The reference list is much larger than the reference list for many technical trade examinations, and candidates may need to move quickly between Florida Statutes, Florida Administrative Code chapters, federal regulations, and Florida Building Code volumes.

Candidates should become familiar with the titles and purposes of each reference before test day. For example, questions involving building code administrators and inspectors should lead toward Chapter 468 and Rule 61G19, while professional regulation questions may require Chapter 455. Ethics questions can point toward Chapter 112, Part III.

Florida DBPR examination rules allow highlighting and permanent tabs with normal chapter headings in approved reference materials, subject to the examination's current reference-material rules. Handwritten or typewritten notes in examination references are prohibited.

The goal of preparation should be to recognize the subject first and then open the correct reference. Searching several books for every question can consume valuable exam time.

  3. Submit the required application to DBPR. Applicants seeking certification through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board must complete the appropriate state application.

  5. Prepare for the Principle and Practice examination. Review the official statutes, administrative rules, code volumes, professional licensing laws, ethics provisions, and regulatory topics.
  6. Schedule the examination. Authorized candidates use the applicable Pearson VUE process to schedule the Florida Principle and Practice examination.

Practice exams turn studying into performance training. Instead of spending your prep time only reading and hoping you remember it, you build the exam rhythm you’ll rely on: read → identify the topic → confirm the controlling requirement → answer → move on. That’s how you make the NEC feel usable under a clock.

Trusted by 50k electricians reflects what consistently works for skilled-trades testing: repetition. When you work enough exam-style problems, you stop getting surprised by wording, you stop wasting time searching, and you start answering with calm confidence because you’ve already practiced the exact process you’ll use on test day.

Exam Details

Florida journeyman electrician exams are commonly administered through local jurisdictions and certificate programs. Many of these exams are NEC-centered and written to evaluate practical installation knowledge across core journeyman areas, including services, feeders, branch circuits, wiring methods, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, equipment rules, special occupancies/conditions, and jobsite safety.

Because jurisdiction requirements vary, candidates typically see a similar style of journeyman exam content even when the administrative details differ. This prep is built around the most transferable, high-impact exam skills:

  • NEC navigation and interpretation: knowing where the rules live and how to apply them correctly to a scenario.
  • Calculation discipline: setting up math cleanly and avoiding avoidable errors under time pressure.
  • Careful reading: recognizing the “one word” that changes the answer (required vs permitted, minimum vs maximum, or a condition that triggers a different rule).
  • Time management: staying on pace across a full exam sitting.

This guide supports those skills through repeated testing. Each exam you take gives you a measurable view of what needs improvement—where you’re losing points, where you’re losing time, and what topics should be your next focus.

Open Book Test

You noted “open book,” and that is consistent with how many Florida jurisdiction exams are administered. For example, Miami-Dade County states that the tests it administers for contractor and trades licensing are open book and timed.

Open book is a major advantage only when you train for it the right way. The exam is not designed for you to slowly look up every answer. It rewards the electrician who can confirm details quickly and keep moving.

What open-book success looks like under real test conditions:

  • Keyword recognition: Identify the key term that points to the right NEC article/table before you touch the book.
  • Fast confirmation: Use your reference to verify the one requirement you need, then answer and move on.
  • Exception awareness: Many wrong answers happen when an exception flips the rule. Practice teaches you to check exceptions consistently.
  • Time discipline: Don’t let one question steal five others. Keep momentum and return only if time allows.

This study guide is built specifically for open-book performance because practice is what makes open book work. The more you repeat the cycle of question → lookup → confirm → answer, the more efficient your navigation becomes and the less time you waste searching.

Licensing Steps

Because Florida journeyman credentials are often issued through local jurisdictions, the steps can vary. A practical pathway many electricians follow looks like this:

  1. Identify the jurisdiction where you will test and work. Confirm the authority that issues the journeyman certificate or license you need.
  2. Meet eligibility requirements. Ensure your work history, apprenticeship documentation, and any required supervision align with that jurisdiction’s standards.
  3. Apply to test. Submit the required application and supporting documentation for approval to schedule.
  4. Schedule your exam. Follow the scheduling process for your local testing program.
  5. Prepare with timed practice. Use practice exams to build speed, accuracy, and pacing in open-book conditions.
  6. Take and pass the exam. Demonstrate NEC-based decision-making under timed conditions.
  7. Complete issuance steps. Finalize any remaining jurisdiction requirements to receive your journeyman credential and maintain it.

This guide supports the step you control the most: exam performance. When your prep is structured around realistic practice, test day feels familiar instead of intimidating.
