Many electricians pursue journeyman certification through a county or city licensing program while state-level electrical contractor licensing is handled through Florida’s professional licensing system.

For journeyman test prep, the most useful approach is to build portable skills that apply across Florida jurisdictions:

  • NEC comfort: knowing how the code is organized and how questions point you to the right location.
  • Scenario interpretation: understanding what the question is actually asking (and what it isn’t asking).
  • Accuracy habits: checking exceptions, reading every qualifier, and selecting the best code-supported answer.
  • Clock management: protecting time so you can finish strong.

This product is written to strengthen those fundamentals so you can sit for your Florida journeyman exam with a method you trust.

Test Information and Study Materials

Timed exams reward performance, not intention. The fastest way to improve performance is to practice the same job the exam demands—then review what you missed until you stop missing it. That’s why this guide includes 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams: enough repetition to build real momentum.

Use the exams in a score-building progression:

  • Phase 1: Baseline and weak-area map (Practice Exams 1–4). Take your first practice exams at a steady pace. Track what you miss and what slows you down. Don’t just mark “wrong”—mark why: misread wording, missed exception, slow lookup, wrong table, rushed math, or concept gap.
  • Phase 2: Build your open-book rhythm (Practice Exams 5–8). Tighten your routine. For each question: identify the topic → go to the most likely code area → confirm the controlling requirement → answer → move on. Your goal is fewer “wandering lookups.”
  • Phase 3: Train pacing under pressure (Practice Exams 9–12). Add realistic timing. Practice skipping and returning. Learn how to keep momentum when a question turns into a time sink.
  • Phase 4: Prove readiness (2 Full Final Exams). Take each final exam in one sitting, timed and distraction-free. Treat it like your dress rehearsal. Review every missed question and fix the pattern before your actual exam date.

The review routine that raises scores:

  • Find the controlling rule for every missed question and read it carefully, including exceptions and definitions.
  • Label the cause of the miss so you stop repeating it (misread, missed exception, slow search, wrong table, rushed calculation).
  • Redo the lookup until you can find the answer quickly and confidently.
  • Retest soon so the correction becomes a habit.

Where journeyman candidates often gain points fastest:

  • Wiring methods and materials: these questions often hinge on one condition. Practice reduces detail-based misses.
  • Branch circuits and conductors: speed improves when you recognize which rules and tables are most likely in play.
  • Grounding and bonding: repetition helps you catch the wording and exceptions that change the answer.
  • Overcurrent protection: disciplined confirmation prevents costly errors.
  • Special occupancies and conditions: repeated exposure reduces surprises and overthinking.

By the time you reach the final exams, the goal is simple: the exam experience should feel familiar—familiar pacing, familiar question style, and a workflow you’ve practiced enough times to trust.

Yes. Open-book exams reward speed and accuracy. Practice exams train you to find answers efficiently, confirm exceptions, and keep your pace steady under timed conditions.

Take a practice exam, review every missed question by locating the controlling rule, label the cause of the miss (misread, missed exception, slow lookup, wrong table, rushed math), then retest. Repetition plus targeted review is where scores climb fastest.

Use them near the end of your study plan as full dress rehearsals. Take each final timed and uninterrupted, then review every missed question and target those weak areas before your scheduled exam date.

No. Results depend on your preparation, experience, and performance on exam day. This guide is designed to make your prep more effective by improving open-book speed, accuracy, and pacing through realistic practice exams.

Exam Details

The Florida Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor examination is part of the state's construction contractor certification program administered through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

The standard examination pathway includes Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractors Trade Knowledge and Business and Finance.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor.
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.
  • Trade Examination: Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractors Trade Knowledge.
  • Additional Examination: Business and Finance.
  • Examination Format: Open book, multiple choice.
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing.
  • Trade Content Areas: Eight structural carpentry and construction subjects.

The trade examination evaluates construction fundamentals, safety, estimating, structural carpentry, trusses, floor systems, doors, windows, metal framing, and exterior finishes.

The Business and Finance examination addresses the administrative, legal, and financial responsibilities associated with operating a contracting business.

Open Book Test

The Florida Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor examination is an open book test. Candidates may use the reference materials authorized by Florida DBPR for the applicable examination.

Open book testing requires preparation because candidates must identify the subject of each question, select the appropriate publication, and locate relevant technical information efficiently.

For example, questions involving truss bracing may require a specialized truss safety guide. Questions about roof framing, exterior weather protection, or construction alterations may involve Florida Building Code provisions.

Authorized reference books must remain properly bound. Underlining and highlighting are permitted, but handwritten and typewritten notes are prohibited.

Moveable tabs, unauthorized loose materials, and electronic reference tablets are not permitted. Candidates cannot add markings to references during examination administration.

Develop familiarity with indexes, technical diagrams, construction tables, and reference organization before testing.

Licensing Steps

Becoming a Florida Certified Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor involves completing the required examinations and satisfying the state's professional certification requirements.

  1. Understand the classification: Review the authorized scope of structural carpentry, wood products, metal framing, doors, windows, and trusses.
  2. Evaluate your experience: Review your framing background, construction responsibilities, supervisory duties, and relevant education.
  3. Organize documentation: Gather records describing qualifying carpentry work and professional construction experience.
  4. Study Trade Knowledge: Prepare for structural framing, floor systems, engineered trusses, metal framing, estimating, and safety.
  5. Prepare for Business and Finance: Review contractor accounting, contracts, financial management, and business responsibilities.
  6. Study authorized references: Review the designated construction manuals, truss publications, OSHA regulations, and building codes.
  7. Complete examination requirements: Follow the applicable examination application, authorization, and scheduling procedures.
  8. Apply for certification: Submit the appropriate specialty contractor application through Florida DBPR.
  9. Complete licensing qualifications: Satisfy applicable experience, financial responsibility, insurance, and background screening requirements.

Examination preparation and professional licensing are separate parts of the certification process. The ACE free demo provides educational study support rather than examination registration or application services.

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractors under Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, and Florida Administrative Code Rule 61G4-15.100.

A Florida Certified Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor is authorized to install wood products or metal framing in a building structure, including rough framing, doors, windows, and structural trusses.

This classification focuses on the structural carpentry trade rather than the broader responsibilities of a General Contractor or Building Contractor.

Work that belongs to another separately regulated trade requires the appropriate professional authorization.

Applicants must meet Florida's applicable examination, professional qualification, character, financial responsibility, and insurance requirements.

Experience involving framing, truss placement, floor assemblies, and related construction work is relevant to understanding the technical responsibilities of this specialty.

Contractors must follow applicable Florida building codes, approved plans, manufacturer installation instructions, and project-specific engineering requirements.

Understanding the limits of the structural carpentry classification helps candidates connect examination preparation with the responsibilities of operating a licensed construction business.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida Structural Carpentry Specialty Contractor trade examination evaluates eight content areas.

Fundamentals – 4%: Review carpentry responsibilities, types of wood products, load-bearing structures, and interior finishing concepts.

Safety – 7%: Study OSHA regulations, ladder safety, truss rigging, fall protection, temporary bracing, and construction hazards.

Estimating and Plan Reading – 7%: Review labor and material estimating, drawing scales, construction details, specifications, and plan interpretation.

Structural Carpentry – 25.5%: Study lumber, engineered wood, straps, connectors, stairs, handrails, permanent bracing, blocking, subfloors, wall systems, and roof assemblies.

Structural Trusses and Floor Systems – 25.5%: Review conventional framing, engineered trusses, truss placement, bracing, connections, roof systems, and floor layouts.

Doors and Windows – 9%: Study opening preparation, door and window bucks, fasteners, shimming, waterproofing, and product approvals.

Metal Framing – 13%: Review steel framing members, structural walls, nonbearing partitions, steel gauges, connections, and bracing.

Exterior Finishes – 9%: Study thermal protection, moisture barriers, rainscreen systems, siding materials, and installation practices.

Florida Sign Specialty Contractor exam prep involves learning to connect field experience with code requirements, technical calculations, and professional responsibilities.

Exam Details

The Florida Sign Specialty Contractor examination is part of the certification program administered by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

The official examination category is Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor. Certification requires examination in both business knowledge and technical and safety subjects.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor.
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.
  • Technical Examination: Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety.
  • Technical Examination Questions: 100 scored multiple-choice questions.
  • Technical Examination Time Limit: 5 hours.
  • Business Examination: Electrical Contractors Business Examination.
  • Business Examination Questions: 50 scored multiple-choice questions.
  • Business Examination Time Limit: 2 hours and 30 minutes.
  • Examination Format: Open book.
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing.
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE.
  • Required Passing Standard: At least 75% on each examination part.

The Technical/Safety examination evaluates electrical principles, construction drawings, wiring protection, wiring materials, workplace safety, electrical signs, structural considerations, and neon systems.

The Business examination addresses estimating, contracts, accounting, insurance, payroll, personnel management, and Florida contracting laws.

Open Book Test

The Florida Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor examinations are open book tests. Candidates may use reference books authorized by Florida DBPR and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

Open book testing still requires effective preparation. Candidates must identify the technical issue described in a question, choose the appropriate reference, and locate the relevant information efficiently.

For example, electrical sign wiring questions may involve the National Electrical Code, while questions about foundations and sign supports may involve structural engineering or concrete references.

Florida permits permanently attached reference tabs but does not permit removable tabs or loose notes. Handwritten and typewritten notes are prohibited, and candidates cannot add markings during an examination.

Only authorized references may be brought into the testing room, with one copy of each permitted publication.

Practice using indexes, chapter headings, definitions, tables, and technical diagrams. Familiarity with reference organization helps reduce unnecessary searching during timed examinations.

ACE provides educational preparation outside the examination room, supporting code navigation and practice-oriented review.

Licensing Steps

Becoming a Florida Certified Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor involves completing the required examinations and satisfying the state's professional licensing qualifications.

  1. Review the license classification: Understand the authorized scope of electrical signs, non-electrical signs, outline lighting, and related structural work.
  2. Evaluate professional experience: Review your electrical, sign installation, construction, and supervisory experience against the applicable state qualification pathways.
  3. Apply for examination authorization: Submit the Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor examination application through Florida DBPR.
  4. Study Technical/Safety: Prepare for electrical principles, wiring requirements, sign structures, neon systems, and construction safety.
  5. Study Business: Review estimating, contracts, accounting, personnel management, and contractor regulations.
  6. Prepare reference materials: Become familiar with the publications authorized for each examination part.
  7. Complete both examinations: Schedule and take the authorized computer-based examinations through Pearson VUE.
  8. Apply for initial certification: Submit the appropriate specialty electrical contractor licensing application after passing the required examinations.
  9. Complete licensing qualifications: Provide experience records, financial documentation, and other materials required by the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

Florida identifies ECLB 8 for Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor examination applications and ECLB 1 for initial certification following examination.

ACE supports examination preparation and technical learning. The free demo does not include examination registration, application processing, or licensing services.

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates sign specialty electrical contractors under Chapter 489, Part II, Florida Statutes, and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

The Florida Certified Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor classification includes structural fabrication, concrete foundation work, erection, installation, alteration, repair, servicing, and wiring of electrical and non-electrical signs and outline lighting.

The classification covers sign-related electrical work within the limits established by Florida law and administrative rules.

Generally, the scope does not include providing or performing electrical work beyond the last disconnecting means or terminal points.

A specific exception permits qualifying electrical entrance work for independently located remote billboards or signs within the statutory electrical capacity and voltage limitations.

This classification differs from Florida's Unlimited Electrical Contractor license, which authorizes a broader range of electrical contracting activities.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old and satisfy the applicable professional experience and examination qualifications.

The licensing process also includes financial responsibility requirements and supporting documentation reviewed by Florida DBPR.

Understanding the limits of the sign specialty classification is important because not every electrical installation or building modification falls within its authorized scope.

Reference Books

The Florida Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor examination identifies the following technical and business references.

  • Florida Contractors Manual, 2021 Edition
    Provides contractor business, administrative, legal, accounting, insurance, employment, and professional practice information. The designated 2025 edition becomes effective for examination use on August 21, 2027.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, OSHA Parts 1926, 1910, and 1904, July 2020 Edition
    Addresses construction safety, workplace hazards, electrical protection, equipment operation, ladders, occupational recordkeeping, and safe work practices. The July 2025 edition becomes the designated examination edition on August 21, 2027.
  • NFPA 70 – National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition
    Provides electrical requirements for wiring methods, circuits, grounding, bonding, equipment, disconnects, electrical signs, outline lighting, and electrical installations.
  • Engineering Sign Structures: An Introduction to Analysis and Design
    Introduces structural design and analysis concepts involving sign supports, poles, mounting systems, connections, anchors, and foundations.
  • NEON, Techniques and Handling
    Covers neon sign components, tubing, electrodes, transformers, fabrication, handling, installation, maintenance, and safety.
  • Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 16th or 17th Edition
    Explains concrete ingredients, mixture proportioning, placement, curing, strength, durability, and construction practices relevant to sign foundations.

Each reference supports different examination subjects. Become familiar with the content and organization of the publications associated with your examination parts.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination evaluates seven primary content areas.

General Theory and Electrical Principles – 23 to 25 Questions: Review electrical calculations, current, voltage, resistance, power, circuits, conductors, and fundamental electrical concepts.

Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation – 5 to 7 Questions: Study construction drawings, electrical diagrams, symbols, installation requirements, and technical specifications.

Wiring and Protection – 13 to 15 Questions: Review circuit protection, conductor requirements, grounding, bonding, disconnecting means, and electrical safety.

Wiring Methods and Materials – 13 to 15 Questions: Study conduits, raceways, conductors, fittings, boxes, wiring systems, and approved installation practices.

OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing and Use of Tools and Equipment – 9 to 11 Questions: Review workplace hazards, electrical testing, ladders, lifting, tools, and protective equipment.

Electrical Signs, Outline Lighting and Structural Considerations – 26 to 28 Questions: Study illuminated signs, electrical equipment, structural supports, mounting, foundation systems, and installation requirements.

Signs Neon – 4 to 6 Questions: Review neon tubing, transformers, electrode connections, handling, maintenance, and related electrical considerations.

Electrical Signs, Outline Lighting and Structural Considerations is the largest individual content category, followed closely by General Theory and Electrical Principles.

Electrical Theory and National Electrical Code Preparation

Electrical fundamentals are essential for understanding how illuminated signs and outline lighting systems operate.

Study Ohm's law, electrical power, series circuits, parallel circuits, and the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance.

Practice calculations involving electrical loads, conductor sizing, and basic circuit conditions.

Become familiar with the National Electrical Code provisions applicable to electrical signs and outline lighting.

Review disconnecting means, grounding, bonding, wiring methods, equipment protection, and appropriate installation practices.

Understanding the principles behind these requirements helps candidates recognize the purpose of electrical safety provisions instead of relying entirely on memorization.

Electrical Signs and Outline Lighting

Electrical signs represent a major subject on the Florida Sign Specialty Contractor examination.

Study illuminated sign assemblies, lighting equipment, wiring connections, electrical components, and installation methods.

Review how power is supplied to sign equipment and how circuits must be protected within the authorized specialty scope.

Become familiar with service access, disconnect locations, grounding, bonding, and equipment support.

Outline lighting introduces additional considerations involving lighting arrangements, electrical connections, and building-mounted installations.

Practice identifying which National Electrical Code provisions apply to the electrical sign or lighting system described in a question.

Sign Structures, Supports, and Concrete Foundations

Sign installation requires structural knowledge because signs must remain stable under the applicable installation conditions.

Study sign poles, brackets, framing, mounting connections, anchor bolts, and foundation components.

Review basic concepts involving loads, support arrangements, and structural connections.

Become familiar with concrete materials, placement methods, curing, reinforcement concepts, and foundation construction.

Practice interpreting drawings that show support dimensions, connection details, and foundation layouts.

Understanding how structural components work together helps candidates connect installation experience with the technical requirements of sign construction.

Neon Sign Systems and Maintenance

Neon signs are a distinct subject in the Sign Specialty Electrical Contractor examination.

Study neon tubing, electrodes, electrical supplies, transformers, connections, and installation procedures.

Review the handling practices associated with fragile glass tubing and specialized sign components.

Become familiar with maintenance considerations, equipment replacement, and electrical safety involving neon systems.

Practice distinguishing neon installation requirements from those associated with other illuminated sign technologies.

Open Book Test

The Florida Plaster and Lath Specialty Contractor trade examination is an open book test. Candidates may use the reference materials authorized by Florida DBPR for the examination.

Florida's examination rules allow underlining and highlighting in approved reference materials. Handwritten and typewritten notes are not permitted, and movable tabs cannot be used.

References must remain properly bound, and only one copy of each approved reference is permitted in the testing room. Candidates cannot add markings to their references during the examination.

For example, a question concerning plaster coverage or material quantities may require an estimating reference. A question involving scaffold safety may involve OSHA construction standards. Technical questions about lath installation may require an ASTM standard or plastering reference.

The classification also includes authorized work involving boilers, unfired pressure vessels, lift station equipment, mechanical piping, process piping, pneumatic control piping, and other specified mechanical systems.

Florida's mechanical contractor scope includes certain fuel piping installations and specific electrical connections associated with mechanical equipment, subject to statutory limitations.

The classification does not provide unrestricted authority to perform general electrical contracting, potable water piping, sanitary sewer construction, or swimming pool piping work.

Applicants seeking state certification must satisfy an approved qualification pathway involving relevant construction experience, education, or other recognized qualifications.

Prepare for the Florida Roofing Contractor examination with a convenient, repetition-based study tool designed to help keep important roofing knowledge fresh throughout your exam preparation. The Florida Roofing Contractor Exam Prep Study Flash Cards set includes 340 flash cards created for candidates who want a practical way to review roofing concepts, terminology, calculations, systems, safety topics, and trade knowledge while preparing for Florida’s contractor licensing examination.

Florida Roofing Contractor exam preparation can involve a large amount of technical material. Candidates need familiarity with multiple roofing systems, Florida building requirements, estimating concepts, safety practices, waterproofing, drainage, flashing, roof materials, and approved examination references. Flash cards provide a simple way to break that material into smaller review sessions that can be repeated throughout your study schedule.

Instead of relying only on long reading sessions, you can use these 340 Florida Roofing Contractor exam prep flash cards to test recall, reinforce important concepts, and identify areas that deserve additional attention. Work through a small group before or after a longer study session, review difficult cards repeatedly, or use the complete set to help structure your preparation by subject.

The Florida Roofing Contractor Trade Knowledge examination is an open-book, computer-based examination. Open-book testing still requires preparation. Candidates need to recognize roofing concepts and know how to navigate the approved books efficiently. Spending too much examination time searching through unfamiliar references can make even an open-book test challenging.

Flash cards can support that process by helping you become more familiar with the vocabulary, systems, materials, procedures, and technical concepts associated with the roofing trade. When you recognize the subject of a question quickly, you can approach your approved references with a clearer idea of where to locate the information you need.

The 340 Florida Roofing Contractor Exam Prep Study Flash Cards can be used alongside approved reference books, practice questions, exam-preparation courses, field experience, and other study materials. They are intended to add active recall and repetition to your preparation rather than replace comprehensive study of the official examination subjects and references.

Included: 340 Florida Roofing Contractor Exam Prep Study Flash Cards.

Exam Details

The Florida Roofing Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination is administered as a computer-based test. Florida identifies Roofing as a Division II construction specialty. Division II contractors are required to pass the applicable General Trade Knowledge examination and the Business and Finance examination as part of the state certification examination requirements.

The Roofing Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination contains 80 scored questions. Candidates are provided 5 hours to complete the Roofing examination. Florida administers the Roofing examination through daily computer-based testing.

The official roofing examination content outline identifies the following major content areas:

  • Built-Up Roofs: approximately 15%
  • Shingles and Shakes: approximately 15%
  • Architectural Metal Roofs: approximately 10%
  • Single Ply Systems: approximately 15%
  • Modified Roofing Systems: approximately 15%
  • Concrete and Clay Tile Roofs: approximately 10%
  • Membrane Waterproofing: approximately 5%
  • Drains and Gutters: approximately 5%
  • Equipment and Safety: approximately 10%

The state examination content information also identifies several general skills candidates should be prepared to use, including reading and interpreting plans and specifications, reading and interpreting codes, and performing basic mathematics. Mathematical knowledge may involve addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, areas, volumes, fractions, decimals, percentages, triangles, square roots, powers, and simple algebraic equations.

The examination outline covers a broad range of practical roofing knowledge. Examples include roof preparation, fasteners, underlayments, flashing, insulation, ventilation, roof slopes, adhesives, sealants, maintenance, repairs, waterproofing, drainage, OSHA requirements, fall protection, roofing equipment, and installation techniques for multiple roofing systems.

Open Book Test

The Florida Roofing Contractor examination is an open-book test. Florida construction examinations are open book and use approved reference materials established by the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Open book does not mean that candidates may bring unrestricted materials into the testing room. Florida publishes a specific Roofing Contractors Trade Knowledge Exam Reference List identifying the books permitted for examination use. Candidates should prepare with the current approved editions and follow all examination rules concerning reference materials.

For the 2026 Roofing Contractor examination, Florida states that only one copy of each approved reference may be brought into the examination. Original editions are required except where the reference list specifically permits a PDF copy. Approved PDF references must be bound in accordance with examination requirements.

Underlining with pen or highlighter is permitted in approved references. Handwritten and typewritten notes are not allowed. Moveable tabs such as removable flags are not permitted, and candidates may not make marks in references during the examination administration.

Because the examination is open book, reference navigation should be part of your preparation. Become familiar with each book’s table of contents, index, major chapters, roofing-system sections, safety information, code provisions, estimating material, and technical tables. Flash cards can support this process by helping you associate a roofing concept with the type of reference where the answer is likely to be found.

Licensing Steps

Florida Certified Roofing Contractor applicants must complete the state licensing process administered through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Construction Industry Licensing Board. Examination preparation is one important part of that process.

  1. Prepare for the required examinations. Certified Roofing Contractor applicants must pass the state certification examinations required for their contractor category.
  2. Apply for the construction examinations. Florida uses Professional Testing, Inc. to register candidates and administer the construction examination application process.
  3. Complete the General Trade Knowledge examination. Roofing candidates take the 80-question, five-hour Roofing Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination through computer-based testing.
  4. Complete the Business and Finance examination. Roofing is a Division II contractor category, and Division II applicants must also pass Business and Finance.
  5. Submit the appropriate licensing application. After meeting the examination requirements, candidates pursuing certification must complete the applicable Certified Roofing Contractor licensing application.
  6. Document qualifying experience or education and experience. Florida requires Certified Roofing Contractor applicants to satisfy the state’s experience and education requirements.
  7. Complete fingerprinting and background requirements. Applicants must submit fingerprints through an approved Livescan provider as part of the licensing process.
  8. Meet financial responsibility requirements. Florida requires applicable financial and credit documentation for certified contractor applicants.
  9. Meet insurance requirements for active licensure. Applicants seeking an active contractor license must satisfy the insurance requirements applicable to their license category.
  10. Receive state approval for licensure. Passing the examinations does not by itself create a Florida contractor license. The applicant must satisfy all applicable state licensing requirements.

State Requirements

Florida regulates Certified Roofing Contractors through the Construction Industry Licensing Board and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation. Candidates seeking certification must meet both examination and licensing requirements.

Florida’s current licensing information states that applicants for Certified Roofing Contractor licensure are required to have four years of experience or a qualifying combination of college and experience. The state application contains the detailed methods of qualification and documentation requirements.

Roofing experience documentation is an important part of the process. Florida’s roofing experience materials address experience in roofing areas such as shingles, metal, tile, concrete, solar tile, single-ply systems, underlayment, insulation, roof penetrations, parapet walls, flashings, and sheathing or framing repairs.

Applicants must also complete a background check and submit fingerprints through a Livescan Service Provider registered with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Financial responsibility and stability requirements apply, and applicants must submit the documentation required by the state.

For active licensing, applicants must also meet applicable public liability, property damage, and workers’ compensation requirements or qualify for an applicable workers’ compensation exemption.

Florida distinguishes between a Certified Roofing Contractor and a Registered Roofing Contractor. Certified contractors follow the state certification examination process. Registered contractors operate under a different licensing path involving a local certificate of competency. Candidates preparing for the Florida state Roofing Contractor examination should make sure they are following the Certified Roofing Contractor pathway applicable to the examination.

Reference Books

The Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation publishes an official Roofing Contractors Trade Knowledge Exam Reference List. The following references are listed for the Roofing Contractor examination for January through December 2026:

  • Walker’s Building Estimator’s Reference Book, 33rd Edition, 2024
    A construction estimating reference used for calculations, estimating concepts, material quantities, and related construction information.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 Part 1926, July 1, 2025
    The federal construction safety reference addressing workplace safety requirements applicable to construction activities, equipment, access, fall protection, and other jobsite safety subjects.
  • SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual, 7th Edition, January 2012
    A technical reference addressing architectural sheet metal applications, details, flashing, and related construction practices.
  • Roofing Construction and Estimating, 13th Printing, 2022
    A roofing trade reference covering roofing construction methods, materials, estimating, and practical roofing applications.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Membrane Roof System, 2023
    A National Roofing Contractors Association reference addressing membrane roofing systems, design considerations, materials, and installation practices.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Metal Panel and SPF Roof Systems, 2024
    An NRCA technical reference covering metal panel roofing and spray polyurethane foam roof systems.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Steep-Slope Roof Systems, 2025
    An NRCA reference addressing steep-slope roofing systems, materials, details, and installation practices.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Architectural Metal Flashing and Condensation and Air Leakage Control, 2022
    An NRCA reference covering architectural metal flashing and methods associated with condensation and air-leakage control.
  • The NRCA Waterproofing Manual, 2020, 2nd Edition
    A technical waterproofing reference addressing waterproofing systems, applications, materials, and construction considerations.
  • Florida Building Code – Building, 2023
    The Florida building code reference containing construction requirements applicable to roofing systems, roof assemblies, materials, structural considerations, and related building provisions.
  • Florida Building Code – Test Protocols for High Velocity Hurricane Zones, 2023
    Florida testing protocols addressing products and assemblies used in High Velocity Hurricane Zone applications.

Test Information and Study Materials

Preparing for an 80-question, five-hour open-book roofing examination requires more than memorizing definitions. A productive study plan combines knowledge review, approved-reference navigation, calculations, code research, and repeated exposure to the roofing systems listed in the state examination outline.

Use the 340 flash cards in smaller groups rather than trying to master the entire set in one sitting. Create separate piles for material you know well, material that needs occasional review, and material that remains difficult. Spend more time on the difficult group while continuing to revisit stronger subjects periodically.

Study according to the official examination categories. Built-up roofs, shingles and shakes, single-ply systems, and modified roofing systems each represent significant portions of the examination. Candidates should also devote time to architectural metal roofs, concrete and clay tile, membrane waterproofing, drains and gutters, and equipment and safety.

Roofing-system study should include installation methods, underlayments, fastening, adhesives, sealants, flashing, insulation, ventilation, deck preparation, penetrations, roof repairs, waterproofing, drainage, and maintenance. The state outline also includes equipment and OSHA safety knowledge, including ladders, scaffolds, hoists, lift trucks, kettles, heat-welding equipment, roof jacks, compressors, pneumatic equipment, and fall protection.

Calculation practice also deserves regular attention. Roofing contractors frequently work with area, quantities, slopes, materials, percentages, and other mathematical applications. Practice completing calculations without relying only on recognition of a formula.

Finally, practice locating information in the approved books. A candidate who understands a roofing concept and knows which reference contains the relevant information can approach an open-book question more efficiently. Exam Details

The Florida Utility Line Contractor examination is intended to evaluate knowledge related to the work performed by utility line contractors. Candidates should be prepared to work with technical standards, construction practices, safety requirements, electrical information, and utility-industry reference materials.

Florida contractor examinations administered through Prov for participating Florida cities and counties are computer-based, timed examinations. The applicable licensing jurisdiction determines which examination a candidate must take for the license or competency card being pursued. Candidates should follow the examination and licensing instructions issued for the jurisdiction in which they are applying.

Preparation for a utility line contractor examination should emphasize both subject knowledge and reference-book navigation. Questions may require candidates to identify the applicable rule, standard, calculation method, safety requirement, or construction practice and then locate supporting information within an authorized reference.

Strong preparation therefore includes regular practice using indexes, tables of contents, article numbers, chapters, definitions, charts, and technical tables. Candidates who know which book covers a particular subject can move through an open-book examination more efficiently than candidates who are opening their references for the first time on test day.

Open Book Test

Florida contractor examinations administered by Prov for participating local jurisdictions are open book and timed. Authorized reference materials may be used during testing, subject to the testing provider’s reference-material rules and the requirements associated with the candidate’s specific examination.

Open-book testing does not eliminate the need to study. The amount of material contained in the Florida Utility Line Contractor reference library makes familiarity with the books essential. Candidates should know which reference addresses electrical installations, which book contains workplace safety rules, where utility-line practices are discussed, and how technical information is organized within each publication.

Prov permits approved reference materials to be prepared using methods such as highlighting, underlining in ink, and permanent tabs. Reference materials are inspected before candidates are admitted to the testing room. Removable tabs, loose papers, unauthorized notes, and other prohibited materials are not permitted under the testing rules.

A useful study method is to assign each reference a specific purpose. For example, use OSHA regulations when reviewing construction safety, the NEC when practicing electrical code questions, the National Electrical Safety Code when reviewing utility safety standards, and the Lineman’s and Cableman’s Handbook when studying practical utility-line work. This helps develop the habit of going directly to the most relevant book.

Licensing Steps

  1. Identify the license or local contractor credential you are pursuing. Florida cities and counties may establish contractor licensing or competency requirements for work performed within their jurisdictions.
  2. Confirm the required examination with the licensing jurisdiction. Candidates should determine which contractor examination is required before scheduling a test.
  3. Complete any local application or authorization requirements. Follow the instructions provided by the jurisdiction responsible for issuing the contractor credential.
  4. Schedule the required examination. Eligible candidates can schedule testing according to the procedures provided by the examination administrator.
  5. Prepare using the applicable reference materials. Study the books, learn how they are organized, and practice locating information under timed conditions.
  6. Take the required examination. Bring only permitted materials and comply with the testing center’s identification, reference-book, calculator, and examination-security requirements.
  7. Complete the remaining licensing requirements. After testing, follow the instructions of the applicable Florida city, county, or licensing authority to complete the licensing process.

Contractor licensing requirements in Florida depend on the type of work being performed and the jurisdiction regulating that work. Candidates using a Utility Line Contractor examination for local contractor qualification should comply with the requirements established by the Florida city or county in which they are seeking licensure or certification.

Test Information and Study Materials

Utility line contractor preparation should be divided into manageable subject areas rather than approached as one large reading assignment. Begin by identifying what each book is best suited for. OSHA material should become your primary safety resource. The NEC and National Electrical Safety Code should become familiar sources for electrical and utility standards. The Lineman’s and Cableman’s Handbook can support practical trade review, while the concrete reference provides specialized construction-material information.

When studying the National Electrical Code, practice locating information by article rather than trying to memorize every requirement. Learn the arrangement of the NEC, including its chapters, articles, definitions, tables, and index. Pay particular attention to the difference between understanding a subject and knowing where the controlling code requirement can be found.

Review major utility components, line construction practices, equipment, field procedures, and the relationship between technical standards and actual utility installations.

Concrete preparation should include basic familiarity with concrete ingredients, mixture characteristics, production, placement, curing, strength, durability, and quality considerations. Rather than memorizing the entire reference, develop an understanding of its organization so technical questions can be researched efficiently.

FAQ Section

What books are included in the Florida Utility Line Contractor Exam Complete Book Set?

The set includes the Contractors Manual, 2025; Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA); National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023; Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 17th Edition; National Electrical Safety Code 2017; and the Lineman’s and Cableman’s Handbook.

Is the Florida Utility Line Contractor exam open book?

Yes. Florida contractor examinations administered through Prov for participating local jurisdictions are open book and timed. Candidates may use authorized references according to the testing provider’s reference-material rules.

Why do I need several books for one utility line contractor exam?

Utility line contracting combines multiple areas of knowledge. Electrical codes, utility safety standards, OSHA requirements, concrete construction, contractor responsibilities, and practical utility-line procedures are covered by different specialized references. Using several books allows the examination to test a broader range of trade knowledge.

Can I bring highlighted or tabbed books into the exam?

Prov's testing rules allow authorized references to contain highlighting, ink underlining, and permanent tabs. Reference materials must comply with the testing provider’s current rules, and materials are inspected before candidates enter the testing room.

Should I memorize the NEC before taking the exam?

No candidate can realistically depend on memorizing an entire electrical code. A stronger preparation strategy is to understand major electrical concepts while learning the structure of the NEC, including how to use article numbers, the table of contents, definitions, tables, and index to locate requirements efficiently.

What is the difference between the NEC and the National Electrical Safety Code?

They are separate standards with different scopes and applications. Candidates should study both as individual references and become familiar with the types of utility and electrical questions that direct them to one code rather than the other.

How should I study OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926?

Start by learning how the construction regulations are organized. Review major safety subject areas and practice finding individual requirements using the table of contents and regulatory numbering system. The objective is to quickly recognize which portion of the regulation applies to a safety question.

Is the Lineman’s and Cableman’s Handbook useful beyond the examination?

Yes. The handbook contains practical utility-industry information covering line work, systems, equipment, terminology, and field practices. It can serve as both an examination-preparation resource and an ongoing technical reference.

How can I prepare for an open-book contractor exam?

Study the material before test day, organize the authorized books, learn which reference covers each subject, practice using indexes and tables, and complete timed reference-navigation exercises. Open-book success depends heavily on being able to find the correct information efficiently.

Does purchasing the book set complete the Florida licensing process?

No. The book set is intended for examination preparation and reference use. Candidates must separately satisfy the licensing, application, examination, and qualification requirements established by the Florida jurisdiction responsible for the contractor credential they are pursuing.

Florida Sheet Metal Contractor Exam Complete Book Set - Trade Books

Prepare for the Florida Sheet Metal Contractor trade examination with a complete set of technical references covering sheet metal fabrication, HVAC duct construction, architectural sheet metal, air distribution, ventilation, exhaust systems, commercial cooking operations, workplace safety, and Florida mechanical-code requirements.

The Florida Sheet Metal Contractor Exam Complete Book Set brings together the books used to study the major knowledge areas associated with sheet metal contracting. These references support preparation for questions involving metal and flexible duct systems, fibrous glass duct construction, architectural sheet metal details, air-conditioning and heating installations, exhaust systems, commercial kitchen ventilation, duct sizing, jobsite safety, contractor administration, and mechanical-code compliance.

Sheet metal contracting requires a combination of fabrication knowledge, installation skill, plan interpretation, airflow understanding, safety awareness, and code navigation. Candidates may need to work with technical drawings, duct dimensions, fittings, pressure classifications, reinforcement schedules, hangers, supports, joints, seams, insulation, equipment connections, ventilation requirements, and architectural metal details.

The included SMACNA publications form an important part of the trade reference library. The HVAC Duct Construction Standards address metal and flexible duct systems. The Fibrous Glass Duct Construction Standards cover the fabrication and installation of fibrous glass duct systems. The Architectural Sheet Metal Manual provides details for flashing, gutters, downspouts, copings, roof edges, wall systems, and other architectural sheet metal applications.

The NFPA standards support preparation involving air-conditioning and ventilating systems, warm-air heating systems, industrial exhaust systems, and commercial cooking ventilation. The Florida Building Code - Mechanical provides statewide mechanical requirements, while OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports study of construction workplace safety.

The Trane Ductulator supports airflow and duct-sizing calculations. Candidates should become comfortable using it to relate airflow, duct dimensions, velocity, and friction loss. The Contractors Manual provides additional material associated with contractor responsibilities and trade-related business practices.

This product includes the listed trade books. Highlighting, tabbing, online courses, live classes, recorded instruction, flash cards, Business and Finance books, and application services are included only when specifically identified as part of another product package.

What You Get

This Florida Sheet Metal Contractor trade book set includes the following references:

  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926
  • Contractors Manual, 2025
  • NFPA 90A, Standard for the Installation of Air-Conditioning and Ventilating Systems, 2024
  • NFPA 90B, Standard for the Installation of Warm Air Heating and Air-Conditioning Systems, 2027
  • NFPA 91, Standard for Exhaust Systems for Air Conveying of Vapors, Gases, Mists, and Noncombustible Particulate Solids, 2020
  • NFPA 96, Standard for Ventilation Control and Fire Protection of Commercial Cooking Operations, 2024
  • SMACNA Fibrous Glass Duct Construction Standards, 8th Edition
  • SMACNA HVAC Duct Construction Standards, Metal and Flexible
  • SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual, 7th Edition
  • Trane Ductulator, 1976 or later
  • Florida Building Code - Mechanical, 2026

Together, these references provide a broad study library for duct construction, ventilation, exhaust systems, commercial kitchen systems, architectural metal work, air distribution, safety, and Florida mechanical requirements.

Exam Details

The Florida Sheet Metal Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination is administered in a computer-based testing format and contains 80 equally weighted questions. Candidates should prepare for questions that measure both technical trade knowledge and the ability to locate information in approved references.

Examination preparation may involve reading and interpreting plans, specifications, schedules, symbols, dimensions, and construction details. Candidates should be prepared to connect drawing information with fabrication requirements, duct construction standards, equipment conditions, and code provisions.

Duct-construction subjects may include rectangular, round, and oval duct systems; metal gauges; reinforcement; pressure classifications; joints; seams; connectors; supports; hangers; access openings; flexible ducts; and fibrous glass duct systems.

Air-distribution questions may require an understanding of airflow, velocity, friction loss, duct sizing, equivalent dimensions, and system performance. The Trane Ductulator is included to support practice with these relationships and help candidates become familiar with common duct-sizing procedures.

Architectural sheet metal subjects may include flashing, counterflashing, copings, roof edges, gutters, downspouts, wall panels, joints, expansion, drainage, penetrations, and transitions. Candidates should understand how sheet metal details control water movement and accommodate building conditions.

Ventilation and fire-safety preparation may involve air-conditioning systems, warm-air heating systems, exhaust systems, and commercial cooking operations. The NFPA standards address different system types, so candidates must determine which publication applies to the question before searching for a requirement.

Workplace-safety questions may involve fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, personal protective equipment, tools, material handling, electrical hazards, and other construction-jobsite responsibilities covered by OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926.

The Florida Building Code - Mechanical supports preparation involving ducts, ventilation, exhaust, appliances, equipment, air distribution, combustion air, clearances, and other regulated mechanical systems.

Open Book Test

The Florida Sheet Metal Contractor trade examination is open book. Candidates may use approved references during the examination when the books comply with the current testing-center requirements.

Open-book testing requires more than bringing the correct publications into the examination room. Candidates must identify the subject of the question, choose the most relevant reference, locate the applicable section or table, interpret the information, and apply it within the available testing time.

A question involving rectangular or round metal duct construction may require the SMACNA HVAC Duct Construction Standards. A question involving fibrous glass duct may require the SMACNA Fibrous Glass Duct Construction Standards.

Questions involving gutters, downspouts, flashing, copings, roof edges, and architectural metal details may require the SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual. Airflow and duct-sizing questions may require the Trane Ductulator.

Air-conditioning and ventilating system questions may require NFPA 90A. Warm-air heating and air-conditioning questions may require NFPA 90B. Industrial exhaust-system questions may require NFPA 91, while commercial cooking ventilation and fire-protection questions may require NFPA 96.

Mechanical-code questions may require the Florida Building Code - Mechanical. Workplace-safety questions may require OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, and contractor-administration subjects may require the Contractors Manual.

Candidates should practice with all books before test day. Review the table of contents, index, definitions, chapters, appendices, figures, diagrams, and technical tables in each reference. Familiarity with the organization of the books can reduce the time spent searching.

Read the surrounding material after locating a possible answer. A requirement may be affected by a definition, exception, system condition, table note, pressure classification, equipment type, or related subsection.

Only references that comply with current rules for editions, binding, highlighting, tabs, notes, attachments, and book condition should be brought into the examination room.

Licensing Steps

Begin by reviewing the qualifications for Florida Certified Sheet Metal Contractor licensure. Candidates should understand the examination, experience, financial, insurance, background, and application requirements associated with the license category.

Complete the applicable examination registration process and obtain the current candidate information for the Sheet Metal Contractor examination. Compare the books in your study library with the reference list for the scheduled examination period.

Create a study plan that divides preparation into manageable subject areas. Useful categories include plans and specifications, metal duct construction, flexible duct, fibrous glass duct, architectural sheet metal, air distribution, ventilation, exhaust systems, commercial cooking systems, mechanical-code requirements, and OSHA safety.

Study the scope and organization of each NFPA standard. Learn when NFPA 90A, NFPA 90B, NFPA 91, or NFPA 96 is most likely to apply. This can help prevent unnecessary searching in the wrong book.

Practice using the SMACNA standards to locate tables for duct gauges, reinforcement, joints, seams, hangers, supports, and pressure classes. Use the Architectural Sheet Metal Manual to review common exterior details and water-management applications.

Complete duct-sizing exercises with the Trane Ductulator. Practice relating airflow, duct dimensions, velocity, and friction loss. Repeated use can help make the tool more familiar during examination preparation.

After completing the required examinations, submit the appropriate Florida licensing application and supporting documentation. Passing the examination does not automatically issue a contractor license.

Applicants must satisfy the applicable qualifications and receive approval before offering or performing work that requires Florida Sheet Metal Contractor certification.

State Requirements

Florida Certified Sheet Metal Contractor applicants must satisfy the requirements established for the license category. These requirements may include passing the applicable examinations, documenting qualifying experience, demonstrating financial responsibility, completing background requirements, maintaining insurance, and submitting the required application materials.

A Florida Sheet Metal Contractor is authorized to perform work within the scope established for the sheet metal trade. The category includes services involving the manufacture, fabrication, assembly, handling, installation, alteration, repair, servicing, and design of qualifying ferrous or nonferrous sheet metal work.

Candidates should understand the boundaries of the license and should not assume that passing the trade examination authorizes work assigned to another contractor category or separately regulated profession.

Applicants should maintain accurate records of employment, sheet metal work, fabrication experience, installation responsibilities, supervisory duties, education, and training. Organized documentation can support a more efficient licensing submission.

The books in this package support examination preparation but do not replace the state application or qualification review. Purchasing the references or passing the examination does not independently authorize regulated contracting work.

Reference Books

  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926
    The federal construction-safety regulations covering fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, personal protective equipment, tools, electrical hazards, material handling, and other workplace requirements.
  • Contractors Manual, 2025
    A contractor reference covering administrative responsibilities, construction practices, business procedures, and regulatory subjects relevant to professional contracting.
  • NFPA 90A, Standard for the Installation of Air-Conditioning and Ventilating Systems, 2024
    A fire-safety standard addressing the installation and operation of air-conditioning and ventilating systems, including ducts, air-handling equipment, and related system components.
  • NFPA 90B, Standard for the Installation of Warm Air Heating and Air-Conditioning Systems, 2027

    A standard addressing commercial cooking exhaust systems, hoods, ducts, fans, grease removal, clearances, fire protection, inspection, and maintenance.

    A technical standard covering the fabrication, reinforcement, closure, support, handling, and installation of fibrous glass duct systems.
  • SMACNA HVAC Duct Construction Standards, Metal and Flexible
    A primary duct-construction reference covering rectangular, round, oval, metal, and flexible duct systems, including gauges, reinforcement, joints, seams, supports, and pressure classes.

    An architectural metal reference covering flashing, copings, gutters, downspouts, roof edges, wall systems, penetrations, drainage details, joints, and expansion.
  • Trane Ductulator, 1976 or Later
    A duct-sizing tool used to relate airflow, duct dimensions, air velocity, and friction loss during HVAC air-distribution calculations.
  • Florida Building Code - Mechanical, 2026
    A Florida mechanical-code reference addressing ventilation, ducts, exhaust systems, appliances, equipment, combustion air, air distribution, and other regulated mechanical installations.

Exam Room Approved Books

Use the SMACNA HVAC Duct Construction Standards to study metal and flexible duct systems. Focus on the relationship among duct dimensions, gauges, pressure classes, reinforcement, joints, seams, hangers, and supports.

Explore ACE by 1 Exam Prep: Meet Your Personal AI Exam Coach.

Personalized AI Exam Preparation for Florida Irrigation Contractors

Traditional irrigation contractor exam preparation often involves reviewing technical manuals, learning hydraulic formulas, studying construction regulations, and answering practice questions independently.

These activities remain important, but interactive learning can help connect technical information with practical construction scenarios.

ACE introduces an AI-supported study experience designed to help Florida Irrigation Contractor candidates organize preparation and focus on subjects requiring additional attention.

The free demo introduces the ACE learning approach as a complement to technical reference books, professional experience, and structured Florida Irrigation Contractor examination preparation.

Why Try the Free ACE AI Tutor Demo?

Experienced irrigation contractors often understand how to install sprinkler heads, connect piping, replace valves, and program controllers. However, licensing examinations require knowledge that extends beyond routine installation work.

For example, an installer may be comfortable troubleshooting residential sprinkler zones but need additional review of hydraulic calculations, pump selection, or irrigation plan interpretation.

Another candidate may understand drip irrigation and landscape watering schedules but require stronger familiarity with plumbing regulations, excavation safety, or backflow prevention.

ACE encourages candidates to recognize these knowledge gaps through question-based learning.

Reviewing the reasoning behind technical answers helps connect field experience with the professional concepts covered by the examination.

For individuals interested in Florida Irrigation Contractor exam prep, the free ACE demo provides an introduction to personalized studying, technical explanations, and consistent preparation habits.

Exam Details

The Florida Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractor examination is part of the state's construction contractor certification framework. The Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR), through the Construction Industry Licensing Board (CILB), oversees the applicable licensing process.

Candidates preparing for the certification examination study both Irrigation General Trade Knowledge and Business and Finance.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractor.
  • Trade Examination: Irrigation Contractors General Trade Knowledge.
  • Trade Examination Questions: 80 multiple-choice questions.
  • Trade Examination Time Limit: 5 hours.
  • Business and Finance Examination: 120 multiple-choice questions.
  • Business and Finance Time Limit: 6 hours and 30 minutes.
  • Examination Format: Open book.
  • Testing Format: Computer-based testing.
  • Examination Registration: Professional Testing, Inc.
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE.
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

The Irrigation General Trade Knowledge examination covers five major categories: Pre-Construction, Construction, Maintenance and Repair, Scheduling and Water Conservation, and Rules, Laws and Codes.

The Business and Finance examination addresses business operations, financial management, accounting, administrative responsibilities, and government regulations affecting contractors.

Preparation for both components helps candidates understand the technical and business responsibilities involved in operating a certified irrigation contracting business.

Open Book Test

The Florida Irrigation Contractor examinations are open book tests. Candidates may bring reference materials specifically authorized for their examination components.

Open book testing does not eliminate the need for preparation. Candidates must still interpret irrigation drawings, solve calculations, identify applicable regulations, and locate technical information efficiently.

Florida permits underlining and highlighting in approved examination references. Handwritten and typewritten notes are prohibited, and removable tabs are not allowed.

All permitted references must remain properly bound. Candidates may bring only one copy of each authorized reference and may not add markings during examination administration.

Printed PDF copies are permitted only where specifically authorized by the examination reference rules and must follow the required binding conditions.

Learning the organization of an irrigation manual before testing can make technical reference lookups more efficient. Candidates benefit from recognizing where to find information about hydraulics, installation practices, system components, and water management.

ACE emphasizes developing these study skills through technical practice and explanatory review. Online AI tutoring tools and general study materials are intended for preparation, not use inside the examination room.

Licensing Steps

Becoming a Florida Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractor involves meeting state qualifications, completing required examinations, and obtaining the appropriate certification.

  1. Understand the certification: Review the authorized scope of Florida irrigation specialty contracting and determine whether it matches your professional goals.
  2. Evaluate your experience: Review qualifying irrigation installation, construction, maintenance, and supervisory experience.
  3. Prepare for the examinations: Study Irrigation General Trade Knowledge and Business and Finance using the applicable content outlines.
  4. Register for testing: Complete the examination registration process through Professional Testing, Inc.
  5. Schedule your examinations: After approval, arrange computer-based testing through Pearson VUE.
  6. Complete the certification application: Submit the appropriate Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractor application through Florida DBPR.
  7. Satisfy remaining qualifications: Complete applicable experience documentation, financial responsibility, background screening, and business qualification requirements.

Florida lists the CILB 5-AC application for individuals seeking Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractor certification. Separate forms apply when a contractor qualifies a business.

Passing the examinations and obtaining contractor certification are separate parts of the licensing process. The ACE free demo introduces educational preparation rather than completing certification applications.

State Requirements

Florida regulates Certified Irrigation Specialty Contractors through Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

Under Rule 61G4-15.100 of the Florida Administrative Code, an irrigation specialty contractor may perform authorized work involving the installation, maintenance, repair, alteration, extension, management, monitoring, auditing, and permitted design of irrigation systems.

The classification includes irrigation piping, fittings, sprinklers, drip irrigation components, valves, controllers, control wiring, rain sensors, water conservation devices, and associated equipment within the authorized scope.

It also covers irrigation main lines downstream of the specified water supply connection and dedicated backflow prevention device, along with incidental excavation work.

The specialty scope excludes irrigation systems used for agricultural purposes and does not authorize water well or pump work reserved to other qualifications under applicable law.

Florida's certified irrigation specialty license provides statewide contracting authority within its scope. The state specialty certification is an alternative to certain local competency credentials, rather than a mandatory statewide credential for every person performing irrigation work.

Applicants seeking certification must be at least 18 years old and satisfy qualifying experience requirements.

One recognized pathway involves four years of experience in the irrigation specialty category, including at least one year as a foreman. Approved accredited college coursework may substitute for up to three years of qualifying experience.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida Irrigation Contractor General Trade Knowledge examination evaluates five principal areas of technical knowledge.

Pre-Construction – 25%: Review site analysis, irrigation design considerations, construction plans, specifications, material takeoffs, and permitting responsibilities.

Topics include soil characteristics, water sources, plant requirements, irrigation symbols, elevation changes, nozzle selection, and hydraulic calculations.

Candidates should understand how flow rates, pressure losses, pipe sizes, and equipment selection affect irrigation system performance.

Construction – 37.5%: Study irrigation installation procedures, site preparation, piping, fittings, valves, controller wiring, sprinklers, water supply connections, and equipment installation.

Additional subjects include trenching, backfilling, pipe joining, system layout, filtration, pumping components, and creating record drawings.

Construction is the largest examination category and requires substantial familiarity with practical irrigation system installation methods.

Maintenance and Repair – 12.5%: Review inspection procedures, sprinkler head adjustments, valve failures, controller problems, piping leaks, filtration issues, and routine maintenance.

Preparation includes recognizing low-pressure problems, electrical faults, pump application issues, and inadequate installation practices.

Scheduling and Water Conservation – 12.5%: Study soil-plant-water relationships, irrigation assessments, water efficiency, scheduling calculations, and conservation practices.

These subjects address how irrigation systems deliver appropriate amounts of water while reducing unnecessary water use.

Rules, Laws and Codes – 12.5%: Review construction safety, electrical safety, Florida plumbing requirements, backflow prevention, water use restrictions, and applicable environmental regulations.

Pre-Construction and Construction together account for 62.5% of the examination content outline. These areas deserve significant attention during technical preparation.

Irrigation hydraulics is an important part of understanding system design and performance.

Candidates preparing for the Florida Irrigation Contractor examination should review flow rates, available pressure, friction loss, pipe sizing, water velocity, and pump selection.

Learning how these concepts relate to one another helps explain why certain irrigation designs perform effectively while others experience poor distribution or inadequate pressure.

Practice interpreting nozzle performance charts, calculating precipitation rates, evaluating zone flow, and understanding pressure changes throughout piping systems.

Technical preparation should also include reading irrigation plans, recognizing common symbols, interpreting scale, and identifying changes in site elevation.

Florida law defines roofing contracting as work involving the installation, maintenance, repair, alteration, and extension of roofing, waterproofing, and protective roof-coating systems within the authorized scope of the classification.

Roofing contractor responsibilities may also involve skylights, roof-deck attachments, and certain repairs to roof sheathing or fascia associated with roofing work.

Contractors must understand the boundaries of their licensed activities and comply with applicable construction regulations, permitting requirements, product approvals, and workplace safety obligations.

Florida's building codes address roofing assemblies, roof coverings, materials, structural connections, wind resistance, and other construction requirements.

High Velocity Hurricane Zone requirements are particularly important for applicable projects in areas subject to specialized roofing testing and installation provisions.

Open Book Test

The Florida Principles and Practices (P&P) examination is an open-book test. Candidates should prepare by becoming familiar with the organization of the applicable Florida references and developing efficient navigation skills.

Open-book testing requires more than knowing that information appears somewhere within a statute, code, or administrative rule. Candidates must recognize the subject of a question, select the correct authority, locate the relevant provision, and determine how it applies.

For example, accessibility questions may involve the Florida Building Code - Accessibility. Energy conservation questions may involve the Florida Building Code - Energy Conservation.

Professional regulation questions may require a Florida Statutes chapter or Florida Administrative Code provision. Ethical conduct questions may involve Chapter 112, Part III, Florida Statutes.

Recommended open-book preparation strategies include:

  • Identify the Category: Determine whether the question involves a building code, statute, administrative rule, ethics provision, or business-related responsibility.

  • Understand Legal Organization: Become familiar with chapters, parts, sections, subsections, definitions, and administrative rule structures.
  • Confirm Applicability: Review scope language, definitions, conditions, and qualifications that affect the requirement.
  • Recognize Scenario Details: Identify the facts that determine which provision applies.
  • Practice Timed Navigation: Develop efficient lookup habits while maintaining accurate interpretation.
  • Review Incorrect Answers: Determine whether mistakes result from selecting the wrong authority or misunderstanding a provision.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized trade examination accepted by participating contractor licensing agencies.

The examination addresses knowledge associated with planning, managing, supervising, and completing commercial building construction projects. Candidates must develop familiarity with both general construction management and specialized building trades.

Major examination preparation areas include:

  • Construction Management: Project organization, field supervision, jobsite coordination, documentation, and construction operations.
  • Project Planning: Scheduling, estimating, contracts, cost control, productivity, and project administration.
  • Construction Safety: OSHA requirements, excavation hazards, fall protection, equipment safety, and workplace responsibilities.
  • Structural Concrete: Concrete requirements, materials, reinforcement, construction practices, and quality control.
  • Reinforcing Steel: Bar placement, supports, splicing, tolerances, identification, and installation procedures.
  • Precast Concrete: Handling, erection, alignment, connections, bracing, and field safety.
  • Post-Tensioning: Unbonded post-tensioning systems, installation procedures, stressing, and field practices.
  • Structural Steel Systems: Steel decking, joists, joist girders, handling, installation, and construction requirements.
  • Wood Construction: Wood trusses, carpentry, framing, materials, and installation practices.
  • Masonry: Brick, block, stone, mortar, layout, and construction methods.
  • Excavation and Site Work: Trenching, underground utilities, grading, equipment, and site safety.
  • Roofing and Exterior Systems: Roofing materials, installation, estimating, flashing, and exterior insulation systems.
  • Building Codes: Commercial building requirements, construction classifications, accessibility, and technical provisions.
  • Building Systems: Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, lighting, and related construction coordination.

The NASCLA examination requires candidates to study multiple technical subjects and understand which reference provides information for a particular question.
