For Florida applicants, the NASCLA examination is accepted through the endorsement process for eligible Division I contractor classifications.

The NASCLA trade examination does not replace the Florida Business and Finance examination, Florida Building Code examination coverage, or the additional requirements associated with Florida contractor licensure.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for obtaining the permitted technical references and bringing them to the examination according to the applicable testing rules.

Open-book testing requires strong reference-navigation skills. The NASCLA reference collection contains extensive information covering construction management, codes, standards, technical manuals, safety regulations, and specialized construction methods.

Candidates must recognize the subject of a question and determine which publication is most likely to contain the applicable information.

For example, structural concrete questions may involve ACI 318-19, while questions about concrete placement and field quality may involve The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction.

Questions involving reinforcing bars may require Placing Reinforcing Bars. Structural steel questions may involve the Steel Deck Institute manual or technical guidance addressing steel joists and joist girders.

Recommended open-book preparation strategies include:

  • Identify the Subject: Determine whether the question involves safety, project management, structural systems, construction methods, or building codes.
  • Select the Appropriate Reference: Choose the publication most closely associated with the question before searching.
  • Learn Reference Organization: Become familiar with tables of contents, indexes, chapter headings, diagrams, and technical tables.
  • Recognize Keywords: Identify terminology that indicates the relevant trade or construction subject.
  • Read Technical Conditions: Review definitions, exceptions, notes, and requirements affecting the correct answer.
  • Practice Timed Navigation: Develop efficient search habits while maintaining accuracy.
  • Review Missed Questions: Return to the appropriate reference and understand the supporting information.

Candidates should prepare with the correct reference editions and follow the current NASCLA examination instructions regarding authorized materials, book condition, tabs, highlighting, annotations, and prohibited inserts.

Florida candidates pursuing contractor licensing through the NASCLA endorsement pathway must complete the applicable trade examination and Florida licensing requirements.

The Florida Electrical Contractors Certification examination is administered in two parts: the Business examination and the Technical and Safety examination. The Technical and Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows five hours for completion. The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows two and one-half hours.

The Technical and Safety examination covers a wide electrical-contracting scope. Candidates should be prepared to interpret codes, safety regulations, technical standards, formulas, diagrams, equipment information, and practical installation scenarios.

Exam Details

The Florida Underground Utility Contractor examination is part of the state's contractor certification program administered through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

The official license classification is Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor.

The standard certification examination process includes Underground Utility Contractors General Trade Knowledge and Business and Finance.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor.
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.
  • Trade Examination: Underground Utility Contractors General Trade Knowledge.
  • Trade Examination Questions: 80 equally weighted multiple-choice questions.
  • Trade Examination Time Limit: 5 hours.
  • Additional Examination: Business and Finance.
  • Examination Format: Open book.
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing.
  • Examination Registration: Professional Testing, Inc.
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE.
  • Technical Content: Eight major underground utility and excavation categories.

The trade examination emphasizes pre-installation planning, excavation, backfill, compaction, pipe installation, fittings, drainage systems, and utility construction equipment.

Questions also involve interpreting plans and specifications, understanding applicable codes, and performing basic construction mathematics.

Open Book Test

The Florida Underground Utility Contractor examinations are open book tests. Candidates may use reference materials authorized by Florida DBPR for the applicable examination.

Open book testing requires thorough preparation. Candidates must understand the question, recognize the relevant construction subject, and locate information efficiently within the approved references.

For example, questions about PVC water mains may involve an AWWA standard, while excavation protection questions may require OSHA regulations.

Florida permits underlining and highlighting in authorized references. Handwritten and typewritten notes are prohibited, and movable tabs are not permitted.

Reference materials must remain properly bound. Certain publications may be brought as bound PDF copies when specifically permitted by the official reference list.

Only one copy of each authorized reference may be brought into the testing room. Candidates cannot add markings during the examination.

Practice locating material through indexes, tables of contents, technical illustrations, pipe specifications, and construction tables.

ACE encourages candidates to strengthen reference-navigation habits through technical explanations and organized review. The AI tutor is designed for preparation outside the examination room.

Licensing Steps

Becoming a Florida Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor involves completing the required examinations and satisfying state licensing qualifications.

  1. Understand the classification: Review the authorized scope involving underground water mains, sewer systems, storm drainage, excavation, and related utility construction.
  2. Evaluate your experience: Review your underground utility installation experience, construction responsibilities, supervisory work, and education.
  3. Organize documentation: Gather employment records describing qualifying utility construction and excavation activities.
  4. Study Trade Knowledge: Prepare for excavation, pipe installation, soil conditions, testing, trenchless methods, equipment, and safety.
  5. Prepare for Business and Finance: Review contractor accounting, estimating, contracts, financial management, and business responsibilities.
  6. Review authorized references: Study the designated underground utility manuals, OSHA standards, pipe specifications, and Florida plumbing code.
  7. Register for testing: Complete the examination application through Professional Testing, Inc.
  8. Complete the examinations: Schedule authorized computer-based testing through Pearson VUE.
  9. Apply for certification: Submit the appropriate Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor application through Florida DBPR.
  10. Complete remaining qualifications: Satisfy applicable experience, background screening, financial responsibility, and insurance requirements.

Florida identifies application CILB 5-N for individuals seeking Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor certification.

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates Underground Utility and Excavation Contractors under Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, through the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

A Florida Certified Underground Utility and Excavation Contractor is authorized to construct, install, and repair specified underground utility systems on public or private property.

The classification includes main sanitary sewer collection systems, main water distribution systems, storm sewer collection systems, and authorized utility lines extending from these main systems.

Permitted construction methods include open excavation, directional drilling, auger boring, jacking and boring, grouting, slip lining, and other applicable trenchless technologies.

The classification also includes certain wet and dry tapping operations and underground utility connections within the limits established by Florida law.

Qualified contractors may install specified empty underground conduits and sleeves where the statutory design and location conditions are satisfied. This authorization does not include installing conductor wiring or connecting to energized electrical systems.

The classification does not authorize the installation of piping used exclusively as part of a regulated fire protection system beyond the statutory boundary.

Applicants must meet Florida's applicable professional qualification requirements. The state's certification process recognizes qualifying construction experience and approved combinations of education and experience.

Contractors must also satisfy the required examinations, financial responsibility standards, background screening, and insurance requirements.

Understanding the scope of this classification helps candidates connect examination preparation with responsible underground infrastructure construction.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Florida Underground Utility Contractors General Trade Knowledge examination evaluates eight major content areas.

Pre-Installation – 20%: Review site inspections, construction plans, shop drawings, utility locations, surveying, soil conditions, water tables, and environmental requirements.

Traffic Control – 5%: Study temporary traffic control, roadway work zones, signs, barricades, detours, flaggers, and safe construction access.

Excavating, Backfill and Compaction – 20%: Review trench construction, excavation equipment, soil properties, dewatering, trench protection, bedding, backfill, grading, and compaction.

Pipe Installation and Repairs – 15%: Study pressure piping, gravity sewers, pipe placement, manholes, catch basins, lift stations, directional boring, slip lining, and pipe repairs.

Piping, Valves and Fittings – 15%: Review pipe materials, valves, fittings, water service connections, fire hydrants, meters, restraints, and associated installations.

Testing, Disinfecting and Job Close Out – 10%: Study pressure testing, gravity sewer testing, flushing, disinfection, bacteriological sampling, documentation, and project closeout.

Drainage Systems – 5%: Review storm drainage installation, repairs, culverts, drainage structures, and connections to existing systems.

Equipment – 10%: Study excavation machinery, lifting equipment, pumps, construction tools, equipment operation, and maintenance.

Pre-Installation and Excavating, Backfill and Compaction are the largest categories, each representing 20% of the trade examination.

Pipe Installation and Repairs and Piping, Valves and Fittings each account for another 15%. Together, these four categories represent 70% of the content outline.

Water Mains, Sewer Systems, and Pipe Installation

Underground utility construction involves different piping materials and installation techniques depending on the system being installed.

Study ductile iron pipe, PVC pressure pipe, concrete pipe, gravity sewer pipe, and associated fittings.

Review pipe bedding, alignment, grade, support, and connection requirements.

Become familiar with pipe slopes, invert elevations, and the use of surveying equipment.

Directional Drilling and Trenchless Construction

Underground utilities can be installed through open trench excavation or approved trenchless construction methods.

Study directional drilling, auger boring, jack-and-bore procedures, slip lining, and related equipment.

These topics help candidates prepare for questions involving utility installations beneath roads, developed properties, and other construction obstacles.

Utility Location, Damage Prevention, and Traffic Control

Before excavation begins, contractors must understand the location of existing underground facilities.

Study Florida's underground facility damage prevention requirements and the responsibilities associated with utility location notifications.

Review methods used to identify buried utilities and document existing site conditions.

Become familiar with temporary traffic control measures involving cones, signs, barricades, detours, and flagging operations.

Practice interpreting plans and recognizing underground utility conflicts.

These subjects connect construction planning with public safety, property protection, and effective jobsite coordination.

Pipe Testing, Disinfection, and Project Closeout

Underground utility projects require testing and documentation to evaluate completed installations.

Study pressure testing, hydrostatic testing, leakage checks, gravity sewer testing, and pipe deflection testing.

Review the purposes of flushing, disinfection, and bacteriological sampling in potable water distribution systems.

Become familiar with as-built drawings, maintenance information, inspection documentation, and closeout procedures.

Practice recognizing how testing requirements differ among pressure piping, sanitary sewers, and storm drainage installations.

Understanding these procedures supports preparation for the complete utility construction process, from initial excavation through final acceptance.

Construction Mathematics and Business Preparation

Underground utility examination questions may require calculating measurements, pipe slopes, trench volumes, material quantities, and project costs.

Practice fractions, decimals, percentages, areas, volumes, and basic algebra.

Review how construction drawings and pipe profiles communicate elevations, dimensions, and installation requirements.

Florida certification also includes Business and Finance preparation involving estimating, accounting, contracts, insurance, and contractor responsibilities.

State Requirements

Florida regulates General Contractors under Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, and the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

A Florida Certified General Contractor has broad contracting authority for construction activities regulated under Chapter 489, subject to limitations established by Florida law.

Certified General Contractors may contract for a wide range of commercial, residential, and other building construction projects within their authorized scope. Certain specialized work remains subject to statutory restrictions and applicable licensing requirements.

Applicants for certified licensure must be at least 18 years old, demonstrate good moral character, and satisfy an approved professional qualification pathway.

One common pathway requires four years of qualifying construction experience, including at least one year of supervisory experience. Approved combinations of education, military service, and professional construction experience may also qualify.

General Contractor applicants must demonstrate experience in four of six identified structural construction categories, including foundations or slabs exceeding 20,000 square feet, masonry walls, steel erection, elevated slabs, column erection, and formwork for structural reinforced concrete.

At least one year of qualifying experience must involve new construction of structures at least four stories in height.

Applicants must also satisfy applicable financial responsibility, examination, fingerprinting, and other licensing requirements.

The classification includes central air-conditioning, refrigeration, heating and ventilating systems, applicable ductwork, boiler and unfired pressure vessel systems, related equipment, piping, insulation, pressure and process piping, and pneumatic control piping when the work is otherwise permitted by law.

A Class B Air Conditioning Contractor is limited to systems of 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 Btu of heating in any one system. The classification includes applicable central air-conditioning, refrigeration, heating, ventilation, ductwork, piping, insulation, controls, and related work within the scope established by Florida law.

The distinction between Air A and Air B should be considered before applying for an examination. Candidates preparing for Class B should understand the capacity limitation, while Class A candidates should prepare for the broader scope represented by that classification.

Florida certified contractor applicants are also subject to application requirements beyond examination preparation. Candidates should complete the current requirements for the specific license and application type they are pursuing.

The Marine Specialty Contractor classification covers work within the scope established by Florida's specialty contractor regulations. This includes construction, repair, alteration, and related activities involving various marine structures.

Examples include fixed and floating docks, boathouses, mooring structures, piers, wharves, boat lifts, boat ramps, seawalls, bulkheads, and related waterfront construction projects.

Depending on the project, marine work can involve timber piles, framing, concrete, masonry, excavation, and other specialized construction operations.

Contractors must understand the boundaries of their authorized work and follow applicable building, permitting, environmental, and construction safety requirements.

The Florida Building Code provides requirements relevant to building construction, structural materials, and applicable facilities. Accessibility provisions may also affect certain construction features.

Marine contractors should also be familiar with safe excavation practices and procedures intended to protect underground utilities during construction activities.

State Requirements

The Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board licenses and regulates construction contractors. Certified contractors may work throughout Florida within the scope of their license, while registered contractors generally operate within the local jurisdictions connected with their registration.

The NASCLA pathway is available through Florida’s certification-by-endorsement process for applicants seeking licensure as a Certified General Contractor, Certified Building Contractor, or Certified Residential Contractor. The NASCLA examination is treated as a trade-knowledge examination for this pathway.

Applicants relying on NASCLA must also pass the Florida Business and Finance examination and attest to passing an examination covering the Florida Building Code. These requirements remain separate from the NASCLA commercial building examination.

Florida contractor applicants are generally required to demonstrate four years of qualifying experience or an approved combination of college education and construction experience. The experience documentation must correspond to the license category requested and show the appropriate level of construction responsibility.

Applicants must also satisfy fingerprinting and background-screening requirements. Financial responsibility and financial stability must be demonstrated through the records required by the Board, including applicable credit reports.

Required insurance must be in place before the license is activated. Depending on the applicant’s circumstances, this may include workers’ compensation coverage or an approved exemption, along with general liability and property-damage insurance.

The Trade Knowledge examination addresses subjects such as foundations, walls, roofs, insulation, windows, post-and-beam structures, roofovers, siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, downspouts, estimating, safety, and Florida building requirements.

Foundation preparation may include excavation, layout, pier-type post footings, forms, concrete placement, reinforcing materials, compaction, grading, concrete finishing, masonry kneewalls, mortar, concrete masonry units, reinforcement, and joint construction.

Wall-system preparation may involve screen walls, framed walls, composite panels, bracing, anchoring, fastening, storm doors, screen doors, flashing, caulking, material compatibility, support spacing, and construction in high-wind conditions.

Roof-system topics may include standing-seam systems, pan roofs, screen roofs, support spacing, structural connections, fastening, flashing, sealing, roof attachments, wind considerations, gussets, panel sizing, and common roof configurations.

Window preparation may include measurement, rough openings, installation in wood, masonry, and metal walls, anchoring, fastening, flashing, sealing, weather resistance, wall reinforcement, and high-wind considerations.

Post-and-beam construction may involve wood and metal systems, patios, carports, roof framing, anchors, fasteners, bracing, structural connections, and safe installation practices. Roofover preparation may include raised systems, flat-down systems, laminated systems, vinyl blanket systems, insulation, ventilation, drainage, spacing, sealing, and weather protection.

Siding and exterior-component preparation may cover vinyl siding, aluminum siding, soffits, fascia, gutters, downspouts, starter strips, furring strips, vents, expansion and contraction, fastening, weather barriers, drainage, and replacement of damaged substrate materials.

The Business and Finance examination focuses on the commercial and administrative side of contracting. Preparation may include accounting, financial statements, bidding, contracts, project administration, business organization, risk management, contractor responsibilities, regulatory requirements, and recordkeeping.

Candidates should also practice construction mathematics, including measurements, areas, volumes, percentages, material quantities, spacing, unit conversions, concrete calculations, estimating, and basic algebra.

Exam Details

Florida's Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is associated with the statewide Certified Electrical Contractor (EC) classification administered by the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

The certification examination consists of two separate parts: Technical/Safety and Business.

  • License Classification: Florida Certified Electrical Contractor (Unlimited).
  • Examination Category: Unlimited Electrical Contractor (UE).
  • Licensing Authority: Florida DBPR and the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.
  • Technical/Safety Examination: 100 scored multiple-choice questions.
  • Technical/Safety Time Limit: 5 hours.
  • Business Examination: 50 scored multiple-choice questions.
  • Business Time Limit: 2 hours and 30 minutes.
  • Passing Score: 75% on each examination part.
  • Examination Format: Open book.
  • Testing Method: Computer-based testing.
  • Testing Provider: Pearson VUE.

The examinations may contain additional unscored pilot questions. Technical/Safety covers electrical knowledge, code interpretation, installation methods, special applications, and safety. Business addresses contracting operations, financial management, and legal responsibilities.

Open Book Test

The Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is an open book test. Both Technical/Safety and Business permit the use of designated references under Florida's electrical contractor examination rules.

Open book testing rewards familiarity with the National Electrical Code and other authorized publications. Candidates must recognize the subject of each question, determine which reference applies, and locate the appropriate provision efficiently.

For example, service load calculations require different code provisions from questions involving fire alarms, hazardous locations, or commercial electrical installations.

Only authorized reference materials are permitted. Handwritten and typewritten notes are prohibited, and removable tabs are not allowed. Permanently attached reference tabs are permitted under the examination rules.

Candidates may bring one copy of each approved reference. Printed PDF materials are permitted only where specifically authorized and properly bound.

Practice using indexes, electrical tables, definitions, chapters, and code articles. ACE encourages candidates to develop effective reference-navigation habits through preparation questions and explanations.

Licensing Steps

Pursuing Florida Certified Electrical Contractor licensure involves the examination process and separate professional qualification requirements.

  1. Understand the classification: Review the statewide Certified Electrical Contractor scope and licensing responsibilities.
  2. Evaluate your qualifications: Review your electrical contracting experience, supervisory responsibilities, technical education, or professional engineering background.
  3. Apply for examination approval: Submit the appropriate application to Florida DBPR.
  4. Prepare for Technical/Safety: Study electrical theory, wiring, protection, calculations, special occupancies, and safety.
  5. Prepare for Business: Review estimating, contracts, accounting, insurance, payroll, and applicable laws.
  6. Study authorized references: Develop familiarity with the National Electrical Code and other approved materials.
  7. Schedule your examinations: Complete the authorized testing process through Pearson VUE.
  8. Apply for initial certification: Submit the appropriate licensing application after completing examination requirements.
  9. Document professional qualifications: Provide experience records, employment verification, job lists, and applicable business information.
  10. Complete board review: Satisfy the applicable financial responsibility and other licensing requirements.

Florida's Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board evaluates initial certification applications separately from examination results.

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates electrical contractors under Chapter 489, Part II, Florida Statutes, and Chapter 61G6, Florida Administrative Code.

The Certified Electrical Contractor classification is the state's unlimited electrical contractor license. Certified contractors may work statewide within their authorized scope, while registered contractors are limited to jurisdictions where their registration is recognized.

Applicants must meet a recognized professional experience pathway. Florida identifies alternatives involving electrical professional engineering experience, electrical contracting management, foreman or supervisory experience, military experience, and qualifying combinations of training and experience.

For the unlimited Certified Electrical Contractor classification, qualifying experience must include at least 40% work involving three-phase services.

Employment verification, job records, and other supporting documentation help establish relevant professional experience.

Applicants must also satisfy the board's financial responsibility and business qualification requirements.

Unlimited electrical contracting differs from restricted specialty classifications such as residential electrical, limited energy, lighting maintenance, and sign specialty contracting.

Understanding the broad scope of the unlimited classification supports preparation for its diverse technical examination topics.

Reference Books

The Florida Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board identifies authorized publications for the Unlimited Electrical Contractor examinations. Important references include:

  • NFPA 70 – National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition
    Provides electrical installation requirements involving services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding, bonding, wiring methods, equipment protection, motors, and special occupancies.
  • Florida Contractors Manual, 2021 Edition
    Provides contractor business information involving accounting, employment, contracts, insurance, construction laws, and management responsibilities.
  • OSHA Regulations, 29 CFR Parts 1926, 1910, and 1904, July 2020 Edition
    Addresses construction and occupational safety, electrical hazards, workplace procedures, protective equipment, and recordkeeping.
  • NFPA 72 – National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition
    Provides requirements for fire alarm systems, signaling equipment, initiating devices, notification appliances, and related installations.
  • NFPA 780 – Standard for the Installation of Lightning Protection Systems, 2017 Edition
    Addresses lightning protection components, installation methods, conductors, connections, and grounding considerations.
  • NFPA 101 – Life Safety Code, 2018 Edition
    Provides life safety requirements involving building occupancy, emergency systems, and protection of building occupants.
  • Fire Alarm Signaling Systems Handbook, 3rd Edition, 2003, or 4th Edition, 2010
    Explains fire alarm technologies, system components, signaling applications, and related technical principles.
  • UL 681 – Installation and Classification of Burglar and Holdup Alarm Systems
    Addresses installation and classification requirements associated with burglar and holdup alarm systems.
  • UL 365 – Police Station Connected Burglar Alarm Units and Systems
    Provides requirements involving police station connected burglar alarm equipment and systems.
  • Engineering Sign Structures: An Introduction to Analysis and Design
    Introduces structural concepts and installation considerations relevant to electrical signs and supporting assemblies.
  • NEON, Techniques and Handling
    Explains neon sign components, handling, fabrication techniques, and installation considerations.
  • Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 16th or 17th Edition
    Provides concrete materials and installation information relevant to electrical equipment foundations and sign structures.
  • Telecommunication Wiring, 3rd Edition, 2001
    Addresses telecommunications wiring principles, cable systems, installation methods, and related low-voltage applications.
  • NTC Blue Book – Low Voltage Systems, 2020
    Provides technical information about low-voltage systems, alarm installations, communication circuits, and related wiring practices.

Other approved business and technical materials include designated legal and accessibility information contained in the Florida Contractors Manual.

Test Information and Study Materials

The Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination evaluates nine major subjects.

General Theory and Electrical Principles – 19 to 21 Questions: Study electrical mathematics, circuits, voltage, current, resistance, power, transformers, and load calculations.

Plan and Specification Reading – 7 to 9 Questions: Review electrical drawings, symbols, schedules, specifications, and construction documentation.

Wiring and Protection – 13 to 15 Questions: Study conductors, circuit protection, grounding, bonding, services, feeders, and electrical protection requirements.

Wiring Methods and Materials – 11 to 13 Questions: Review raceways, cables, conduits, fittings, boxes, and approved installation methods.

Special Occupancies and Situations – 13 to 15 Questions: Study electrical requirements involving hazardous locations, healthcare facilities, pools, emergency systems, and other special applications.

OSHA, Safety, Testing, Tools and Equipment – 8 to 10 Questions: Review electrical testing, protective equipment, construction safety, and safe working procedures.

Life Safety and Accessibility – 4 to 6 Questions: Study life safety provisions, emergency considerations, and applicable accessibility requirements.

Electrical Signs and Outline Lighting – 2 to 4 Questions: Review illuminated signs, electrical connections, lighting installations, and structural considerations.

Alarms and Limited Energy – 14 to 16 Questions: Study alarm circuits, fire alarm systems, signaling, communication wiring, and low-voltage applications.

Electrical Theory and Contractor Calculations

Electrical theory is foundational to the unlimited contractor examination. Candidates must understand electrical relationships and apply calculations to real installation scenarios.

Review Ohm's law, electrical power, resistance, current, and voltage. Practice single-phase and three-phase calculations and study the relationship between voltage, current, and apparent power.

Develop familiarity with service and feeder load calculations, demand factors, voltage drop, conductor sizing, and transformer calculations.

Study how electrical loads affect circuit design, equipment selection, and the application of relevant National Electrical Code provisions.

ACE supports focused practice by encouraging candidates to review calculation methods and understand the reasoning behind solutions.

National Electrical Code Navigation

The National Electrical Code is a central technical reference for Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor exam preparation.

Study its organization, including general requirements, wiring methods, equipment installations, and special occupancies.

Practice locating information involving conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, box fill, and conduit fill.

Become familiar with the use of code tables, definitions, exceptions, and cross-references.

When answering practice questions, identify the installation condition before choosing a code article. This approach encourages a more consistent method of applying electrical requirements.

Services, Feeders, Motors, and Transformers

Unlimited electrical contracting involves an extensive range of power distribution equipment.

Study electrical services, service equipment, feeders, branch circuits, disconnects, and overcurrent protection.

Review motors, motor controllers, transformers, and equipment connection requirements.

Practice identifying relevant code provisions for conductor sizing and electrical equipment protection.

Develop familiarity with three-phase electrical systems because experience involving three-phase services is an important part of Florida's unlimited contractor qualification framework.

Special Occupancies, Alarms, and Safety

Florida's unlimited electrical examination covers technical situations beyond ordinary residential wiring.

Review special occupancies, emergency systems, swimming pool electrical installations, and electrical equipment in hazardous environments.

Study fire alarm components, notification devices, initiating circuits, signaling systems, and low-voltage wiring.

Become familiar with workplace safety requirements, electrical testing procedures, and the proper use of protective equipment.

These subjects help candidates develop a broader understanding of electrical contracting responsibilities across different building types and applications.

Business Examination Preparation

The Business examination evaluates knowledge required to manage an electrical contracting company.

Study estimating and bidding, purchasing, contract scheduling, insurance, bonding, contracting laws, and personnel management.

Review payroll, tax responsibilities, financial statements, accounting, and construction business records.

Practice recognizing how project costs, business expenses, and contractual responsibilities affect electrical contracting operations.

Preparing for both Technical/Safety and Business supports the full examination pathway toward Florida Certified Electrical Contractor licensure.

Exam Details

Open Book Test

The Florida Solar Contractor examinations are open book tests. Candidates may use the reference books authorized by Florida DBPR for the applicable examination.

Open book testing still requires careful preparation. Candidates must recognize the technology described in a question, determine which reference is relevant, and locate technical information efficiently.

A question about photovoltaic wiring may involve an electrical reference, while a question about solar pool heating may require a solar thermal manual. Roof attachment questions may involve specialized roofing publications.

Authorized references must remain properly bound. Florida permits underlining and highlighting but prohibits handwritten and typewritten notes.

Moveable tabs, unauthorized loose materials, and electronic tablets are not permitted. Candidates cannot add markings to references during the examination.

Practice using tables of contents, indexes, diagrams, electrical tables, and installation details before examination day.

Licensing Steps

Florida State Requirements

Florida regulates solar contractors under Chapter 489, Part I, Florida Statutes, through the Construction Industry Licensing Board.

A Florida Certified Solar Contractor is authorized to perform specified installation, alteration, repair, maintenance, relocation, and replacement work involving solar panels and related equipment for potable solar water heating, swimming pool solar heating, and photovoltaic systems.

The classification includes authorized work on solar systems serving public or private properties, subject to applicable construction and licensing requirements.

It differs from the narrower Rooftop Solar Heating Installation Specialty Contractor classification, which focuses on specified residential solar thermal applications.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old, demonstrate good moral character, and satisfy an approved professional qualification pathway.

Florida recognizes four years of qualifying construction experience or approved combinations of experience, education, and military service. Applicable qualification pathways include supervisory experience.

Applicants must also satisfy examination, financial responsibility, background screening, and insurance requirements.

Contractors performing solar work must operate within the scope of their certification and meet applicable permitting and construction requirements.

Understanding these responsibilities helps candidates connect examination preparation with the professional demands of operating a licensed solar contracting business.

Reference Books

  • Walker's Building Estimator's Reference Book, 33rd Edition, 2024
    Provides construction estimating guidance involving labor, materials, equipment, measurements, and project cost calculations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations, OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, July 1, 2025
    Addresses construction safety, rooftop hazards, fall protection, ladders, electrical awareness, and workplace equipment.

    Provides technical information about photovoltaic system planning, components, electrical calculations, and solar power applications.
  • Solar Water & Pool Heating Manual, 2006

  • Photovoltaic Systems, 3rd Edition, 2012

    Provides guidance on membrane roof assemblies, roofing details, penetrations, and weather protection around rooftop installations.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Metal Panel and SPF Roof Systems, 2024
    Addresses metal panel and spray polyurethane foam roofing systems relevant to rooftop equipment installation.
  • The NRCA Roofing Manual: Steep-Slope Roof Systems, 2025
    Covers steep-slope roofing materials, flashing, attachment methods, underlayment, and roof penetration considerations.
  • Florida Building Code – Plumbing, 2023 Edition
    Provides requirements for plumbing materials, piping, water heating connections, and applicable installation methods.
  • Florida Building Code – Residential, 2023 Edition
    Addresses residential roof structures, construction requirements, building systems, and related safety provisions.

These publications cover photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technology, construction safety, roofing, plumbing, and estimating. Familiarity with their organization supports more effective preparation for the open book examination.

Test Information and Study Materials

Swimming Pools – 25%: Review site surveys, collector orientation, pool and spa heating design, collector installation, piping systems, electrical controls, system activation, troubleshooting, and safety.

Domestic Hot Water – 25%: Study solar thermal collector selection, hot water system design, storage, heat exchangers, piping, freeze protection, installation, commissioning, and maintenance.

Photovoltaics – 50%: Review solar module orientation, photovoltaic design, grid-connected systems, standalone systems, hybrid configurations, installation, commissioning, maintenance, and electrical safety.

Photovoltaics represents half of the trade examination content outline, making electrical solar technology a major preparation priority.

Swimming pool solar heating and domestic hot water systems each account for one-quarter of the outline, so candidates also need substantial familiarity with solar thermal applications.

Preparing for Photovoltaic System Questions

Photovoltaic systems convert sunlight into electrical energy through solar modules connected to additional electrical equipment.

Study module types, array configurations, inverters, conductors, circuit protection, disconnects, and grounding.

Review the differences between direct current and alternating current and how inverters support connected electrical loads.

Become familiar with grid-connected, standalone, and hybrid photovoltaic systems.

For battery-supported applications, review battery types, energy storage, charge controllers, and system monitoring.

Practice calculations involving voltage, current, electrical power, energy production, and basic system sizing.

Develop an understanding of how shading, orientation, location, and environmental conditions influence photovoltaic performance.

Solar Pool Heating and Hydraulic Systems

Solar swimming pool heating involves circulating pool water through collectors that absorb solar energy.

Study collector placement, orientation, shading, system sizing, and the relationship between collector area and heating requirements.

Review pumps, valves, piping, circulation controls, and the effects of pressure and flow rate.

Become familiar with how solar heating equipment integrates with existing pool filtration and circulation systems.

Practice recognizing potential installation problems involving piping connections, equipment placement, and system operation.

Understanding these concepts helps candidates approach questions involving both solar collector installation and pool equipment interaction.

Domestic Solar Water Heating Systems

Domestic solar water heating systems use solar collectors to heat water for building applications.

Study direct and indirect systems, heat exchangers, storage tanks, circulation pumps, and temperature controls.

Review the differences between active and passive systems and the importance of proper collector sizing.

Become familiar with piping materials, insulation, thermal expansion, pressure relief, and freeze protection.

For indirect systems, review heat transfer fluids, pressure testing, and maintenance considerations.

Practice identifying how the components of a solar domestic hot water system work together to collect, transfer, and store thermal energy.

Rooftop Installation, Weather Protection, and Safety

Solar equipment installations frequently involve roof structures and elevated construction activities.

Study roof attachments, mounting systems, penetration methods, flashing, and sealants.

Review the relationship between solar equipment loads, supporting structures, and wind-related construction requirements.

Become familiar with roofing system differences that affect attachment and waterproofing methods.

Construction safety is another important subject. Review OSHA requirements involving ladders, fall protection, electrical hazards, tools, and material handling.

Understanding these considerations supports technical examination preparation and safer installation planning.

Electrical Calculations and Construction Mathematics

The Solar Contractor trade examination includes basic mathematics and the interpretation of plans, specifications, and codes.

Practice electrical formulas involving voltage, current, resistance, and power.

Review percentages, decimals, fractions, measurements, areas, and volumes.

Become familiar with calculations involving photovoltaic string configurations, collector areas, and piping systems.

Study construction drawings and diagrams to recognize equipment locations, dimensions, and installation conditions.

Consistent calculation practice helps candidates build confidence in technical problem-solving.

Business and Finance Examination Preparation

Florida Solar Contractor candidates also prepare for the Business and Finance examination.

This examination addresses responsibilities associated with running a licensed contracting business, including estimating, contracts, accounting, financial management, insurance, and construction regulations.

Study how labor, materials, equipment, and overhead influence project costs.

Florida recognizes different air conditioning contractor classifications based on the scope and capacity of the systems contractors are authorized to work on.

Florida Class A Air Conditioning Contractor

A Class A Air Conditioning Contractor is authorized to perform a broad range of central air conditioning, heating, ventilation, and refrigeration contracting activities within the statutory scope of the license.

Unlike Class B, the Class A classification is not restricted by the 25-ton cooling and 500,000-BTU heating limitations.

This classification is relevant to contractors seeking broader authority to install, maintain, repair, alter, and design qualifying HVAC systems.

Florida Class B Air Conditioning Contractor

A Class B Air Conditioning Contractor works within a more limited system-capacity classification. Florida defines the Class B scope as systems involving no more than 25 tons of cooling and 500,000 BTU of heating in any one system.

Class B contractors may perform qualifying installation, repair, maintenance, alteration, and related HVAC activities within their authorized scope.

Neither classification automatically authorizes work outside its statutory definition, including certain plumbing, fuel-line, and electrical power wiring activities.

Exam Details

Florida administers the Unlimited Electrical Contractor certification examination through the Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board. The certification examination consists of two examination parts: a Business section and a Technical/Safety section.

The Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and provides 5 hours of testing time. The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and provides 2½ hours of testing time. The state examination program may also include additional pilot questions that are not counted toward the candidate’s score.

Both portions are administered as computer-based examinations through Pearson VUE after the candidate receives approval from the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

The official Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination content outline identifies the following subject ranges:

  • General Theory and Electrical Principles: 19 to 21 questions
  • Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation: 7 to 9 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 13 to 15 questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 11 to 13 questions
  • Special Occupancies and Situations: 13 to 15 questions
  • OSHA, Safety, Procedures for Testing and Use of Tools and Equipment: 8 to 10 questions
  • Life Safety and Americans with Disabilities Act: 4 to 6 questions
  • Electrical Signs, Outline Lighting, and Structural Considerations: 2 to 4 questions
  • Alarms/Limited Energy: 14 to 16 questions

  1. Apply for approval to take the certified electrical contractor examination. Candidates submit the applicable examination application to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and select the Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination category.
  2. Receive authorization to test. After the examination application is approved, candidates become eligible to schedule the applicable examination sections.
  3. Schedule the examinations. Florida electrical certification examinations are offered in computer-based format through Pearson VUE.
  4. Pass the Technical/Safety examination. Unlimited Electrical Contractor candidates must complete the 100-question Technical/Safety examination.
  5. Pass the Business examination. The Business examination is required for electrical certification categories and consists of 50 scored questions.
  6. Submit the initial certified licensure application. After passing both examination parts, candidates must apply for initial certification as an electrical contractor.
  7. Document qualifying experience. The initial application requires evidence that the applicant meets the experience requirements for the Certified Electrical Contractor category.
  8. Provide required supporting documentation. Applicants must submit the experience, financial, business, and other documentation required by the licensing application.
  9. Complete Board review. Initial certified licensure applications are reviewed through the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board process.
  10. Receive approval for licensure. Passing both examination sections is an important step, but candidates must also satisfy the applicable licensing requirements before receiving certification.

State Requirements

Florida’s Certified Electrical Contractor category is commonly associated with the Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination. Applicants must meet one of the experience pathways established by the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.

Qualifying pathways include three years of management experience in the trade within the preceding six years; four years of experience as a foreman, supervisor, or contractor in the trade within the preceding eight years; qualifying electrical professional-engineer experience; certain Armed Forces or governmental electrical experience; six years of qualifying comprehensive training, technical education, or broad electrical contracting experience; or an approved combination of qualifying experience.

For the Certified Electrical Contractor category, the qualifying experience must include at least 40 percent of work involving three-phase services. This category-specific requirement is important when documenting electrical experience for the state application.

Florida requires applicants to provide evidence supporting the experience claimed. Depending on how the experience was obtained, documentation may include W-2 forms, employer verification forms, and job lists. Applicants using qualifying job lists are expected to document representative projects for the experience period claimed.

The state licensing process also addresses financial responsibility and information about the business the applicant intends to qualify. Passing the examination does not replace these application requirements. Candidates should treat examination preparation and licensing documentation as separate parts of the overall certification process.

Reference Books

Florida publishes an official Electrical Contractors’ Reference List identifying which references are approved for each electrical certification category. The Unlimited Electrical Contractor category is identified as UE on the state reference chart.

  • Florida Contractors Manual, 2021 Edition
    A Florida contracting reference used for selected legal, accessibility, safety-recordkeeping, and contractor-related subjects applicable to the Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination.
  • MANCOMM Code of Federal Regulation, Title 29 (OSHA) Parts 1926, 1910, 1904, July 2020 Edition
    A federal workplace and construction safety reference covering OSHA requirements relevant to electrical contracting, jobsite safety, equipment, testing procedures, and occupational safety.
  • NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition
    The primary electrical code reference used for wiring, protection, conductors, equipment, installations, special occupancies, electrical systems, and other electrical-code requirements.
  • NFPA 72, National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2019 Edition
    A fire alarm and signaling reference covering systems, devices, circuits, installation requirements, testing, and related signaling concepts.
  • NFPA 780, Lightning Protection Code, 2017 Edition
    A reference covering lightning protection systems, protection methods, components, and related installation requirements.
  • NFPA 101, Life Safety Code, 2018 Edition
    A life-safety reference addressing building and occupancy safety concepts relevant to the examination.
  • Fire Alarm Signaling Systems Handbook, Bukowski & Moore, 3rd Edition 2003 or 4th Edition 2010
    A technical reference covering fire alarm signaling systems, components, application, and system principles.
  • UL 681, Installation and Classification of Burglar and Holdup Alarm Systems
    A reference addressing the installation and classification of burglar and holdup alarm systems.
  • UL 365, Police Station Connected Burglar Alarm Units and Systems
    A reference addressing burglar alarm units and systems connected to police-station applications.
  • Engineering Sign Structures, An Introduction to Analysis and Design
    A reference addressing structural analysis and design concepts applicable to electrical sign structures.
  • NEON, Techniques and Handling
    A specialty reference covering neon systems, techniques, installation considerations, and handling practices.
  • Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 16th or 17th Edition
    A construction reference addressing concrete materials, mixtures, and related technical considerations that may apply to electrical installations and structural support work.
  • Telecommunication Wiring, 2001, 3rd Edition
    A reference covering telecommunications wiring methods, systems, and installation principles.
  • NTC Blue Book Low Voltage Systems, 2020 Edition
    A low-voltage systems reference used for limited-energy and related electrical topics included within the Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination.

Test Information and Study Materials

A successful study routine for the Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination should combine trade knowledge with practical reference navigation. Because the Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions across several electrical subject areas, candidates should avoid concentrating all of their preparation on only one familiar topic.

Begin by dividing the 200 flash cards into smaller study groups. A set of 20 to 30 cards can be easier to review consistently than the complete deck at once. As you become comfortable with a group, mix older cards back into newer groups so earlier material remains active.

Spend substantial time on general electrical theory and electrical principles because the official content outline assigns 19 to 21 questions to that area. Review relationships involving voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, and other core electrical principles. Calculation practice should involve actually solving problems rather than simply reading completed examples.

Code navigation should be another regular part of your preparation. Wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, and special occupancies and situations together represent a large portion of the Technical/Safety examination. Learn how the National Electrical Code is arranged and practice moving between articles, tables, definitions, exceptions, and related sections.

Do not ignore alarms and limited-energy material. The official outline allocates 14 to 16 questions to alarms and limited energy. The state reference list includes multiple alarm and low-voltage resources, so these subjects deserve meaningful preparation alongside traditional power and wiring topics.

Safety should also remain part of your study routine. OSHA, testing procedures, and the use of electrical tools and equipment account for 8 to 10 questions. Review safe work practices together with the approved OSHA reference so that safety concepts and reference locations become familiar.

Plan and specification reading can be strengthened by practicing how to interpret drawings, symbols, schedules, notes, and electrical project information. The goal is to understand what a plan communicates and connect that information to code and installation requirements.

Use the flash cards for active recall, but pair them with your books. When a card reveals a weak topic, find that subject in the applicable approved reference and review the surrounding material. This turns a missed flash card into an opportunity to strengthen both technical understanding and reference-navigation ability.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor candidates build a more organized approach to examination preparation. Electrical contracting covers an extensive range of technical material, and consistent structure can make that material easier to review and retain.

The Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor Exam Prep Study Flash Cards provide 200 opportunities for active recall. Instead of simply rereading electrical material, flash-card study requires you to retrieve an answer, recognize uncertainty, and identify topics that deserve additional work.

1 Exam Prep supports trade-focused review by encouraging candidates to combine electrical knowledge with practice-oriented preparation. This can include electrical theory review, code navigation, calculations, plan interpretation, safety study, alarm and limited-energy topics, and familiarity with the approved examination references.

Reference navigation is particularly important because Florida’s Unlimited Electrical Contractor examinations are open book. Candidates benefit from knowing how to move through their references efficiently rather than relying on unfamiliar books during the examination. Regular reference practice can help you associate specific topics with the books and sections most likely to contain the information you need.

The flash cards also make it easier to maintain consistency. You can study a manageable number each day, track difficult concepts, revisit missed material, and combine short review sessions with longer periods of code and calculation practice. This type of structured preparation can help candidates approach the examination with stronger familiarity and a more organized study foundation.

FAQ Section

How many Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor study flash cards are included?

This product includes 200 Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor Exam Prep Study Flash Cards.

Is the Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor exam open book?

Yes. Both the Business and Technical/Safety portions of Florida’s electrical certification examination are open book. Only approved references that meet the examination rules may be used.

How many questions are on the Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety exam?

The Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions. Additional unscored pilot questions may also appear.

How long is the Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety exam?

Candidates receive 5 hours for the Technical/Safety examination.

Is there also a Business exam?

Yes. Florida electrical certification requires a Business examination in addition to the applicable Technical/Safety examination. The Business section contains 50 scored questions and provides 2½ hours of testing time.

What score do I need to pass?

Florida’s electrical examination information identifies a minimum passing score of 75 percent for both the Business and Technical/Safety sections.

Is the Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor exam computer based?

Yes. Florida administers the electrical certification examinations in computer-based format through Pearson VUE after the candidate has received authorization to test.

What subjects are covered on the Technical/Safety exam?

The official content outline includes electrical theory and principles, plan and specification interpretation, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, special occupancies, OSHA and safety, life safety and accessibility, electrical signs and structural considerations, and alarms and limited-energy systems.

Can I bring study notes into the examination?

No. Florida’s electrical examination rules prohibit class notes, formulas, sample questions, loose-leaf study materials, and similar unauthorized materials. Candidates should use only the approved examination references permitted for their category.

Can I use tabs in my reference books?

Permanently attached tabs may be used. Removable tabs, pull-off labels, and Post-it-style notes are not permitted under the examination rules.

Do I need experience with three-phase electrical work?

Yes. Applicants for the Certified Electrical Contractor category must document qualifying experience that includes at least 40 percent of work involving three-phase services.

Should I study the approved reference books in addition to using these flash cards?

Yes. The flash cards are intended to supplement comprehensive preparation. Because the examinations are open book, candidates should also become comfortable locating information in the approved electrical references, particularly the National Electrical Code and the other books assigned to the Unlimited Electrical Contractor category.

How should I use the 200 flash cards?

Divide the cards into manageable groups and review them repeatedly. Separate difficult cards for additional study, then use your approved books to research topics you miss. Combining flash-card recall with code navigation and problem solving creates a more complete exam-preparation routine.

Licensing Steps

  5. Review the current exam information and approved reference list before testing.

  7. Complete the required examination parts.

Examination preparation is one part of the licensing process. Applicants must also satisfy the qualification and application requirements established for Florida certification.

State Requirements

Florida defines a Residential Contractor as a contractor whose services are limited to the construction, remodeling, repair, or improvement of one-family, two-family, or three-family residences that do not exceed two habitable stories above no more than one uninhabitable story, along with accessory-use structures connected with those residences.

This scope distinguishes the Residential Contractor classification from Florida's Building Contractor and General Contractor classifications. A Building Contractor may perform a broader range of residential and commercial construction within the statutory limits of that classification, while a General Contractor has a broader scope still.

Understanding the correct classification is important because the license determines the type of work a contractor is authorized to perform. Candidates should choose the classification that matches their intended scope before beginning the examination and application process.

  8. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Florida reviews the applicant's qualifications before issuing certification.
  9. Obtain certification before contracting statewide. A Florida certified specialty electrical contractor license authorizes work statewide within its approved scope.

State Requirements

The Florida Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board regulates electrical contractors and certified specialty electrical contractors. Certified licenses are statewide, allowing a properly licensed contractor to work within the authorized classification throughout Florida.

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor specialty scope includes installation, repair, alteration, addition to, replacement of, or design of electrical wiring, fixtures, appliances, apparatus, raceways, conduit, and related electrical components in one-, two-, three-, or four-family residences not exceeding two stories in height, including accessory-use structures associated with those residences.

The electrical service within the Residential Electrical Contractor specialty scope is limited to a single-phase, 400-ampere single service.

Florida recognizes the NASCLA Residential Electrical Exam as substantially similar to the Residential Specialty technical examination for endorsement. Applicants using this substantially similar examination pathway must also hold an out-of-state license associated with a comparable scope and satisfy Florida's certification requirements.

Florida law provides several possible experience and education pathways for electrical contractor certification. These include at least three years of qualifying management experience in the trade within the preceding six years, with permitted educational equivalency; four years of qualifying supervisory or contractor experience within the preceding eight years; or six years of qualifying comprehensive training, technical education, or supervisory experience within the preceding 12 years. Additional qualifying pathways exist for certain professional engineers and combinations of eligible experience and education.

Applicants for Florida certification must also satisfy applicable character, financial responsibility, credit, insurance, business, and application requirements. The Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board reviews the application and supporting documentation before certification is issued.

Florida's NASCLA endorsement pathway should not be confused with automatic reciprocity. The Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board does not treat NASCLA examination passage alone as automatic authorization to perform electrical contracting work in Florida.

A productive Florida NASCLA Residential Electrician study plan should combine code navigation, electrical theory, calculations, safety, residential construction, and contractor business knowledge. The books in this package provide references for each of those areas.

Start with the 2023 NEC. Study dwelling-unit services, feeders, branch circuits, load calculations, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, receptacles, lighting outlets, wiring methods, cables, raceways, boxes, appliances, motors, and electrical equipment.
