The Florida Roofing Inspector examination is a specialized technical examination for professionals pursuing certification to perform roofing inspections under Florida's building-code regulatory system. Florida building code inspectors are regulated through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board within the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Roofing inspection in Florida requires a detailed understanding of roof assemblies and rooftop structures as well as conditions created by Florida's wind and weather environment. Candidates should be prepared to evaluate roof coverings, materials, underlayment, flashing, attachment, drainage, re-roofing work, rooftop structures, and installation requirements.

The ICC FR Florida Roofing Inspector examination contains 70 multiple-choice questions and allows 3 hours for completion. It is an open-book examination.

The references associated with this online practice-question product are the Florida Building Code - Building, 2023 and the Florida Building Code - Residential, 2023. These references support preparation for commercial and residential roofing requirements under Florida's current 8th Edition building-code framework.

Effective roofing inspector preparation requires more than memorizing isolated roofing rules. Candidates should understand how roofing materials, installation methods, wind resistance, flashing, drainage, structural support, and code requirements work together to form a complete roof assembly.

What You Get

  • Online Practice Questions: Practice-oriented preparation for the Florida Roofing Inspector ICC FR examination.
  • Florida Roofing Code Review: Preparation involving roof coverings, materials, installation, re-roofing, drainage, rooftop structures, and wind-related requirements.
  • HVHZ Preparation: Review of roofing requirements associated with Florida's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone.
  • Code Navigation Practice: Questions designed to improve familiarity with the Florida Building Code - Building and Florida Building Code - Residential.
  • Inspection-Focused Study: Preparation centered on identifying compliant and noncompliant roofing conditions.
  • Access Period: 3 months access included.

Exam Details

The Florida Roofing Inspector ICC FR examination contains 70 multiple-choice questions. Candidates receive 3 hours to complete the examination.

The official examination content outline includes:

  • Administration: 6%
  • Materials: 4%
  • Fire Classifications: 4%
  • Roof Coverings: 14%
  • Roofing Installations: 28%
  • Re-roofing: 12%
  • High-Velocity Hurricane Zones: 18%
  • Roof Drainage: 6%
  • Rooftop Structures: 8%

Roofing Installations is the largest category at 28% of the examination. Candidates should devote substantial preparation time to installation requirements, fastening, underlayment, flashing, roof assemblies, material limitations, slopes, penetrations, attachment, and manufacturer-related installation provisions.

High-Velocity Hurricane Zones represent 18% of the exam. Florida roofing inspectors need to understand requirements that apply in areas subject to enhanced wind-performance provisions, including roof assembly attachment, approved products, roof coverings, flashing, and other wind-related installation requirements.

Roof Coverings represent 14%, while Re-roofing accounts for 12%. Rooftop Structures represent 8%, Administration and Roof Drainage each represent 6%, and Materials and Fire Classifications each account for 4%.

The examination therefore emphasizes both the physical installation of roof systems and the Florida-specific conditions that affect their performance.

Open Book Test

The Florida Roofing Inspector ICC FR examination is an open-book test.

This product uses the Florida Building Code - Building, 2023 and Florida Building Code - Residential, 2023 for preparation. Candidates should become familiar with the organization of both code volumes and know where roofing requirements are generally located.

Open-book testing does not eliminate the need for strong code familiarity. With 70 questions and 3 hours, candidates have an average of a little more than two and a half minutes per question.

A question involving commercial roof assemblies, reroofing, rooftop structures, or High-Velocity Hurricane Zone provisions may require the Building volume. Residential roofing questions may direct the candidate toward the Residential volume.

Practice should include locating requirements for roof coverings, flashing, underlayment, fastening, drainage, slope, weather protection, fire classification, and roof assemblies.

Tables, exceptions, product requirements, material limitations, and special Florida provisions should receive focused attention. Candidates should also practice recognizing when a question is asking about ordinary Florida roofing requirements versus requirements specific to a High-Velocity Hurricane Zone.

Licensing Steps

  1. Confirm the Florida Roofing Inspector certification category. Roofing Inspector is a recognized Florida building code inspector classification.
  2. Meet the applicable qualification requirements. Applicants must qualify through one of Florida's accepted experience, education, certification, or training pathways.
  3. Submit the appropriate application. Roofing Inspector applications are processed through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  4. Receive approval for the examination process. Applicants must complete the applicable Board approval requirements before taking required state licensing examinations.
  5. Prepare for the technical examination. Study the Florida Building Code roofing provisions, residential roofing requirements, HVHZ provisions, re-roofing, roof drainage, and rooftop structures.
  6. Take the ICC FR Florida Roofing Inspector examination. The examination contains 70 multiple-choice questions and allows 3 hours.
  7. Complete the Florida Principles and Practice examination when required. Applicants pursuing initial Florida inspector certification by examination must satisfy the applicable state examination requirement.
  8. Complete remaining certification requirements. Florida reviews examination results and required qualification documentation before issuing certification.

State Requirements

Florida Roofing Inspectors are regulated through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board within the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Florida requires building code inspectors to hold certification appropriate to the inspection category in which they perform regulated work. Roofing Inspector is a specialized category focused on roof systems and related construction.

Applicants seeking certification must satisfy Florida's applicable eligibility requirements. Qualification can depend on relevant construction or inspection experience, education, existing certifications, or other approved pathways.

Applicants seeking certification by examination must pass the applicable technical examination. Florida also requires the Florida Principles and Practice examination for applicable initial licensing pathways.

Florida currently makes ICC National Certification examinations available to Florida candidates through ICC's PRONTO remote-proctored testing platform.

The Florida Principles and Practice examination is administered separately through Florida's approved testing process.

Passing the ICC FR technical examination by itself does not automatically issue a Florida Roofing Inspector certification. Applicants must also satisfy Florida's application, eligibility, examination, and other licensing requirements.

Reference Books

  • Florida Building Code - Building, 2023
    Supports preparation involving commercial roof assemblies, roof coverings, re-roofing, rooftop structures, drainage, structural requirements, High-Velocity Hurricane Zone provisions, materials, weather protection, fire classifications, and related Florida roofing requirements.
  • Florida Building Code - Residential, 2023
    Supports preparation involving residential roof coverings, underlayment, flashing, roof slopes, fastening, roof assemblies, re-roofing, weather protection, and roofing provisions applicable to residential construction.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Florida Roofing Inspector study plan should begin with Roofing Installations, the largest category at 28% of the examination.

Review roof deck preparation, underlayment, flashing, fasteners, attachment methods, roof covering installation, roof slope requirements, penetrations, transitions, edges, and other installation details.

Candidates should understand that the roof covering is only one component of a complete roof assembly. Decking, underlayment, flashing, fastening, ventilation, drainage, and penetrations all affect overall roof performance.

Underlayment deserves focused study. Florida roofing requirements address the placement, type, attachment, and integration of underlayment with roof coverings and flashing.

Flashing should also receive substantial preparation. Roof-to-wall intersections, valleys, penetrations, chimneys, edges, and other transitions must be protected against water intrusion.

A roofing inspector should be able to recognize whether flashing is properly positioned and integrated with the roofing materials so water is directed away from vulnerable locations.

High-Velocity Hurricane Zones represent 18% of the examination. Candidates should understand that Florida's HVHZ provisions impose additional requirements intended to address high-wind performance.

Study roof-covering attachment, approved systems, fasteners, flashing, product approval, and other provisions that can differ from ordinary non-HVHZ construction.

Miami-Dade and Broward Counties are associated with Florida's High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. Candidates should be prepared to recognize when HVHZ requirements apply and when the general Florida Building Code provisions apply instead.

Wind resistance is a central roofing issue throughout Florida. Roof assemblies must be designed and installed to resist uplift forces produced by wind, with attachment requirements varying according to the roof system, location, design pressures, and approved assembly.

Roof Coverings represent 14%. Candidates should study common systems such as asphalt shingles, tile, metal roofing, built-up roofing, modified bitumen, single-ply systems, and other code-recognized roof coverings.

Different roof-covering systems have different slope limitations, underlayment requirements, fastening methods, attachment requirements, and weather-protection details.

A roofing inspector should understand both the general code requirements and the importance of approved installation instructions for specific systems.

Re-roofing represents 12%. Review removal of existing coverings, roof-deck condition, re-covering limitations, flashing replacement, damaged materials, structural conditions, and requirements that apply when an existing roof is replaced or recovered.

Re-roofing questions often require candidates to distinguish between repair, replacement, and roof recovering. The condition of the existing roof and the number or type of roof coverings already installed can affect what work is permitted.

Rooftop Structures account for 8%. Candidates should be familiar with code requirements affecting equipment, supports, rooftop construction, access, clearances, structural attachment, and other components installed above the roof surface.

Rooftop equipment can affect drainage and roof integrity. Penetrations and support systems should be coordinated with the roofing assembly so weather protection is maintained.

Roof Drainage represents 6%. Review roof slopes, drains, gutters, scuppers, secondary drainage where applicable, overflow provisions, and methods for directing water away from the building.

Standing water can contribute to roof deterioration and structural loading. Inspectors should understand how proper slope and drainage contribute to long-term roof performance.

Fire Classifications represent 4%. Candidates should review roof-covering fire classification concepts and understand how roof assemblies are classified for fire performance.

Materials also represent 4%. Study approved roofing materials, identification, product standards, compatibility, storage, and code limitations.

Florida inspectors frequently encounter product approval information. Roofing materials and systems should correspond to approved products and installations applicable to the project conditions.

Administration represents 6%. Candidates should understand the inspector's relationship to approved plans, permits, required inspections, manufacturer instructions, product approvals, and code enforcement procedures.

A roofing inspector should compare the installed roof with the approved construction documents and applicable code requirements. Work that differs from approved plans may require evaluation or correction before approval.

The Florida Building Code - Building, 2023 should be used actively during preparation. Practice locating Chapter 15 roofing provisions as well as related structural and Florida-specific requirements.

The Florida Building Code - Residential, 2023 should be used for residential roof assemblies and roof covering provisions within its scope.

Practice distinguishing between commercial and residential roofing requirements. Similar roof systems may be addressed differently depending on the building type, code volume, roof covering, and location.

When a practice question is missed, determine why. The error may involve choosing the wrong code volume, overlooking an HVHZ requirement, missing a slope limitation, misreading an installation requirement, or failing to identify the correct roofing material.

Organize missed questions by category. If Roofing Installations produce repeated errors, focus additional study there. If HVHZ, re-roofing, drainage, or roof coverings are weaker, build separate review sessions around those subjects.

As examination day approaches, move into mixed-topic practice. A roofing inspector exam may switch rapidly between roof covering types, installation requirements, re-roofing, wind provisions, drainage, fire classifications, rooftop structures, and administration.

With 70 questions in 3 hours, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and 34 seconds per question. Efficient code navigation can preserve extra time for more detailed roofing scenarios and Florida-specific provisions.

The included 3 months access gives candidates time to progress through code familiarization, topic-focused study, weak-area review, mixed-question practice, and timed preparation.

Florida defines a Modular Plans Examiner as a person authorized to review plans for manufactured or modular buildings and the systems incorporated into them when the buildings are designed and constructed to comply with the Florida Building Code under Part I of Chapter 553, Florida Statutes.

Applicants must be at least 18 years of age and meet Florida's applicable character and professional qualification requirements.

Florida requires qualifying experience for the Modular Plans Examiner credential. One pathway is three years of plans examiner experience with local or state government.

An alternative pathway allows three years of qualifying plans examination experience with an independent inspection or plans-review agency under contract with a state department.

Florida also recognizes qualifying experience as a registered or certified state general, building, or residential contractor, or as a job superintendent, project manager, or quality-control manager working in an appropriate supervisory capacity involving building, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing personnel or subcontractors on residential or commercial projects.

Modular construction is regulated differently from ordinary site-built construction because significant portions of the building may be completed inside a manufacturing facility before being transported to the final location.

The state modular building program addresses plan review, approved construction documents, inspections, manufacturing controls, certification, and other requirements intended to ensure that factory-built structures comply with the Florida Building Code.

For a plans examiner, this means reviewing more than the building shell. Systems incorporated into modular construction can include electrical, plumbing, mechanical, fuel-gas, accessibility, structural, and life-safety components.

Traps, Interceptors, Separators, Special Piping, and Storage Systems represent 11%. Review trap seals, prohibited traps, grease interceptors, oil separators, indirect waste, special waste systems, and other specialized commercial plumbing installations.

Commercial buildings may include kitchens, laboratories, health care facilities, industrial processes, and other uses that require plumbing systems beyond ordinary domestic fixtures.

Water Heaters represent 10%. Review water-heating equipment, temperature and pressure relief protection, discharge piping, installation location, supports, pans, access, connections, and applicable safety provisions.

Gas-fired water heaters may require coordination between the IPC and IFGC. Candidates should be able to identify when fuel-gas piping, combustion air, or venting provisions must also be reviewed.

Storm Drainage represents 7%. Review roof drains, secondary drainage, leaders, conductors, storm piping, roof areas, sizing, and approved discharge arrangements.

Plans examiner preparation should include storm-drainage calculations and table navigation. A proposed system may require verification of roof area, rainfall conditions, pipe size, number of drains, and secondary drainage provisions.

Health Care Plumbing represents 5%. Candidates should become familiar with specialized plumbing requirements associated with health care facilities and related systems.

Health care facilities can contain plumbing and piping systems that require special materials, arrangements, equipment, or protection. Candidates should recognize when specialized code sections apply.

General Requirements represent 5%. This category can include plan completeness, permits, approved materials, piping protection, structural protection, testing, installation requirements, and general code administration.

A plans examiner should verify that submitted documents contain enough information for a complete review. Missing pipe sizes, unclear fixture counts, incomplete riser diagrams, absent accessibility dimensions, or missing system calculations can prevent a proper determination of compliance.

Plumbing riser diagrams are an important study area. Candidates should practice tracing water supply, sanitary drainage, and vent systems through a building and understanding the relationships among fixtures, branches, stacks, and mains.

For water distribution systems, review how fixture-unit demand, pipe length, available pressure, elevation, and other design conditions affect sizing.

For sanitary drainage, understand how drainage fixture units relate to pipe capacity and how horizontal and vertical piping may be sized differently.

For vent systems, understand how fixture arrangements and drainage connections affect permitted vent methods and sizing.

The 2021 International Plumbing Code should be used actively throughout preparation. Rather than reading the code straight through, work practice questions and locate the specific provisions that control the answer.

The 2021 International Fuel Gas Code should be used for fuel-gas piping, gas-fired appliances, combustion air, and venting questions. Learn to recognize when a plumbing plan-review question crosses into fuel-gas requirements.

The ICC A117.1-2017 standard should be reviewed regularly for accessible fixture and facility requirements. Accessibility questions often depend on exact dimensions, so familiarity with the standard's organization is useful.

Tables deserve substantial practice. The plumbing and fuel-gas codes use tables for pipe sizing, fixture units, drainage capacity, vent sizing, fuel-gas systems, and other technical requirements.

When using a table, always confirm the title, units, conditions, and footnotes. A candidate can locate the correct table and still reach the wrong answer by applying the wrong row or column.

When a practice question is missed, determine why. The error may involve weak code navigation, selecting the wrong reference, misunderstanding system operation, overlooking an exception, or using a table incorrectly.

Organize missed questions by category. If water supply remains difficult, dedicate additional review there. If accessibility, drainage, venting, water heaters, or special piping produce repeated errors, build focused study sessions around those subjects.

As exam day approaches, use mixed-topic practice. A real plans examiner exam can move quickly from fixtures to water distribution, then vents, drainage, accessibility, storm systems, or fuel-gas requirements.

  • Services
  • Branch Circuit and Feeder Requirements

  • Equipment for General Use
  • Special Occupancies

Branch Circuit and Feeder Requirements include conductor sizing, ampacity, calculated loads, overcurrent protection, grounded and grounding conductors, voltage considerations, and required circuit arrangements.

Equipment for General Use can include motors, transformers, panelboards, switchboards, luminaires, appliances, generators, and other equipment commonly shown on commercial electrical plans.

Branch circuits and feeders are another major subject. Candidates should review feeder sizing, branch-circuit conductors, overcurrent protection, continuous loads, multiwire branch circuits, grounded conductors, equipment grounding conductors, and required circuits.

Plans examiners should be comfortable checking whether proposed conductors and overcurrent devices are properly coordinated with the calculated load and connected equipment.

Grounding and bonding should receive dedicated study. Review grounding electrode systems, grounding electrode conductors, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, grounded conductors, separately derived systems, and effective fault-current paths.

Wiring Methods and Distribution Systems can involve raceways, cables, conductors, supports, boxes, pull boxes, junction boxes, conduit fill, conductor fill, temperature limitations, and protection from physical damage.

The Florida Building Plans Examiner ICC 3B examination contains 80 multiple-choice questions. Candidates receive 3 hours and 30 minutes to complete the examination.

  • General Administration: 5%
  • Building Planning: 21%
  • Footings and Foundations: 8%
  • Floor Construction: 4%
  • Wall Construction and Coverings: 12%
  • Roof/Ceiling Construction: 4%
  • Public Safety and Special Construction: 46%

Public Safety and Special Construction is the largest category at 46% of the examination. Candidates should devote significant study time to fire protection, means of egress, accessibility, special construction, occupant safety, fire-resistance-rated assemblies, and other life-safety requirements.

Building Planning is the second-largest category at 21%. This area includes occupancy classification, construction type, allowable height and area, mixed occupancies, fire separation, building configuration, interior environment, and other planning requirements that affect the overall design.

Wall Construction and Coverings represent 12%, while Footings and Foundations account for 8%. General Administration represents 5%, and Floor Construction and Roof/Ceiling Construction each represent 4%.

The distribution of topics reflects the role of a plans examiner. The work is not limited to structural calculations or framing details. A building plans examiner must review both structural and life-safety provisions and understand how multiple code sections work together within a complete design.

Open Book Test

The Florida Building Plans Examiner ICC 3B examination is an open-book test.

For the 2021 examination cycle, the official references include the 2021 International Building Code and either ACI 318-19 or the applicable ICC Concrete Manual for structural concrete topics.

Open-book testing rewards strong reference-navigation skills. Candidates have 80 questions and 3 hours and 30 minutes, so efficient use of the references is important.

A question involving occupancy classification, construction type, fire resistance, accessibility, means of egress, or allowable building area should direct the candidate toward the IBC. A question involving concrete reinforcement, structural concrete design requirements, anchorage, or concrete construction may require ACI 318-19 or the ICC Concrete Manual.

Candidates should practice locating requirements through chapter organization, indexes, tables, definitions, exceptions, and cross-references. Building plans examination frequently requires using several code sections together rather than relying on a single isolated provision.

For example, a proposed commercial building may require review of occupancy classification, construction type, allowable area, sprinkler status, fire separation, egress, accessibility, structural design, and special construction. Plans-examiner preparation should reflect that interconnected process.

  1. Confirm the Florida Building Plans Examiner certification category. Florida regulates plans examiners by discipline, including building, electrical, mechanical, and plumbing categories.

State Requirements

Florida plans examiners are regulated through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board within the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Florida requires certification to perform plan review in applicable categories, including building, electrical, mechanical, and plumbing.

    The primary code reference for preparation involving building administration, occupancy classification, construction types, allowable height and area, fire resistance, means of egress, accessibility, structural systems, foundations, walls, floors, roofs, and special construction.

    Supports practical understanding of concrete quality, structural concrete provisions, reinforcement, construction practices, inspection considerations, and application of concrete requirements associated with the 2021 IBC and ACI 318-19.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Florida Building Plans Examiner study plan should begin with Public Safety and Special Construction, which represents 46% of the examination.

Means of egress should receive substantial attention. Candidates should understand occupant load, exit access, exits, exit discharge, travel distance, common path of egress travel, corridors, doors, stairs, ramps, guards, handrails, and other egress components.

Plans examiners must verify that proposed egress systems are correctly sized and arranged for the occupancy and occupant load. This requires more than locating a single dimensional requirement; multiple sections and tables may need to be applied together.

Accessibility should also receive focused study. Candidates should understand accessible routes, entrances, doors, parking, toilet facilities, changes in level, ramps, and other accessibility scoping provisions relevant to building plan review.

Special construction can include a variety of systems and building features with dedicated code requirements. Candidates should learn how to recognize when a design triggers a special construction chapter or specialized provision.

Building Planning represents 21% of the exam. Begin with occupancy classification because occupancy frequently drives other code decisions.

Footings and Foundations represent 8%. Study soil-related requirements, footing dimensions, foundation walls, reinforcement, anchor bolts, dampproofing, waterproofing, piles, piers, and special foundations.

General Administration represents 6%. Candidates should understand project administration, permits, inspections, approved construction documents, alternative materials and methods, special inspections, certificates of occupancy, and general code-enforcement responsibilities.

For example, a question involving occupancy should direct attention toward classification provisions. A question involving exit width should point toward means of egress. A fire-rated wall question should suggest the fire-resistance chapters, while concrete reinforcement may require the structural concrete reference.

The Residential Plumbing Inspector is responsible for evaluating residential plumbing systems for compliance with applicable adopted codes and standards. Inspection duties can include checking piping systems, approved materials, fixtures, water supply, drainage, vents, water heaters, joints, connections, and related plumbing installations.

The current Residential Plumbing Inspector examination contains 60 multiple-choice questions and allows 2 hours for completion. The exam is an open-book test. For the 2021 code cycle, the required reference is the International Residential Code, 2021.

The major examination categories are General Requirements, Fixtures, Water Heaters, Water Supply and Distribution, Sanitary Drainage, and Vents. Water supply, drainage, and venting make up a large portion of the exam, so candidates should spend substantial study time on those subjects.

The practice questions in this product are built around the 2021 International Residential Code. The goal is to help candidates strengthen code familiarity while also practicing the inspection-focused reasoning needed to recognize compliant and noncompliant residential plumbing installations.

What You Get

  • Code Navigation Practice: Preparation designed to improve familiarity with locating plumbing requirements efficiently.

  • Reference: International Residential Code, 2021.
  • Access Period: 3 months access included.

Exam Details

The ICC Residential Plumbing Inspector examination contains 60 multiple-choice questions. Candidates receive 2 hours to complete the test.

The current examination content areas include:

  • General Requirements: 14%
  • Fixtures: 8%
  • Water Heaters: 11%
  • Water Supply and Distribution: 22%
  • Sanitary Drainage: 23%
  • Vents: 22%

Sanitary Drainage is the largest single category at 23% of the examination. Candidates should be familiar with drainage piping, sizing, slope, cleanouts, building drains, fixture drains, branches, stacks, materials, connections, and installation requirements.

Water Supply and Distribution and Vents each represent 22%. Together with Sanitary Drainage, these three categories account for more than two-thirds of the examination content.

General Requirements account for 14%. This category can include permits, piping protection, approved materials, inspections, testing, structural protection, and general installation requirements.

Water Heaters represent 11%, while Fixtures account for 8%. Candidates should prepare for questions involving water-heater installation, temperature and pressure protection, fixture requirements, connections, clearances, and approved plumbing components.

Open Book Test

The ICC Residential Plumbing Inspector examination is an open-book test.

For the 2021 examination version, the required reference is the International Residential Code, 2021. Candidates may use approved references during the exam in accordance with ICC testing rules.

Open-book testing still requires efficient preparation. With 60 questions and a 2-hour limit, candidates have an average of about 2 minutes per question. Searching randomly through the IRC for every answer can consume valuable time.

A better strategy is to identify the plumbing subject before opening the code. A drainage question should immediately point toward sanitary drainage provisions. A venting question should direct attention to the vent chapters, while a fixture or water-heater question should suggest a different area of the IRC.

Practice should also include using the code's index, tables, definitions, and cross-references. Many inspection questions require candidates to find a specific dimensional requirement, sizing rule, material limitation, or exception.

During preparation, attempt each practice question before looking up the answer. Then use the IRC to confirm the applicable requirement. This strengthens both plumbing knowledge and code-navigation ability.

  1. Confirm the Florida Residential Plumbing Inspector certification category. Florida regulates building code inspectors by inspection discipline and category.
  2. Meet the applicable qualification requirements. Applicants must qualify through an accepted experience, education, certification, or Board-approved training pathway.
  3. Submit the appropriate Florida application. Building code inspector applications are processed through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  4. Receive approval for the required examinations. Candidates must satisfy the state's application requirements before completing the necessary examination process.
  5. Prepare for the ICC Residential Plumbing Inspector examination. Study the 2021 International Residential Code and the official plumbing inspector content areas.
  6. Take the ICC 1P technical examination. The exam contains 60 multiple-choice questions and provides 2 hours.
  7. Complete the Florida Principles and Practice examination. Florida applicants seeking inspector certification by examination must also satisfy the separate state examination requirement.
  8. Complete remaining certification requirements. Florida reviews examination results and all required application, experience, education, training, and certification documentation before issuing a license.

State Requirements

Residential Plumbing Inspectors in Florida are regulated through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board under the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Florida requires building code inspectors to hold certification in the inspection category in which they work. Residential Plumbing Inspector certification applies to residential plumbing inspections within the applicable state and code scope.

Applicants seeking initial certification by examination must meet one of Florida's approved qualification pathways. These may involve construction or inspection experience, post-secondary education combined with experience, existing certifications, or Board-approved training programs.

Florida's experience-based pathways include qualifying construction or inspection work in the category sought. Other routes allow combinations of post-secondary education and experience or additional approved qualifications.

Florida applicants seeking certification by examination must pass an appropriate International Code Council technical examination and the separate Florida Principles and Practice examination.

The ICC Residential Plumbing Inspector exam addressed by this product is the technical examination component. Candidates preparing for Florida licensure should plan separately for the Florida Principles and Practice examination.

Florida currently makes ICC National Certification examinations available to Florida candidates through the PRONTO remote-proctored testing platform. The Florida Principles and Practice examination continues to be available through Florida's separate approved testing process.

Passing the ICC technical examination alone does not automatically issue a Florida Residential Plumbing Inspector certification. Applicants must also satisfy the applicable experience, education or training, application, state examination, and other certification requirements.

Reference Books

  • International Residential Code, 2021
    The required reference for the 2021 Residential Plumbing Inspector examination. It supports preparation involving general plumbing requirements, fixtures, water heaters, water supply and distribution, sanitary drainage, vents, piping materials, testing, and other residential plumbing inspection requirements.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong ICC Residential Plumbing Inspector study plan should begin with the three largest content areas: Sanitary Drainage, Water Supply and Distribution, and Vents.

Sanitary Drainage represents 23% of the examination. Candidates should understand how wastewater moves through residential piping systems and how the IRC regulates sizing, slope, materials, cleanouts, connections, and installation.

Review fixture drains, branch drains, drainage stacks, building drains, building sewers, cleanout locations, drainage fittings, and approved piping materials.

Drainage inspection questions often require candidates to determine whether a piping arrangement, size, slope, or fitting is acceptable. Practice identifying the specific condition in the question before selecting a code section.

Water Supply and Distribution represents 22%. Candidates should review potable water piping, distribution systems, pressure, materials, valves, connections, fixture supply, protection against contamination, and sizing concepts.

Residential plumbing inspectors should understand how water enters a dwelling and is distributed to fixtures and equipment. Questions can involve pipe sizing, pressure, protection, materials, accessibility, and installation conditions.

Backflow protection and cross-connection control are important water-supply concepts. Candidates should understand how potable water systems are protected from contamination and which installations require protective devices or methods.

Vents also represent 22%. Vent systems protect trap seals and support proper drainage-system performance. Candidates should understand vent sizing, vent connections, vent terminations, wet venting, individual vents, common vents, and other permitted arrangements.

Venting questions can be challenging because the answer may depend on both the fixture arrangement and pipe size. Practice visualizing the complete system instead of focusing only on a single pipe.

General Requirements account for 14%. This category includes broader plumbing inspection responsibilities such as permits, testing, approved materials, piping protection, structural protection, and installation requirements.

Piping must be protected from physical damage, corrosion, freezing, stress, and strain. Candidates should understand how plumbing installations interact with building framing and how the code protects both the piping and the structure.

Water Heaters represent 11%. Study water-heater installation, location, temperature and pressure relief protection, discharge piping, connections, clearances, pans, supports, and other applicable residential requirements.

Water-heater questions may require close attention to the installation condition. A requirement can differ depending on location, fuel type, surrounding construction, or equipment configuration.

Fixtures account for 8%. Review fixture materials, required fixtures, clearances, installation, supports, connections, faucets, traps, and fixture-specific requirements.

Inspection-focused preparation should include recognizing whether fixtures are properly installed, accessible, supported, connected, and supplied with appropriate drainage and water connections.

The 2021 International Residential Code should be used actively throughout preparation. Practice locating plumbing requirements by topic rather than trying to memorize the entire code.

One effective method is to read a practice question and identify the main keyword. Terms such as cleanout, trap, vent, fixture, water heater, supply piping, or drainage stack can help point toward the correct chapter or section.

Tables deserve special attention. Plumbing codes frequently use tables for pipe sizing, fixture-unit relationships, developed lengths, spacing, and other requirements. Practice reading both table headings and footnotes carefully.

Definitions can also affect the correct answer. Plumbing terminology is precise, and two similar words may refer to different parts of a system. When a question seems ambiguous, checking the code definition can help clarify the intended meaning.

When a practice question is missed, determine why. The issue may be weak code navigation, misunderstanding of system operation, overlooking a table note, confusing drainage with vent requirements, or missing an exception.

Organize missed questions by category. If sanitary drainage remains difficult, focus additional study there. If venting or water distribution produces repeated errors, dedicate separate review sessions to those topics.

As preparation progresses, combine categories into mixed-question sets. A realistic exam may switch from a water-heater question to drainage, then fixtures, vents, water supply, or general requirements.

Because the exam contains 60 questions in 2 hours, time management matters. Candidates should answer familiar questions efficiently and preserve extra time for complicated code lookups or table interpretation.

The ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector examination evaluates knowledge of residential construction and inspection requirements contained in the International Residential Code. The exam covers code administration, building planning, footings and foundations, floor construction, wall construction and coverings, roof and ceiling construction, penetrations, and public safety.

For Florida candidates seeking certification as a residential building inspector, the ICC technical examination is part of a broader state licensing process administered through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board. Florida applicants seeking licensure by examination must complete the applicable technical examination as well as the Florida Principles and Practice examination.

The ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector exam contains 60 multiple-choice questions and allows 2 hours for completion. It is an open-book examination. The 2021 examination version uses the 2021 International Residential Code as its primary reference.

Practice questions can help candidates become more comfortable locating residential code provisions related to foundations, framing, walls, roofs, structural connections, safety, stairs, guards, openings, and other inspection topics.

Successful open-book preparation is not simply a matter of owning the code book. Candidates should learn how the IRC is organized, recognize which chapter or section is likely to contain the answer, and practice distinguishing between similar requirements. The goal is to develop enough code familiarity that reference searches become targeted rather than random.

What You Get

  • Online Practice Questions: Practice-oriented preparation for the Florida Residential Building Inspector ICC 1B technical examination.
  • 2021 IRC Review: Questions designed around residential building inspection subjects covered by the 2021 International Residential Code.
  • Code Navigation Practice: Preparation designed to improve familiarity with locating residential code provisions efficiently.
  • Inspection-Focused Review: Practice involving foundations, floors, walls, roofs, building planning, code administration, and public safety.
  • Reference: International Residential Code, 2021.
  • Access Period: 3 months access included.

Exam Details

The ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector examination based on the 2021 International Codes contains 60 multiple-choice questions. Candidates receive 2 hours to complete the examination.

The official 2021 examination content outline is divided among the following major categories:

  • Code Administration: 4% of the examination
  • Building Planning: 8%
  • Footings and Foundations: 16%
  • Floor Construction: 14%
  • Wall Construction and Coverings: 27%
  • Roof/Ceiling Construction and Penetrations: 14%
  • Public Safety: 17%

Wall Construction and Coverings is the largest category at 27% of the examination. Candidates should therefore devote substantial preparation to wall framing, bracing, structural connections, headers, openings, exterior coverings, interior finishes, and related inspection requirements.

Public Safety accounts for 17%. Public-safety preparation can involve stairs, guards, handrails, emergency escape and rescue openings, glazing, smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms, fire-resistance-related provisions, and other requirements intended to protect occupants.

Footings and Foundations account for 16%, making foundation inspection another major study area. Candidates should understand footing dimensions and placement, foundation wall requirements, anchorage, reinforcement, concrete and masonry concepts, crawl spaces, drainage, dampproofing, and related residential construction requirements.

Floor Construction and Roof/Ceiling Construction and Penetrations each represent 14% of the exam. These categories require familiarity with framing members, spans, bearing, connections, openings, sheathing, roof framing, ceiling construction, and penetrations through assemblies.

Building Planning and Code Administration make up smaller percentages but remain important because each question contributes to the candidate's overall examination result.

Open Book Test

The ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector examination is an open-book test.

For the 2021 examination version, the primary examination reference is the 2021 International Residential Code. Candidates should prepare with the same code edition associated with the exam version they register to take.

Open-book testing rewards familiarity with the organization of the IRC. Candidates should know where major subjects are located and how to move from a question to the appropriate code chapter efficiently.

For example, a question involving footing dimensions should immediately suggest the foundation provisions. A question involving wall framing, bracing, or coverings should lead toward the wall-construction sections. Questions involving stairs, guards, emergency escape openings, or safety glazing should direct the candidate toward building-planning and safety provisions.

Do not plan to read entire chapters during the examination. Practice identifying key terms in each question and using those terms to narrow the code search. The faster the candidate can identify the correct code subject, the more time remains for interpreting the actual requirement.

During preparation, pay attention to tables, exceptions, figures, definitions, and cross-references. ICC questions may require more than finding a familiar phrase; candidates may need to apply a table or determine whether a specific exception changes the general rule.

Licensing Steps

  1. Confirm the Florida residential inspector certification pathway. Florida building inspectors are regulated through the Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board under the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.
  2. Meet the applicable education and experience requirements. Florida applicants must qualify under one of the experience, education, certification, or approved training pathways applicable to the residential inspector category.
  3. Submit the appropriate Florida application. Applicants seeking initial certification must complete the applicable Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board application process.
  4. Receive authorization for required examinations. Florida candidates must be approved for the examinations required for their certification pathway.
  5. Prepare for the ICC technical examination. For the 2021 ICC 1B exam, study the International Residential Code, 2021 and the official residential building inspector content areas.
  6. Take the ICC Residential Building Inspector technical exam. The 2021 1B examination contains 60 multiple-choice questions and allows 2 hours.
  7. Complete the Florida Principles and Practice examination. Florida applicants seeking a new inspector license by examination must also satisfy the state's Principles and Practice examination requirement.
  8. Submit or complete remaining licensing documentation. Florida reviews the candidate's examination results and other required qualifications before issuing a standard inspector certification.

State Requirements

Florida building code inspectors are regulated by the Florida Building Code Administrators and Inspectors Board through the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

A building inspector performs inspections of construction for compliance with applicable building codes. Florida requires inspectors performing regulated building-code inspection work to hold the appropriate state certification.

For initial certification by examination as an inspector or plans examiner, Florida generally requires qualifying construction or inspection experience in the category sought, or an accepted combination of post-secondary education and experience. Residential inspector applicants may also qualify through specific Board-approved training pathways when applicable.

Florida's application materials identify experience pathways that can include a minimum of four years of construction and/or inspection experience in the category sought, or an accepted combination of post-secondary education and experience totaling three years. Other qualification routes exist for applicants with existing certifications or Board-approved training.

Florida requires applicants seeking licensure by examination to pass an appropriate technical examination administered by the International Code Council as well as the Florida Principles and Practice examination.

The ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector examination is the technical examination addressed by this online practice-question product. The practice questions are not a substitute for preparation for the separate Florida Principles and Practice examination.

Florida currently makes ICC National Certification examinations available to Florida candidates through ICC's remote-proctored PRONTO testing platform. The Florida Principles and Practice examination is administered separately through the state's approved testing process.

Applicants should also distinguish a Florida building code inspector certification from a Florida home inspector license. These are different professional categories with different scopes and licensing requirements.

Reference Books

  • International Residential Code, 2021
    The primary reference for the 2021 ICC 1B Residential Building Inspector examination. It covers residential building planning, foundations, floors, wall construction, roof and ceiling construction, safety provisions, structural requirements, and other code requirements applicable to one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses within the IRC scope.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong ICC 1B study plan should begin with the examination content outline rather than reading the IRC from front to back without priorities. The outline shows where the largest share of questions is concentrated and can help candidates organize their study time accordingly.

Wall Construction and Coverings deserves substantial attention because it represents 27% of the examination. Review wood framing, studs, plates, headers, wall bracing, sheathing, fasteners, openings, veneer and exterior covering requirements, and structural connections.

Practice identifying how wall loads transfer downward through framing and into foundations. Residential inspection questions often require an understanding of how components connect, bear, and transfer loads rather than simple recognition of individual pieces.

Footings and Foundations account for 16%. Review footing placement, minimum dimensions, foundation walls, concrete and masonry construction, anchorage, crawl-space conditions, drainage, dampproofing, and protection against moisture.

Foundation questions may require candidates to use tables. Practice locating and interpreting tabular information rather than relying on memory alone.

Floor Construction represents 14%. Candidates should understand joists, beams, girders, bearing, spans, fastening, notching and boring restrictions, floor sheathing, and connections.

Learn to distinguish between requirements that apply to different framing materials. Dimensional lumber, engineered wood products, and other structural components may have different limitations and installation requirements.

Roof and Ceiling Construction also represents 14%. Study rafters, ceiling joists, ridge boards, ties, trusses, bearing, connections, openings, roof sheathing, and penetrations.

Roof questions can require candidates to interpret slope, spans, framing configuration, or structural relationships. Practice visualizing how roof loads transfer through walls and foundations.

Public Safety accounts for 17%. Review stairs, risers, treads, landings, handrails, guards, emergency escape and rescue openings, glazing, smoke alarms, carbon monoxide alarms, and related life-safety requirements.

Dimensions matter in public-safety questions. Candidates should become comfortable locating exact code requirements for heights, widths, openings, clearances, and other dimensional limits rather than relying on approximate memory.

Building Planning accounts for 8%. This category can include room dimensions, ceiling heights, light and ventilation, fire separation, dwelling separation, glazing, means of egress, and other planning requirements.

Code Administration accounts for 4%. Although smaller, candidates should understand the scope and administration of the IRC, permits, inspections, construction documents, approvals, and the authority and responsibilities associated with code enforcement.

A useful open-book strategy is to practice recognizing keywords. If a question uses terms such as guard, handrail, footing, anchor bolt, rafter, header, emergency escape, or wall bracing, those words can serve as navigation clues.

During practice, avoid immediately looking up every answer. First determine what you believe the answer should be and identify the code subject. Then use the IRC to confirm the requirement. This approach develops both technical knowledge and reference-navigation ability.

When a question is missed, identify the reason. The issue may be lack of code knowledge, choosing the wrong chapter, overlooking an exception, misreading a table, or failing to notice a condition in the question.

Create a study list of recurring weak areas. If wall bracing produces repeated mistakes, return to that subject. If stairs, foundations, or roof framing are more difficult, dedicate additional practice to those sections.

Timed practice can also help. The official exam provides 2 hours for 60 questions, which averages about 2 minutes per question. Some questions may be answered quickly, allowing additional time for complex table lookups or code interpretation.

Trade-focused preparation also helps candidates see residential buildings as complete systems. Footings support foundations, foundations support floors and walls, walls support roof systems, and every part of the structure must also satisfy safety and code requirements.

Only authorized references may be used during the examination. Candidates should prepare the exact books and editions included on the Florida Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board examination reference list for the test date and license category.

For the current testing cycle, the approved reference list includes NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition. Beginning August 21, 2027, Florida will transition the electrical examination reference to NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition.

This package includes the 2026 NEC and is particularly suited to candidates preparing in advance for that transition. Students testing before the transition date should also prepare using the 2023 NEC required for the current exam.

The approved electrical reference list contains additional materials covering subjects such as occupational safety, Florida contractor requirements, fire and life safety, and other technical areas. The precise authorized books depend on the examination category.

Florida permits only approved references in the examination environment. Candidates should not assume that the Master Electrician Study Guide, Calculations Study Guide, flash cards, simulated practice exams, or course materials can be taken into the official examination simply because the exam is open book.

The NEC tabs included with this package are designed to help candidates practice efficient code navigation. Students should repeatedly locate services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, conductor tables, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, motors, transformers, equipment, special occupancies, definitions, and calculation-related sections.

Open-book testing still requires strong preparation. A five-hour Technical/Safety examination with 100 scored questions demands efficient use of time. Candidates need to recognize the subject first and then move directly toward the most likely code article, table, or approved reference.

Students should become comfortable using the NEC table of contents, index, Article 100 definitions, article numbering, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references. Repeated navigation practice can reduce the amount of time spent searching during the examination.

Licensing Steps

Begin by deciding whether the Florida Certified Electrical Contractor license is the appropriate credential for your professional goals. A certified contractor may perform authorized electrical contracting throughout Florida, while a registered contractor is limited to the jurisdictions associated with the registered local competency credential.

An applicant for the Florida certification examination must be at least 18 years old. Florida allows a person to take the certification examination before completing the full experience review required for initial licensure.

Apply to take the Certified Electrical Contractor examination through the Department of Business and Professional Regulation using the applicable Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board examination application.

Schedule and complete both examination sections. The Florida Certified Electrical Contractor examination includes the Business section and the Technical/Safety section, both administered through computer-based testing.

Prepare for the Technical/Safety section with the applicable NEC edition and every other authorized technical reference. Candidates taking the examination beginning August 21, 2027 should prepare with the 2026 NEC.

Use the Master Electrician Study Guide for advanced trade review and complete the Calculations Study Guide regularly. Electrical calculation practice should include services, feeders, loads, conductors, motors, transformers, voltage drop, raceway fill, box fill, and three-phase systems.

Use flash cards for active recall between longer study sessions. Attend live instructor-led NEC sessions and use the recorded videos to revisit calculations, theory, code navigation, and other challenging subjects.

Complete simulated practice examinations under realistic timing. Practice sustaining concentration for a five-hour technical examination while balancing direct trade knowledge with efficient reference research.

After passing both parts of the state examination, apply for initial Certified Electrical Contractor licensure. Examination scores used for the initial licensing application generally must not be more than three years old at the time the license application is filed.

Applicants must then demonstrate that they satisfy one of Florida’s statutory education and experience pathways. Florida provides several combinations of management experience, supervisory experience, electrical training, technical education, and professional engineering experience.

The experience submitted for a Certified Electrical Contractor license must include at least 40 percent work involving three-phase services. Applicants should maintain detailed records that clearly establish the nature, level, and duration of qualifying electrical work.

Complete all remaining licensing requirements, including the documentation and financial or credit information required by the initial-license application, before operating as a Certified Electrical Contractor.

State Requirements

Florida regulates certified and registered electrical contractors through the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board and the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Florida does not issue a statewide credential formally titled Master Electrician. The Certified Electrical Contractor license is the principal statewide credential for broad electrical contracting authority and is the closest statewide licensing category to the master-level electrical contractor role.

A certified contractor may perform authorized work throughout Florida. A registered electrical contractor operates under a local competency credential registered with the state and is limited to the applicable counties or municipalities.

Florida law provides several experience pathways for certified electrical contractor applicants. One pathway requires at least three years of proven management experience in the trade, or education considered equivalent to part of that experience, within the six years immediately before application.

Another pathway requires at least four years of experience as a supervisor or contractor in the electrical trade within the eight years immediately before application. Florida also recognizes qualifying supervisory experience obtained in electrical work with the United States Armed Forces.

A separate pathway allows at least six years of comprehensive training, technical education, or supervisory experience associated with an electrical contracting business within the preceding 12 years. Qualifying electrical experience with the military or a governmental entity may also apply under the statutory standards.

A professional engineer who has been licensed for at least three years during the applicable 12-year period and is qualified through education, training, or experience to practice electrical engineering may also qualify under the statutory pathway.

Florida allows combinations of several of the approved experience, training, education, and supervisory qualifications when they satisfy the applicable licensing requirements.

For Certified Electrical Contractor applicants, at least 40 percent of the required experience must involve three-phase services. This is a specific experience component and should be clearly supported in the applicant’s documentation.

The Florida electrical examination currently uses the 2023 NEC. Effective August 21, 2027, the examination reference list will transition to the 2026 NEC. This package is designed specifically around that upcoming 2026 code cycle.

Reference Books

  • NFPA 70 National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition
    The primary electrical code book included with this package and the NEC edition Florida is scheduled to begin using for electrical contractor examinations on August 21, 2027. It covers services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, conductors, wiring methods, motors, equipment, special occupancies, special conditions, and other electrical installations.
  • Master Electrician Study Guide
    An advanced electrical preparation resource included for review of electrical theory, NEC concepts, installations, calculations, troubleshooting, and master-level trade knowledge.
  • Calculations Study Guide
    A focused preparation resource covering electrical mathematics, service and feeder calculations, conductor sizing, motors, transformers, voltage drop, raceway fill, box fill, three-phase systems, and systematic problem solving.

Test Information and Study Materials

An effective Florida master-level electrical study plan should combine NEC navigation, electrical theory, calculations, safety, business knowledge, active recall, instructor guidance, and timed simulated testing.

Begin with the NEC overview. Learn how the 2026 National Electrical Code is organized and practice moving from a technical question to the applicable chapter, article, definition, table, exception, or cross-reference.

Divide technical preparation into services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, motors, transformers, equipment, special occupancies, special conditions, electrical safety, and calculations.

Use the Calculations Study Guide consistently. Practice identifying known values, selecting formulas, locating applicable code requirements, performing each mathematical step, and checking the result.

Because Florida specifically requires Certified Electrical Contractor experience involving three-phase services, candidates should also be comfortable with three-phase electrical theory and calculations.

Use flash cards for frequent active-recall practice involving formulas, definitions, electrical terminology, conductor concepts, motors, transformers, grounding, and other technical information.

Live instructor-led NEC training provides structured guidance through advanced code topics and electrical calculations. Recorded videos allow candidates to pause explanations, replay examples, and revisit difficult subjects.

Complete simulated practice examinations under realistic conditions. After every practice exam, review missed questions and questions that took too long. Identify whether the weakness involved calculations, electrical theory, code navigation, safety, terminology, or trade knowledge.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep supports Florida master-level electrical candidates through an organized combination of printed study resources, instructor-led NEC education, electrical calculation practice, reference-navigation training, flash cards, and simulated practice examinations.

The NEC overview helps students understand how the National Electrical Code is structured before they begin working through difficult technical questions. This foundation helps candidates connect electrical subjects with articles, tables, definitions, exceptions, and cross-references.

The included 2026 NEC and tabs provide a current-code preparation platform for electricians planning ahead for Florida’s August 21, 2027 examination transition. Regular navigation practice helps candidates become more efficient at locating technical information.

The Calculations Study Guide helps candidates develop repeatable problem-solving methods for loads, services, feeders, conductors, motors, transformers, voltage drop, raceway fill, box fill, and other mathematical applications.

The Master Electrician Study Guide provides advanced trade-focused review, while flash cards reinforce formulas, terminology, definitions, and electrical concepts through active recall.

Live instructor-led sessions provide structured guidance, while recorded videos give working electrical professionals flexibility to revisit challenging topics. Simulated practice examinations combine theory, calculations, reference navigation, pacing, and test strategy.

No exam-preparation package can guarantee a passing examination score or license approval. Results depend on the applicant’s qualifying experience, preparation, examination performance, and completion of Florida licensing requirements. This package provides an organized preparation system for electricians pursuing advanced Florida electrical contractor responsibilities and preparing for the 2026 NEC examination cycle.

FAQ Section

The package includes NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition, NEC tabs, flash cards, a Master Electrician Study Guide, a Calculations Study Guide, an online instructor-led NEC course, simulated practice exams, an NEC overview, and live and recorded videos.

Does Florida issue a statewide Master Electrician license?

Florida does not issue a statewide license formally titled Master Electrician. The primary statewide electrical contracting credential is the Certified Electrical Contractor license administered through the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.

Is the Florida electrical contractor examination open book?

Yes. Florida’s Electrical Contractors’ Licensure Examination allows approved references during testing. Candidates should bring only the authorized references listed for their examination category.

How many parts are on the Certified Electrical Contractor exam?

The examination has two parts: a Business section and a Technical/Safety section.

How many questions are on the Florida electrical contractor exam?

The Business section contains 50 scored questions and allows two and one-half hours. The Technical/Safety section contains 100 scored questions and allows five hours.

When will Florida begin using the 2026 NEC for electrical contractor exams?

Florida is scheduled to begin using NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2026 Edition, for its Electrical Contractors’ Licensure Examination on August 21, 2027.

Which NEC is used before August 21, 2027?

The current Florida electrical contractor examination uses NFPA 70, National Electrical Code, 2023 Edition.

What experience is required for a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor license?

Florida provides several qualifying pathways based on management experience, supervisory electrical experience, training, technical education, professional engineering experience, or qualifying combinations of those credentials.

Is three-phase experience required?

Yes. For the Certified Electrical Contractor category, at least 40 percent of the qualifying experience must involve work with three-phase services.

Can a Florida Certified Electrical Contractor work statewide?

Yes. A Certified Electrical Contractor may perform authorized electrical contracting throughout Florida. Registered Electrical Contractors are limited to the jurisdictions associated with their registered local credentials.

Are simulated practice exams included?

Yes. The online course includes simulated practice exams designed to strengthen electrical knowledge, calculations, NEC navigation, pacing, and testing discipline.

Are live and recorded NEC lessons included?

Yes. The package includes live instructor-led NEC training and recorded videos that can be replayed while reviewing electrical theory, calculations, code concepts, and advanced trade subjects.

Florida Residential Electrical Inspector ICC 1E Exam Details

The ICC 1E Residential Electrical Inspector examination is administered by the International Code Council (ICC). Florida recognizes this national certification examination as a technical examination within its building code inspector certification process.

The examination evaluates the ability to interpret and apply residential electrical code requirements involving services, conductors, circuits, wiring methods, electrical equipment, and specialized installations.

Examination Overview:

  • Exam Name: Residential Electrical Inspector.
  • Exam ID: 1E.
  • Testing Organization: International Code Council (ICC).
  • Number of Questions: 60 multiple-choice questions.
  • Time Allowed: 2 hours (120 minutes).
  • Examination Type: Open Book.
  • Code References: 2021 International Residential Code and 2020 National Electrical Code.
  • Additional Reference: Ugly's Electrical References, any edition.
  • Florida Testing Platform: ICC PRONTO remote-proctored examination system.

The examination measures practical knowledge of residential electrical installations and the ability to identify code requirements applicable to inspection situations.

Open Book Test

The Florida Residential Electrical Inspector ICC 1E examination is an open book test. Candidates may consult permitted examination references according to ICC testing policies.

Open-book testing requires more than knowing where information appears in a codebook. Candidates must understand electrical terminology, identify relevant installation conditions, and interpret code requirements correctly.

  • Using the National Electrical Code index and article structure efficiently.

Applicants must be at least 18 years of age and demonstrate good moral character. Applicants must also satisfy an applicable education and experience qualification pathway.

Qualifying professional experience may involve construction-related work, hands-on technical activities, or other experience recognized under Florida's certification requirements. The specific eligibility pathway determines the documentation needed.

Florida's requirements for Residential Inspector certification recognize applicable construction-related experience without requiring supervisory experience involving operational control and direction under the affected experience pathway.

Applicants seeking certification by examination must complete the required technical examination and the Florida Principles and Practice examination. Individuals who already hold an active qualifying Florida inspector certification may be exempt from repeating the Principles and Practice examination when adding another category.

Passing the ICC 1E examination demonstrates technical examination competency but does not independently grant Florida inspector certification. The state certification process includes separate eligibility, documentation, and application requirements.

Exam Details

The Florida Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board examination is administered in two parts: a Business examination and an Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination. Both portions are computer-based examinations scheduled through the state’s authorized testing provider after the candidate receives approval from the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

The Business examination contains 50 scored questions and allows two and one-half hours. The Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination contains 100 scored questions and allows five hours. Additional pilot questions may appear and do not count toward the candidate’s final score.

A minimum score of 75 percent is required on both the Business and Technical/Safety examinations.

The Business examination includes the following published subject ranges:

  • Maintaining Cash Flow: 3 to 5 questions
  • Estimating and Bidding a Job: 5 to 7 questions
  • Interpretation of Contracts and Agreements: 4 to 6 questions
  • Purchasing Control: 0 to 2 questions
  • Contract Scheduling: 3 to 5 questions
  • Obtaining Insurance and Bonding: 4 to 6 questions
  • Complying with Contracting Laws and Rules: 5 to 7 questions
  • Personnel Management: 3 to 5 questions
  • Payroll and Sales Tax Laws: 6 to 8 questions
  • Financial Statements and Reports: 4 to 6 questions
  • Management Accounting: 2 to 4 questions

The Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination includes the following published subject ranges:

  • General Theory and Electrical Principles: 19 to 21 questions
  • Plan and Specification Reading and Interpretation: 7 to 9 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 13 to 15 questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 11 to 13 questions
  • Special Occupancies and Situations: 13 to 15 questions
  • OSHA, Safety, Testing Procedures, Tools, and Equipment: 8 to 10 questions
  • Life Safety and Americans with Disabilities Act: 4 to 6 questions
  • Electrical Signs, Outline Lighting, and Structural Considerations: 2 to 4 questions
  • Alarms and Limited Energy: 14 to 16 questions

General theory is the largest individual category. Candidates should be prepared to work with voltage, current, resistance, power, alternating current, series and parallel circuits, transformers, motors, generators, power factor, conductor relationships, and electrical calculations.

Wiring and protection topics may include services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, equipment ratings, short-circuit considerations, and disconnecting means. Wiring-method questions may involve raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, conductor fill, support, physical protection, and environmental conditions.

Special occupancies and situations require familiarity with NEC requirements that modify or supplement general installation rules. Preparation may include hazardous locations, healthcare facilities, assembly occupancies, agricultural buildings, marinas, emergency systems, generators, fire pumps, renewable-energy systems, and other specialized electrical installations.

Open Book Test

Both portions of the Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination are open-book tests. Candidates may bring the approved references assigned to the Business and Technical/Safety sections when the materials comply with the official examination rules.

Only authorized references may be taken into the testing room. Original editions are required unless an official reference is specifically permitted as a printed PDF. Approved PDF materials must be printed and securely bound in an acceptable spiral notebook or qualifying multi-ring binder.

Permanently attached tabs may be used to organize reference books. Removable tabs, pull-off labels, sticky notes, loose papers, class notes, separate formulas, sample questions, and independent study materials are not allowed.

The 2023 National Electrical Code is currently assigned to the Unlimited Electrical Contractor Technical/Safety examination. The official reference schedule identifies a transition to the 2026 NEC beginning August 21, 2027.

Licensing Steps

  1. Review the Unlimited Electrical Contractor classification. Confirm that the license matches the broad electrical contracting work you intend to perform.
  2. Meet the minimum age requirement. Applicants for the state examination must be at least 18 years old.
  3. Submit the examination application. Apply through the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation for approval to take the Certified Electrical Contractor examination.
  4. Receive authorization to test. The department reviews the application and forwards approved candidate information to the examination provider.
  5. Schedule both examination portions. Register for the Business examination and the Unlimited Electrical Technical/Safety examination.
