  8. Apply for initial certification. Submit the Certified Electrical Contractor application after completing the examination requirement.
  9. Document qualifying experience. Provide the education and work-experience records required by the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board.
  10. Submit the remaining documents. Complete the financial, credit, business, insurance, background, and supporting-document requirements.
  11. Complete the Florida Building Code course requirement. Electrical contractors must complete the required Florida Building Code education associated with initial certification.

State Requirements

The Florida Unlimited Electrical Contractor certification is regulated by the Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board within the Department of Business and Professional Regulation.

Florida law defines an electrical contractor as a person who conducts business in the electrical trade and has the experience, knowledge, and skill to install, repair, alter, add to, or design electrical wiring, fixtures, appliances, apparatus, raceways, conduit, and related systems that generate, transmit, transform, or use electrical energy.

The scope applies to private and public property and includes excavation, paving, and other work incidental to electrical contracting. It also includes work performed by Florida specialty electrical contractors. Work belonging to another separately licensed trade must be subcontracted unless the electrical contractor also holds the required credential for that trade.

Applicants must pass the state examination before applying for initial certification. Passing both examination sections does not automatically issue the license. The Board reviews the complete experience, education, financial, business, insurance, background, and application documentation.

Experience records should identify employers, supervisors, project dates, project types, electrical systems, service sizes, installation responsibilities, code duties, supervision, estimating, project management, and the applicant’s level of responsibility.

After certification, contractors must comply with Florida contracting laws, Electrical Contractors’ Licensing Board rules, business-qualification requirements, insurance obligations, continuing education, renewal requirements, and applicable electrical and building codes.

Electrical plans examiners may work for municipal or county building departments or through authorized arrangements serving governmental code-enforcement functions. The Florida journeyman electrician study path should begin with NEC navigation. Many exam questions depend on finding the correct article quickly and reading the exact language carefully. General electrical theory is another important study area. Candidates should review voltage, current, resistance, power, series and parallel circuits, electrical units, basic formulas, and practical field applications. These concepts support many code and calculation questions, especially when a problem requires understanding what the numbers represent rather than simply memorizing a rule.

Services, feeders, and branch circuits should receive steady review. Students should practice service load concepts, feeder rules, branch-circuit requirements, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, required outlets, grounding and bonding, and equipment grounding conductor requirements. These subjects often require candidates to connect several parts of the NEC to reach the correct answer.

Wiring methods and materials are common journeyman-level topics. Candidates should review raceways, cables, boxes, cabinets, panelboards, fittings, supports, conductor fill, box fill, burial requirements, working clearances, and installation limitations. These questions often test the candidate’s ability to identify proper installation methods and apply NEC tables correctly.

Motors, transformers, equipment, lighting, signs, and special occupancies should also be included in the study plan. Motor questions may involve disconnects, controllers, overload protection, short-circuit and ground-fault protection, conductors, and branch-circuit rules. Special occupancies and special equipment can include requirements that differ from ordinary wiring installations, making NEC navigation practice especially important.

A strong study routine should combine reading, code lookup, calculation review, and practice with exam-style questions. Students should avoid waiting until the final days before the exam to open the NEC.
